title: Default JavaScriptEncoder escapes every non-ASCII byte in wire envelopes as \u00XX, making operator-facing strings unreadable
userImpact: When the LLM (Claude/Cursor/Windsurf) receives a tool response, every non-ASCII character is double-escaped: a client name 'José García' renders as 'José García', a detail-row description 'W-2 — Box 1 wages' becomes 'W-2 — Box 1 wages', and the SDK's localized German error 'Datenbank nicht zugänglich' becomes 'Datenbank nicht zugänglich'. The LLM has to mentally decode these escapes (it can, but burns tokens and frequently quotes the escaped form back to the operator). Worst case is Cyrillic/CJK client names that become unreadable strings of \u04XX escapes, defeating the entire purpose of returning the name to the model.
description: WrapToolHandler.cs line 69 constructs `new JsonSerializerOptions { WriteIndented = false }` with no Encoder override. System.Text.Json's default is `JavaScriptEncoder.Default`, which is the most conservative encoder — it escapes everything outside ASCII and HTML-sensitive chars (`<`, `>`, `&`, `'`, `+`). Every Serialize call at lines 102 and 157 therefore produces output like '{"userMessage":"Field §24 required"}' instead of '{"userMessage":"Field §24 required"}'. The redaction layer (WireLog.Redact) doesn't touch this — it operates on key names, not value encoding. The MCP spec sends responses as JSON over stdio, so the LLM sees the escaped form verbatim. WireLog.cs:127 has the same defaulting (disk log uses default encoder too, harder to grep). FieldAccessMapLoader.cs:80 builds its OWN options object via BuildJsonOptions() and may set the right encoder there — worth checking. The fix is one line: `Encoder = JavaScriptEncoder.UnsafeRelaxedJsonEscaping` (or the `Create(UnicodeRanges.All)` variant if you want to keep HTML escaping but allow Unicode passthrough — the safer choice given user-supplied data flows through the envelope).
recommendation: Change WrapToolHandler.cs:69-72 to `new JsonSerializerOptions { WriteIndented = false, Encoder = JavaScriptEncoder.Create(UnicodeRanges.All) }` (the bracket-balanced choice — passes through Unicode but still escapes HTML-sensitive chars, which matters because some MCP clients embed responses in HTML chrome). Add `using System.Text.Encodings.Web; using System.Text.Unicode;`. Mirror the change in WireLog.cs:127 so the disk log is also human-readable when an operator opens it. Add one assertion in WrapToolHandlerTests (or McpDiscoveryRoundtripTests for an end-to-end pin): set up an error envelope that contains '§' in the userMessage and assert the returned JSON contains the literal '§' byte sequence and does NOT contain '§'. Skip changing UnsafeRelaxedJsonEscaping over the safer ranges variant — there's no consumer that needs the relaxed mode and the safer one matches what MCP spec implementations use.
rationale: Prior audits focused on what WireLog.Redact strips (which keys) but never on how Serialize escapes value bytes. The two issues are orthogonal — one redacts, the other mangles every surviving non-ASCII byte. The default encoder is a notorious .NET footgun specifically for systems that round-trip user data.

verdict.reasoning:
Verified at src/LacertMCP.Server/Errors/WrapToolHandler.cs:69-72 — `new JsonSerializerOptions { WriteIndented = false }` with no `Encoder` set. .NET's `JavaScriptEncoder.Default` escapes every non-ASCII codepoint as `\uXXXX` plus HTML-sensitive chars. Both Serialize calls at lines 102 and 157 use this options bag. WireLog.cs:127 has the identical defect (the disk log).

Grep for `Encoder|JavaScriptEncoder|UnsafeRelaxed|UnicodeRanges` returns ZERO matches across src/ — nothing in the codebase has set an Encoder. FieldAccessMapLoader's BuildJsonOptions (line 80) only sets PropertyNameCaseInsensitive / AllowTrailingCommas / ReadCommentHandling — also defaults to JavaScriptEncoder.Default but it's only used for Deserialize, so irrelevant.

Grepped audit-findings.json + audit-findings-r2.json for encoder/JavaScriptEncoder/escape/unicode/non-ascii/wire-envelope/readable — no prior finding addresses this. The closest neighbor (r2-doctor-Unicode-glyphs) is about console codepage rendering for `chcp 65001`, completely orthogonal to JSON string encoding. The redaction work in P15-001/P14-018/019 covers key filtering, never value-byte encoding.

Real-world impact assessment:
1. MCP transport is JSON-RPC over stdio. The string returned from WrapToolHandler.Run becomes the `content[0].text` field — the LLM sees `Jos\u00E9 Garc\u00EDa` rather than `José García`.
2. U.S. tax-pro market has heavy Latino client demographics — accented names are everyday inputs.
3. DetailRow.Description text routinely contains em-dashes (`Form 2106 — Employee Business Expenses`) and section signs (`§24`) — these escape too.
4. Token cost is real: `\u00E9` is typically 5 tokens vs 1 for `é` in Claude/GPT tokenizers — meaningful for large detail-row reads.
5. Operator opening disk log to debug sees `\u00E9` instead of `é`, degrading the troubleshooting story.

Fix is genuinely one line per call site plus a using statement. `UnicodeRanges.All` (keep HTML escaping, allow Unicode passthrough) is the correct conservative choice — UnsafeRelaxedJsonEscaping would also escape less, but the safer-ranges variant is bracket-balanced with the audit's framing and matches what MCP-spec implementations typically use.

Minor caveat to the finding: it lists FieldAccessMapLoader.cs:80 as worth checking but that path only Deserializes, so it doesn't need the encoder. Otherwise the analysis is sound.
verdict.refinedRecommendation:
Fix in two sites with a shared helper to avoid drift:

1) src/LacertMCP.Server/Errors/WrapToolHandler.cs:69-72 — change to:
```
private static readonly JsonSerializerOptions JsonOptions = new JsonSerializerOptions
{
    WriteIndented = false,
    Encoder = JavaScriptEncoder.Create(UnicodeRanges.All),
};
```
Add `using System.Text.Encodings.Web; using System.Text.Unicode;`.

2) src/LacertMCP.Server/Logging/WireLog.cs:127 — mirror the same Encoder so disk logs are operator-readable when opened in a text editor.

3) Choose UnicodeRanges.All over UnsafeRelaxedJsonEscaping — keep HTML-sensitive char escaping (`<`, `>`, `&`, `'`, `+`) for defense-in-depth in case a future MCP client embeds responses in HTML chrome. There's no consumer that needs the relaxed mode.

4) Add ONE assertion (suggest McpDiscoveryRoundtripTests or a new tiny test in WrapToolHandlerTests):
   - Throw a LacerteSDKError with userMessage containing `§` and `José`, run WrapToolHandler.Run on a handler that throws it, assert the returned JSON contains the literal `§` and `é` bytes and does NOT contain `\u00A7` or `\u00E9`.
   - This pins the encoder so a future refactor of JsonOptions can't silently revert.

5) Skip changes to FieldAccessMapLoader.cs and FieldAccessCommand.cs BuildJsonOptions — they only Deserialize, encoder is irrelevant there. Also skip HeartbeatWriter.cs:162 unless an operator-readability angle is added (likely cheap to do alongside).

6) DECISIONS.md addendum (1 sentence): "Wire envelopes and disk logs use JavaScriptEncoder.Create(UnicodeRanges.All) so accented client names and em-dash detail-row descriptions remain operator-readable rather than escaping as \uXXXX; HTML-sensitive chars still escape as a defense-in-depth measure."

No behavior risk: changing encoder only affects how non-ASCII bytes are represented in the output string — the resulting JSON is still valid per RFC 8259 and any conformant parser produces the same Unicode codepoint either way.

title: Remediation strings reference a phantom MCP tool `lacerte_register` that doesn't exist
userImpact: When auth gates fire (9006 AppNotRegistered, 9007 LoginExpired, 9101 ReAuthRequired, and three SDK NotSignedIn variants), the operator-facing remediation says `Run lacerte_register` — that name looks identical to the snake_case-converted MCP tool names (`lacerte_session_status`, `lacerte_client_create`, etc.), so an LLM client will reliably try to call it as a tool. There is no `lacerte_register` MCP tool; registration is a CLI command (`lacerte-mcp register`). The LLM will loop on tool-not-found, the operator will see `tools/call` errors instead of the real fix.
description: There are at least 8 sites that say `Run lacerte_register` (or `Re-run lacerte_register and click Accept`). All of them are misleading the LLM into hunting for an MCP tool that the server never registers — no `[McpServerTool] LacerteRegister(...)` exists anywhere in `Tools/`. The actual registration path is the operator-side CLI binary `lacerte-mcp register`. Worse, register is the one operation the LLM CANNOT perform on the operator's behalf (it requires interactive Intuit dialogs), so the name confusion blocks the only working remediation.
recommendation: Replace every `lacerte_register` mention in `SyntheticStatusCodes.cs` and `StatusCodes.cs` (and the matching session manager comment) with the unambiguous CLI form `lacerte-mcp register`. While there, harmonize with the existing `lacerte-mcp login` form already used at SyntheticStatusCodes.cs line 193 (`lacerte-mcp login (or lacerte_register)` → `lacerte-mcp login (or lacerte-mcp register)`). The fix is one find-replace across two files plus a regression test asserting no remediation string contains the underscore-form.
rationale: Round 1 / round 2 covered remediations being too vague (DBxError name-the-file finding) and the synthetic-vs-SDK distinction being buried, but nobody noticed that the canonical remediation string itself names a tool that doesn't exist — confusing both the LLM (looks like an MCP tool) and the operator (looks like a CLI command that doesn't quite work).

verdict.reasoning:
Verified directly. The remediation strings literally say "Run lacerte_register" (underscore form) at 7 distinct sites:

SyntheticStatusCodes.cs:
- L144 (9006 AppNotRegistered) — "Any tool other than lacerte_register was called..."
- L145 (9006 AppNotRegistered) — "Run lacerte_register once to grant consent and sign in."
- L151 (9007 LoginExpired) — "Run lacerte_register to re-authenticate..."
- L193 (9101 ReAuthRequired) — "Run lacerte-mcp login (or lacerte_register) to refresh..."

StatusCodes.cs (SDK-side TPSDKStatus remediations):
- L264 (200 ConsentDenied) — "Re-run lacerte_register and click Accept..."
- L276 (202 RegVersionBlocked) — "Upgrade Lacerte... then re-run lacerte_register."
- L282 (203 NotSignedIn) — "Run lacerte_register (or open Lacerte and sign in)..."

Plus a comment at LacerteSessionManager.cs:1325 referencing the same string.

MCP tool naming verified: SessionTools.cs has methods like LacerteSessionStatus → snake_cased on the wire as lacerte_session_status, LacerteSetContext → lacerte_set_context. There is NO LacerteRegister method anywhere in src/LacertMCP.Server/Tools/ (Grep confirmed). Registration is a CLI verb in src/LacertMCP.Cli/Commands/RegisterCommand.cs invoked as `lacerte-mcp register`.

The hyphen-vs-underscore distinction is load-bearing in this codebase: every other place that mentions a CLI command uses the dashed form (`lacerte-mcp register`, `lacerte-mcp unregister`, `lacerte-mcp login`, `lacerte-mcp doctor`). The underscore form is reserved for tool names. The 7 remediation strings break this convention precisely where an LLM is most likely to act on them.

Ironically, the P15-007 fix comment at BridgeInputValidation.cs:110-113 explicitly states: 'the 9006 "Run lacerte_register" remediation sent LLM clients into infinite loops' — but the fix only re-routed bad-shape appIds to a new code; the broken remediation string itself is unchanged for the genuine 9006 case.

Prior audit check: searched audit-findings.json and audit-findings-r2.json for any task addressing the underscore-vs-hyphen remediation naming. P15-007 only changed the status code (9006 → 9103) for bad-shape appIds; it left every remediation string verbatim. No Phase-14 or Phase-15 task touches the canonical "Run lacerte_register" wording. New finding.

Materiality: HIGH. (1) The LLM literally sees this string and is highly likely to attempt `tools/call {name: "lacerte_register"}` → tool-not-found loop. (2) Affects the four most common operator failure modes: fresh install, expired auth, re-auth required, consent denied. (3) Fix is mechanical (~8 string replacements) and a one-line regression test. (4) Increases trust in the API's remediation hygiene generally — operators learn the difference between MCP tool calls and CLI ceremonies, which is one of the project's documented core architectural distinctions (CLAUDE.md two-mode discipline + DECISIONS.md 2026-05-30 "One-time CLI lacerte-mcp register").

Not bikeshedding — this is a string-level bug that breaks an actual user moment (operator-facing remediation that an LLM will misinterpret as a callable tool).
verdict.refinedRecommendation:
Mechanical fix across two files plus a regression test:

(1) SyntheticStatusCodes.cs — 4 string updates:
- L144: "Any tool other than `lacerte-mcp register` was called before a successful Register() landed."
- L145: "Run `lacerte-mcp register` once to grant consent and sign in."
- L151: "Run `lacerte-mcp register` to re-authenticate (consent is one-time; only the sign-in needs refresh)."
- L193: "Run `lacerte-mcp login` (or `lacerte-mcp register`) to refresh the auth ticket." (the existing L193 already inconsistently mixes the two forms — harmonize)

(2) StatusCodes.cs — 3 string updates:
- L264 (ConsentDenied): "Re-run `lacerte-mcp register` and click Accept on the consent dialog."
- L276 (RegVersionBlocked): "Upgrade Lacerte to the minimum supported build, then re-run `lacerte-mcp register`."
- L282 (NotSignedIn): "Run `lacerte-mcp register` (or open Lacerte and sign in) to refresh the login token."

Use backticks consistently — this matches the style already used at L169 (UnknownFieldAccess: "Run `lacerte-mcp field-access discover`...") and L205 (InvalidAppId: "...run `lacerte-mcp unregister` then `lacerte-mcp register`..."). The backticked form gives LLM hosts a strong visual signal "this is a shell command, not a tool name."

(3) LacerteSessionManager.cs:1325 — update the inline comment to match: "...the operator-friendly 'Run lacerte-mcp register to re-authenticate' string..."

(4) BridgeInputValidation.cs:112 — update the P15-007 explanatory comment ("the 9006 'Run lacerte_register' remediation...") since after this fix the historical wording in the comment no longer matches anything in the codebase. Replace with: "...the 9006 'Run lacerte-mcp register' remediation..." OR drop the literal quote and reference SyntheticStatusCodes.AppNotRegistered by name.

(5) Regression test in StatusCodesTests / SyntheticStatusCodesTests:

```csharp
[Fact]
public void Remediations_NeverNameNonexistentMcpTool_LacerteRegister()
{
    // Guard rail: no remediation string may say "lacerte_register" because there is
    // no LacerteRegister MCP tool — an LLM following that string will tools/call
    // a non-existent name and loop. The CLI ceremony is `lacerte-mcp register`.
    var allRemediations =
        SyntheticStatusCodes.StatusTable.Values.Select(v => v.Remediation)
        .Concat(StatusCodes.StatusTable.Values.Select(v => v.Remediation))
        .Where(r => r != null);
    var offenders = allRemediations
        .Where(r => Regex.IsMatch(r!, @"\blacerte_register\b"))
        .ToList();
    Assert.Empty(offenders);
}
```

This sentinel prevents regression: future contributors adding a new remediation string can't reintroduce the underscore form without a test failure.

(6) Out of scope but worth a follow-up note: do a similar sweep for any OTHER remediation string that names a snake_case identifier that ISN'T a real MCP tool. Spot-checked the current StatusTable and found none beyond `lacerte_register`, but the regression test above could be generalized to "every snake_case `lacerte_*` token in any remediation must match the wire-name of a registered McpServerTool method" — that's a stronger invariant worth filing separately.

Docs follow-up: docs/research/agents/05-error-mapping.md and 02-auth-flow.md also use `lacerte_register` in the same remediation columns (research docs, not user-facing) — leave them as historical research artifacts unless the round-3 doc-consistency sweep grabs them. The shipped server's user-facing strings are what matter for the LLM loop.

title: README claims `register` calls ITPRegistration.Register(); actual code returns exit 3 with '[partial] not yet wired'
userImpact: A tax pro follows the README's setup ceremony step 4, runs `lacerte-mcp register --app-name "Operator Lacerte MCP" --tax-year 2024`, sees the GUID print, exit-code 3, and a `[partial]` message on stderr saying the Intuit consent ceremony is not actually wired. README never warns them. They will assume their install is broken, file a bug, or worse — set LACERTE_LIVE=1 in Claude Desktop and discover at first tool call that nothing works.
description: README line 117 promises `register` 'Mints an AppID GUID, persists it to Windows Credential Manager, calls `ITPRegistration.Register()`, and prints the GUID for backup.' Line 230 repeats: 'on Windows + live SDK calls `ITPRegistration.Register(...)` which surfaces the consent + Intuit dialogs to the interactive shell.' Line 286-287 troubleshoots 'register opened no dialog' by telling the operator to switch to an interactive PowerShell — but no shell change will help, because `RegisterCommand.InvokeLiveRegister` (line 111-114) writes `[partial] AppID minted, but the Intuit consent ceremony is not yet wired into the CLI (Phase 9 task #63)` and returns exit 3. `LoginCommand.Run` (line 73-75) is identical. Same goes for the troubleshooting section's `lacerte-mcp login` 24h-refresh fix (line 293) — login is also stubbed. The README sells a complete onboarding flow that the code explicitly is not delivering.
recommendation: Either (1) add a prominent v0.1.0 status banner at the top of `## Lacerte SDK install` and `### lacerte-mcp register` sections: 'Phase 9 caveat: the Intuit consent ceremony is not wired yet — `register` mints the AppID and exits 3 with a `[partial]` stderr message. Live mode is not bootable until Phase 9 task #63 lands. Sim mode works fully today.' (2) Replace the 'opened no dialog' troubleshooting entry with an entry titled '`register` exits 3 with `[partial]` message' that explains exit-3 is the documented Phase-9-incomplete state. (3) Add the `1` / `3` exit codes to the CLI table at line 220-227 so operators wrapping the CLI in PowerShell `if ($LASTEXITCODE -eq 0)` don't silently swallow the partial state.
rationale: This is the single most expensive operator-onboarding bug in the project — the canonical setup ceremony in the README does not match what the code does, and the gap is a multi-hour debugging session for a non-developer tax pro. Prior audits surfaced the exit-3 design (P15-028) but did not flag the README contradiction it left behind. The exit code is also undocumented in the CLI table so PowerShell wrappers can't even alarm correctly.

verdict.reasoning:
Confirmed by direct reads of all cited locations:

(1) RegisterCommand.cs:91-115 — `InvokeLiveRegister` on `PlatformID.Win32NT` (line 104-114) does NOT call `ITPRegistration.Register()`. It writes `[partial] AppID minted, but the Intuit consent ceremony is not yet wired into the CLI (Phase 9 task #63)` to stderr and returns exit 3. The XML doc comment on the class (line 13) even says "(on Windows + live SDK) calls ITPRegistration.Register(...)" — that part is also misleading.

(2) LoginCommand.cs:42-76 — identical pattern. Windows branch writes `[partial] Login refresh not yet wired (Phase 9 task #63)` to stderr and returns exit 3. README line 293's "Fix" telling operators to run `lacerte-mcp login` does not work.

(3) README.md line 117 — "calls `ITPRegistration.Register()`, and prints the GUID for backup." False today.
README.md line 230 — "on Windows + live SDK calls `ITPRegistration.Register(...)` which surfaces the consent + Intuit dialogs". False today.
README.md line 286-287 — troubleshooting entry titled "`lacerte-mcp register` opened no dialog (or hangs)" diagnoses non-interactive shell. But the code path that fires on Windows (line 104-114) cannot surface a dialog regardless of shell, because ITPRegistration is never called. The diagnosis sends operators on a wild-goose chase.
README.md line 293 — "Fix" tells operator to run `lacerte-mcp login` to refresh 24h ticket. login is also `[partial]` exit-3 — the fix recipe does not work.
README.md line 218-227 — CLI table has no exit-code column; the doctor entry has its own 0/1/2 contract spelled out in line 274-278 but register/login have no documented exit codes, so a PowerShell wrapper `if ($LASTEXITCODE -eq 0)` treats the silent-no-op exit-3 partial state as a hard failure (not bad) but a less-careful `if (-not $?)` wrapper or one that only catches non-zero loses context about WHY.

P15-028 (audit-findings-r2.json line 683) is the prior task that introduced the exit-3 + `[partial]` behavior. Its refinedRecommendation explicitly included a README "Exit codes" subsection edit (item #3 in the recommendation) — but a grep of README.md for "Phase 9", "partial", or "exit 3" shows ZERO mentions. The code half of P15-028 landed; the documentation half did not. So the README still actively sells the original lie ("calls ITPRegistration.Register()") and the troubleshooting section now actively misleads operators away from understanding the real problem.

Not a duplicate of any other finding: P14-065 was about masking the GUID in stdout. P15-028's docs follow-through was not completed. No other Phase-14/15 entry touched these README lines.

Operator impact is concrete and acute: tax pro follows step 4, sees exit 3 + `[partial]` on stderr, reads troubleshooting entry that does not match their symptom (their symptom is `[partial]` not `opened no dialog`), tries the prescribed shell change, nothing happens, then tries `lacerte-mcp login`, gets another `[partial]` exit-3, sets `LACERTE_LIVE=1` anyway hoping it works, discovers at first tool call it doesn't. Multi-hour confusion before they grep the code. The fix is pure docs and prevents this.

meaningfullyImproves: YES. This is the canonical onboarding ceremony in the project, and the docs lie about it.
verdict.refinedRecommendation:
Three coordinated README edits (no code changes — code already correctly returns exit 3 per P15-028; this finding is solely about the docs follow-through that P15-028 specified but never landed).

(1) README.md line 113-118 (Lacerte SDK install step 4) — Replace the current promise with a status-banner version:
```
4. **Run the one-time registration** ceremony:
   ```powershell
   & src/LacertMCP.Cli/bin/x64/Debug/lacerte-mcp.exe register --app-name "Operator Lacerte MCP" --tax-year 2024
   ```
   **Phase 9 caveat (v0.1.x):** Today this mints the AppID GUID and persists it to Windows Credential Manager, then exits **3** with a `[partial]` message on stderr explaining the Intuit consent ceremony is not yet wired (tracked as Phase 9 task #63 in `Todo.md`). The full live-mode boot path is not available until Phase 9 ships. **Simulation mode (the default off-Windows and on-Windows when `LACERTE_LIVE` is unset) works fully today** — you only hit the Phase-9 gap if you try to flip `LACERTE_LIVE=1`.
   Once Phase 9 lands, this command will additionally call `ITPRegistration.Register()` to surface the Intuit consent + sign-in dialog and exit 0.
```

(2) README.md line 228-236 (`### lacerte-mcp register`) — Append an "Exit codes" subsection:
```
**Exit codes:**
- `0` — fully complete (Phase 9+: AppID minted AND Intuit ceremony succeeded; today: only on non-Windows where the ceremony is intentionally skipped for cross-platform dev convenience).
- `1` — hard failure (IO error writing the AppID store; --confirm-style guard tripped).
- `3` — **partial / Phase 9 incomplete:** AppID was minted and persisted, but the Intuit consent ceremony was not invoked. Today this is the expected outcome on Windows. Wrapping PowerShell scripts must treat exit 3 as "AppID step ready, live-mode boot blocked until Phase 9 ships" — not as a hard failure to retry.
```
Repeat the same exit-code block (with login-specific wording — code 3 means the 24h ticket refresh did not actually fire, tools will return `TicketExpired (9103)` once the existing ticket lapses) under `### lacerte-mcp login` at line 238-244.

(3) README.md line 283-293 (Troubleshooting) — Replace the existing "opened no dialog (or hangs)" entry (which gives the wrong diagnosis for the v0.1.x exit-3 state) with TWO entries:

```
### `lacerte-mcp register` exits 3 with `[partial]` on stderr (v0.1.x expected state)

- **Symptom:** The command prints the AppID, then a `[partial] AppID minted, but the Intuit consent ceremony is not yet wired into the CLI (Phase 9 task #63)` line on stderr, and exits 3.
- **Diagnosis:** This is the documented v0.1.x state — Phase 9 task #63 has not landed. The AppID half succeeded; the Intuit consent half is a stub.
- **Fix:** Use simulation mode (do not set `LACERTE_LIVE=1`) until Phase 9 ships. Watch `Todo.md` Phase 9 #63 (Bridge/Registration.cs) for the upgrade. Once it lands, re-run `lacerte-mcp register` and the consent dialog will surface.

### `lacerte-mcp register` opened no dialog after Phase 9 lands (or hangs)

- **Symptom:** Post-Phase-9, the command exits 0 but no Intuit consent window appeared.
- **Diagnosis:** Run from a **non-interactive** shell (SSH session, Windows service, scheduled task) — the Intuit ITPRegistration COM call needs a desktop session to surface its UI.
- **Fix:** Open a normal interactive PowerShell on the operator's desktop session and re-run `lacerte-mcp register`. Confirm with `lacerte-mcp status` that `registered: true`.
```

Also fix the immediately following entry ("Tools start returning `NotSignedIn` after a day") — the "Fix" tells the operator to run `lacerte-mcp login`, which today also exits 3 with `[partial]`. Add a one-line "Until Phase 9 ships, `lacerte-mcp login` also exits 3 with `[partial]` — there is no manual ticket refresh available in v0.1.x; the only workable mode today is simulation." after the existing Fix bullet.

Skip: a full v0.1.x deprecation banner at the top of the README — out of proportion for a single phase gap. Skip: any code change to RegisterCommand/LoginCommand — P15-028 already landed the exit-3 + stderr routing correctly. This finding is purely the docs half of P15-028 that never shipped.

Why this meaningfully improves the operator moment: the tax-pro follows step 4, sees exit 3 + `[partial]` on stderr, then opens troubleshooting and reads an entry that diagnoses a DIFFERENT symptom (non-interactive shell), tries the wrong fix, fails, tries `lacerte-mcp login` per the next troubleshooting entry, gets another `[partial]` exit 3, gives up and either sets `LACERTE_LIVE=1` hoping it'll work (it won't — first tool call returns NotSignedIn 9101) or files a bug. This is a multi-hour failure mode for a non-developer audience. The docs fix is 30 minutes of work and turns the failure into a one-screen "ah, Phase 9 isn't done yet, I'll use sim mode" decision.

title: Three different default app names (`Lacerte MCP` / `LacerteMCP` / `Operator Lacerte MCP`) across server, CLI, and env table
userImpact: Intuit ties the consent to AppName + AppID together. If an operator runs `lacerte-mcp register` (defaults to 'Operator Lacerte MCP') without setting LACERTE_APP_NAME in Claude Desktop config, the running MCP server defaults to 'Lacerte MCP' — a different string — when subsequently calling SDK APIs. The SDK is likely to reject the call with an auth/identity mismatch, and the operator will see opaque `NotSignedIn` errors despite a freshly-registered AppID. README compounds it by documenting a third default ('LacerteMCP', no space) in the env-var table.
description: RegisterCommand.cs:25 and LoginCommand.cs:24 default `--app-name` to `"Operator Lacerte MCP"`. LacerteSessionManager.cs:310 and :339 use `_appName ?? "Lacerte MCP"` when LACERTE_APP_NAME is unset — a different string with a space. README.md line 93 env table says default is `LacerteMCP` (no space at all). Neither the CLI commands nor the server actually read `LACERTE_APP_NAME` to seed their defaults — the CLI's `--app-name` flag has a hard-coded `() => "Operator Lacerte MCP"` literal, ignoring any env var the operator set in their MCP host config. Three different strings means an operator who omits the env var lands in mismatch territory; an operator who sets the env var lands in 'CLI ignores my env, server reads it' territory.
recommendation: (1) Pick ONE default — recommend `Operator Lacerte MCP` since it's already in the README install snippet at line 61. (2) Change RegisterCommand.cs:25 and LoginCommand.cs:24 to default to `Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("LACERTE_APP_NAME") ?? "Operator Lacerte MCP"`. (3) Change LacerteSessionManager.cs:310/339 fallback `"Lacerte MCP"` to `"Operator Lacerte MCP"`. (4) Fix README env-var table line 93 default `LacerteMCP` → `Operator Lacerte MCP`. (5) Add a doctor probe that warns when LACERTE_APP_NAME differs from the AppName the persisted AppID was registered with (requires persisting the AppName alongside the AppID, which is cheap).
rationale: Subtle correctness bug that erodes trust silently — the operator sees `lacerte-mcp status` show `registered: yes` and the server show `live` mode, but every tool call fails because the SDK identity tuple is mismatched. None of the diagnostic surfaces (doctor, status, session_status) catch this. The three-way drift is exactly the kind of slapped-together inconsistency Round-3 was asked to find.

verdict.reasoning:
Verified all five citations directly:

(1) RegisterCommand.cs:25 — hard-codes `() => "Operator Lacerte MCP"`. CONFIRMED.
(2) LoginCommand.cs:24 — hard-codes `() => "Operator Lacerte MCP"`. CONFIRMED.
(3) LacerteSessionManager.cs:310 — `_appName ?? "Lacerte MCP"` (with space). CONFIRMED.
(4) LacerteSessionManager.cs:339 — `_appName ?? "Lacerte MCP"` (with space). CONFIRMED.
(5) README.md:93 env-var table — Default column literally says `LacerteMCP` (no space). CONFIRMED.

Additional verified evidence amplifying the drift:
- README.md:61 (install snippet operators paste): `"Operator Lacerte MCP"` (a fourth datapoint that DOES agree with the CLI literal).
- README.md:115 (register example): `--app-name "Operator Lacerte MCP"`.
- README.md:293 (recovery instructions): `--app-name "Operator Lacerte MCP"`.
- docs/research/agents/02-auth-flow.md:23, 103: `"Operator Lacerte MCP"`.
- .env.example:5: `LACERTE_APP_NAME=LacerteMCP` (matches README table default of `LacerteMCP`, but disagrees with README install snippet and CLI default).
- src/LacertMCP.Tests/Parity/fixtures/example-recording.json:25: `"appName": "Lacerte MCP"` (matches the SERVER fallback string, not the CLI default — so the parity recording fixture is also locked to the silent-fallback variant).
- StatusCommand.cs:71 reads `LACERTE_APP_NAME` from env for display only — confirming the CLI knows about the env var but doesn't use it for register/login defaults.
- LacerteSessionManager.cs:220 + :274 confirm only the server reads `LACERTE_APP_NAME`.

The asymmetry described in the finding is exact: server reads env, CLI ignores env, three different default literals. An operator who pastes the README install snippet (which sets `LACERTE_APP_NAME=Operator Lacerte MCP`) will get the server using "Operator Lacerte MCP" but the CLI's `lacerte-mcp register` ignoring it (still defaulting to the literal "Operator Lacerte MCP" — coincidentally matching, BUT only because the literal happens to equal the env value). An operator who follows .env.example (which sets it to `LacerteMCP`) will get server using "LacerteMCP" but CLI using "Operator Lacerte MCP" — guaranteed mismatch.

Not a duplicate of any prior task:
- P14-065 (audit-findings.json:~1412): GUID-masking in stdout, unrelated to AppName drift.
- R2 finding about .env.example LACERTE_APP_ID: doc cleanup for AppID guidance, did not flag the AppName drift; in fact its recommended replacement text would re-cement `LACERTE_APP_NAME=LacerteMCP` even though README install snippet uses `Operator Lacerte MCP`.
- R2 finding about LACERTE_DEFAULT_TAX_YEAR: separate var, different problem (not read at all). The AppName case is the inverse: read by server only, ignored by CLI, with three diverging documented defaults.
- Phase-14 P14-016/P14-033 only added missing rows to the README env table; they did not catch that the *default value* column itself contradicts the install snippet 32 lines above it.

Meaningful improvement assessment (strict bar): YES. This is exactly the trust-eroding silent inconsistency Round-3 was asked to catch. The recommended doctor-probe addition (warn when env != registered AppName) plus the simple literal alignment closes a class of opaque NotSignedIn / consent-mismatch failures that the existing `lacerte-mcp status` and `doctor` surfaces do not catch today. The fix is cheap (4 literal edits + 1 doctor probe + 1 README cell) and the recovery moment it improves is real: an operator at 11pm staring at `status: registered=yes, mode=live` and every tool call returning 9101 has no diagnostic surface that points at the AppName mismatch. Severity-wise, "high" is defensible because the operator-visible failure mode (NotSignedIn) is opaque and the doctor remediation does not currently mention AppName at all — but I'd note the finding's "SDK is likely to reject" framing is slightly speculative (Intuit's actual enforcement of AppName-must-match-consent-record is not 100% confirmed in the docs cited). The doc/test/CLI drift on its own justifies the fix regardless.
verdict.refinedRecommendation:
Adopt the original 5-step plan with three tightening edits:

1. **Pick `Operator Lacerte MCP` as the One True Default.** Reasoning: it is already what the README install snippet (line 61), the register example (line 115), the recovery instructions (line 293), and the auth-flow research doc (02-auth-flow.md:23, 103) all use. The other two strings (`Lacerte MCP`, `LacerteMCP`) appear only in code fallbacks, the README env-table cell, .env.example, and one test fixture — strictly fewer touch-points to update.

2. **CLI literal edits (sim-safe, no Windows, no SDK):**
   - `src/LacertMCP.Cli/Commands/RegisterCommand.cs:25` — change `() => "Operator Lacerte MCP"` to `() => Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("LACERTE_APP_NAME") ?? "Operator Lacerte MCP"`. This makes the CLI honor the same env var the server reads.
   - `src/LacertMCP.Cli/Commands/LoginCommand.cs:24` — same change. Critical for the cron-driven 24h refresh path: if the operator's MCP-host env sets `LACERTE_APP_NAME` to anything non-default, a cron `lacerte-mcp login` would otherwise refresh with the wrong identity tuple.

3. **Server fallback edits:**
   - `src/LacertMCP.Server/Session/LacerteSessionManager.cs:310` — change `_appName ?? "Lacerte MCP"` to `_appName ?? "Operator Lacerte MCP"`.
   - `src/LacertMCP.Server/Session/LacerteSessionManager.cs:339` — same change. Extract `const string DefaultAppName = "Operator Lacerte MCP"` at the top of the class so future drift is impossible.

4. **Doc + fixture alignment (4 edits):**
   - `README.md:93` env table — change Default column from `LacerteMCP` to `Operator Lacerte MCP`.
   - `.env.example:5` — change `LACERTE_APP_NAME=LacerteMCP` to `LACERTE_APP_NAME=Operator Lacerte MCP` (note: this OVERRIDES the suggestion in the prior R2 finding about LACERTE_APP_ID, which inadvertently preserved the `LacerteMCP` literal — call that out in the DECISIONS entry below).
   - `ARCHITECTURE.md:173` — env table currently has no Default column for `LACERTE_APP_NAME` (just Purpose); leave as-is OR add a Default column for consistency. Keep scope tight: skip unless ARCH cleanup is in the same PR.
   - `src/LacertMCP.Tests/Parity/fixtures/example-recording.json:25` — change `"appName": "Lacerte MCP"` to `"appName": "Operator Lacerte MCP"` AND regenerate any test that compares against this fixture. Verify no test asserts the literal "Lacerte MCP" — if any do, update them (this is one reason the drift survived).

5. **Doctor probe (the real trust-restoring deliverable):**
   - Persist the registered AppName alongside the AppID in `AppIdStore` (cheap — same Windows Credential Manager target or %APPDATA% JSON file, just add an `app-name` field).
   - At register-time, write both. At server-startup-time, if `LACERTE_APP_NAME` is set AND differs from the persisted AppName, log one stderr warning: `[startup] LACERTE_APP_NAME='<env>' differs from registered AppName='<persisted>' — Intuit consent record is tied to '<persisted>'. Re-run 'lacerte-mcp register --reset' to align.`
   - Add a doctor probe: `[CHECK] AppName/env alignment — env='Operator Lacerte MCP' matches persisted AppName 'Operator Lacerte MCP'` (PASS) vs `[FAIL] AppName drift — env='X', persisted='Y'. Tools will fail with NotSignedIn (9101). Fix: unset LACERTE_APP_NAME OR re-run 'lacerte-mcp register --reset --app-name "<intended>"'.`

6. **Tests (all sim-safe, in `RegisterCommandTests`, `LoginCommandTests`, `LacerteSessionManagerTests`, new `DoctorProbeTests`):**
   - Register/Login defaults: when `LACERTE_APP_NAME` env unset → CLI uses `Operator Lacerte MCP`.
   - Register/Login env honored: when `LACERTE_APP_NAME=Foo` → CLI passes "Foo" to Run().
   - Server fallback: with env unset and `_appName==null`, `Register()` WireLog payload + `_bridge.Register` arg are both `Operator Lacerte MCP`.
   - Doctor probe: env vs persisted mismatch produces FAIL row with the remediation string above.
   - Round-trip: register with env='X', then a fresh CLI invocation with env='X' login → no drift warning; with env='Y' → drift warning.

7. **DECISIONS.md entry** (dated today): `AppName default is "Operator Lacerte MCP" — one literal across CLI defaults, server fallbacks, README, .env.example, and parity fixtures. CLI honors LACERTE_APP_NAME so the env var the server reads is the same one the CLI defaults from. Mismatch between persisted AppName and env LACERTE_APP_NAME is a doctor-probe FAIL.`

title: Six distinct list-envelope shapes across read tools makes the LLM relearn the contract per call
line: SubclientsTools.cs:28-34, StatesTools.cs:28-34/45-51, FormsTools.cs:27-33, StatusTools.cs:26-33, EFileTools.cs:60-62, MetadataTools.cs:109-117/159-163, SessionTools.cs:127-156, ClientsTools.cs:50-61, TablesTools.cs:41-54, DetailsTools.cs:85-96
userImpact: An LLM (or curious operator scripting in PowerShell) sees a different envelope for every list-returning tool. Some have full pagination ({rows,total,limit,offset,hasMore,nextOffset,count,clients}), some have {count,subclients}, some {count,states}, some {count,efStatuses}, some {count,codes}, some {count,fields}, some {count,modules}, some {count,datapaths}. To page or count rows, the LLM has to memorize which name the array uses. A model that learned `result.rows` from one tool will hit `result.efStatuses` on the next and fall back to enumerating keys. Cross-tool sharing of paging code becomes impossible.
description: Tools split into three shape families: (a) full-pagination tools (ClientsTools, TablesTools, DetailsTools) emit rows+total+limit+offset+hasMore+nextOffset+count plus a SECOND alias key (clients, subclients duplicated); (b) named-array+count tools (SubclientsTools 'subclients', StatesTools 'states'/'stateSubclients', FormsTools 'forms', StatusTools 'statuses', EFileTools 'efStatuses', SessionTools 'modules'/'datapaths', MetadataTools 'fields'/'codes'); (c) DetailsTools has both styles (rows-as-paged + count). Even within the full-pagination family, ClientsTools serializes the same array under BOTH `rows` and `clients`, doubling the payload size for no benefit.
recommendation: Pick one shape and apply it everywhere. Recommended: every list-returning tool emits {rows: [...], total, limit, offset, hasMore, nextOffset}. Drop the per-tool aliases (subclients/forms/efStatuses/codes/fields/modules/datapaths) and the legacy `count` field. The `legacy` comments in TablesTools/DetailsTools/ClientsTools already acknowledge the cleanup is overdue ('remove in v0.2'); ship that cleanup before more tools accrete more shapes. The CHANGELOG note costs less than the cumulative LLM confusion of every tool call going forward.
rationale: Round-2 P14-082 flagged pagination unevenness in EF/details/forms specifically; this finding generalizes to ALL list tools and surfaces the duplicate-array (rows+clients) bug + the 8 distinct array names. Round 1 did not catch the rename inconsistency.

verdict.reasoning:
Verified by reading all 9 cited tool files. The envelope-shape inventory is accurate as a snapshot of TODAY'S code: SubclientsTools returns `{clientNumber, count, subclients}`, StatesTools returns `{clientNumber, stateAbbrev, count, states}` and `{..., count, stateSubclients}`, FormsTools `{clientNumber, count, forms}`, StatusTools `{clientNumber, count, statuses}`, EFileTools `{count, efStatuses}`, MetadataTools `{module, moduleName, table, year, count, fields}` and `{count, codes}`, SessionTools `{count, modules}` and `{root, rootExists, count, datapaths}`. ClientsTools/TablesTools/DetailsTools emit the full paginated envelope with the legacy duplicate `count` (+ `clients` alias in ClientsTools).

Prior rounds DO overlap significantly. Round-2 P15-040 and P15-047 explicitly identified the same six tools (EFileTools/DetailsTools/FormsTools/SubclientsTools/StatesTools/StatusTools) and recommended retrofitting them with Pagination.Page<T> — and both rounds CHOSE to keep the named aliases (subclients/forms/efStatuses/etc.) as additive v0.1 back-compat with v0.2 cleanup deferred. So the broad 'shape inconsistency' complaint is mostly an explicit prior design choice, not a new finding.

However, two genuinely NEW components survive:

1) **The P15-047 retrofit was marked [x] complete in Todo.md but the actual code change was NOT applied to 5 of 6 tools.** Only DetailsTools.cs has the `int limit = 100, int offset = 0` parameters and `Pagination.Page<T>` wrapper (line 65-96, references audit P15-040/P15-047). SubclientsTools/StatesTools/FormsTools/StatusTools/EFileTools are unchanged — zero `limit`, `offset`, or `Pagination` references. This is a closed-but-not-actually-fixed audit gap, which is a meaningful usability finding (the inconsistency P15-047 promised to resolve is still present in production code).

2) **ClientsTools serializes the SAME array under BOTH `rows` AND `clients` keys** (lines 52 + 60), literally doubling the response payload for a ~100-row default page. This is wire-size waste neither P15-040 nor P15-047 flagged — they discussed keeping the legacy alias as a separate field referencing the same data structurally; the duplicate-emission-in-JSON aspect was missed. For a 100-row default page of DATA1 (~1-2 KB per row), this is roughly 100-200 KB of literally duplicated JSON per `lacerte_client_list` call.

Usability-wise, both matter: (1) the LLM still has to relearn the envelope per tool because the promised cleanup didn't actually land; (2) the duplicated `clients` array wastes context-window budget on every call to the most-frequently-called read tool. Recommend reframing the finding away from a wholesale 'rename all aliases' (which prior rounds explicitly rejected) and toward the two narrower, concrete gaps that DID slip through.
verdict.refinedRecommendation:
Two concrete, narrow fixes. Frame as a P15-047 follow-up rather than re-litigating the v0.1 back-compat design.

(A) **Finish the P15-047 retrofit that was marked done but never applied.** Apply DetailsTools.cs:65-96's exact pattern to the 5 tools where it's still missing — SubclientsTools, StatesTools (both methods), FormsTools, StatusTools, EFileTools. Each is a 4-line edit:
  - Add `int limit = 100, int offset = 0, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default` parameters
  - Wrap `var page = Pagination.Pagination.Page(rows, limit, offset);`
  - Emit `{ ...existing context keys, rows = page.Rows, total = page.Total, limit, offset, hasMore, nextOffset, count = page.Rows.Count, <legacyAlias> = page.Rows }`
  - Update [Description] to mention `Supports limit/offset pagination; returns {rows, total, limit, offset, hasMore, nextOffset}`
  Mirror DetailsTools.cs's exact phrasing so the LLM sees one canonical template.

(B) **Fix the duplicate-array payload bug in ClientsTools.cs:60.** The current return emits `rows = page.Rows` AND `clients = page.Rows` — same List<T> instance serialized twice. Drop the second emission and keep ONLY `rows` (the canonical pagination key). Justification: the v0.1 'legacy' contract is the named field, but ClientsTools is the ONLY paginated tool that emits BOTH the canonical AND legacy key for the array; TablesTools and DetailsTools only emit `rows` (no `tables`/`details` alias) plus the legacy `count` integer. ClientsTools is the outlier and the duplication doubles response size for the most-frequently-called read tool. If preserving any back-compat key is required, keep `count` only — that's already TablesTools/DetailsTools' precedent.

(C) **Add a guardrail test** in `src/LacertMCP.Tests/Tools/PaginationContractTests.cs` (new) that calls each `lacerte_*_read` / `lacerte_*_list` tool, deserializes the envelope, and asserts the six pagination fields (`rows`, `total`, `limit`, `offset`, `hasMore`, `nextOffset`) are all present and the response does NOT contain a duplicate array under any other top-level key. This prevents both (a) the silent-skip pattern that closed P15-047 without code changes and (b) future re-introduction of duplicate-array aliases.

Explicitly OUT OF SCOPE for this finding (already decided by prior rounds, do not relitigate): renaming `subclients`/`forms`/`efStatuses`/`statuses`/`states`/`stateSubclients`/`modules`/`datapaths`/`fields`/`codes` to `rows`. That breaking change is deliberately deferred to v0.2 per DECISIONS.md pagination ADR; raising it as a new finding ignores the explicit prior decision.

title: Eight error remediations point to a non-existent MCP tool `lacerte_register` — LLM will hit tool-not-found loops
userImpact: When auth lifecycle errors fire (NotSignedIn 203, AppNotRegistered 9006, LoginExpired 9007, ConsentDenied 200, RegVersionBlocked 202, ReAuthRequired 9101), the LLM is told to `Run lacerte_register`. No MCP tool of that name exists — registration is a CLI verb (`lacerte-mcp register`). Modern MCP hosts let the LLM try calling unknown tools and surface `tool not found`, putting the LLM into a confused loop where it can either invent the tool or eventually deduce the operator must run a shell command. The error path that fires MOST often (24h expiry) is the one with the broken remediation.
description: Six remediation strings in StatusCodes/SyntheticStatusCodes use phrasing like `Run lacerte_register` or `Run lacerte_register to re-authenticate`. The LLM reads these as actionable tool names (consistent with the `lacerte_*` naming convention used for every real MCP tool). The actual recovery path is an out-of-band shell command, and the message gives no signal that this is a CLI command vs an MCP tool. ReAuthRequired 9101 already shows the right pattern (`Run lacerte-mcp login (or lacerte_register)`) — proving the team knows the distinction; the inconsistency is just unfinished.
recommendation: Bulk-rename the 6 remediations to `Ask the operator to run the shell command \`lacerte-mcp register\` (or \`lacerte-mcp login\` for a ticket refresh) — this is a CLI command, not an MCP tool.` Verb-prefix with `Ask the operator to run the shell command` (or similar) so the LLM never confuses CLI verbs with MCP tools. Audit grep for `Run lacerte_` across the codebase as a regression seam.
rationale: Prior rounds covered error envelope structure (origin discriminator, severity, etc.) but did not audit the actual remediation TEXT for callable-tool accuracy. This is the single most-followed error in the operator lifecycle (every 24h).

verdict.reasoning: Verified directly. SIX remediation strings reference a non-existent MCP tool `lacerte_register`: SyntheticStatusCodes.cs:145 (AppNotRegistered 9006) "Run lacerte_register once to grant consent and sign in.", :151 (LoginExpired 9007) "Run lacerte_register to re-authenticate...", and StatusCodes.cs:264 (ConsentDenied 200) "Re-run lacerte_register and click Accept...", :276 (RegVersionBlocked 202) "...then re-run lacerte_register.", :282 (NotSignedIn 203) "Run lacerte_register (or open Lacerte and sign in)...". (SyntheticStatusCodes.cs:193 ReAuthRequired 9101 also contains `lacerte_register` but at least leads with `lacerte-mcp login` — proves the team knows the right pattern.) NO MCP tool named `lacerte_register` exists — confirmed by grepping every `[McpServerTool]` method under src/LacertMCP.Server/Tools; the closest tools are `lacerte_session_status`, `lacerte_set_context`, etc. Registration is exclusively a CLI verb (`lacerte-mcp register`, RegisterCommand.cs). The naming convention `lacerte_<verb>` (snake_case auto-derived) makes `lacerte_register` indistinguishable from real tools — an LLM host will absolutely try to call it and hit tool-not-found, then either invent the tool or eventually deduce the shell-command path. NOT a Phase-14 or Phase-15 duplicate: P15-007 fixed the WRONG-CODE side (BridgeInputValidation no longer routes appId-shape failures to 9006/AppNotRegistered, instead emitting new 9103/InvalidAppId), but it left the StatusInfo remediation TEXT for 9006/9007/200/202/203 unchanged. Prior rounds audited envelope structure (origin discriminator, severity, redaction), env-var consistency (P14-016 — `LACERTE_DEBUG` -> `LACERTE_DEBUG_WIRE`), and `LACERTE_BRIDGE_LOG` phantom-var fix, but none audited remediation text for callable-tool accuracy. The 24h LoginExpired path is the single most-fired auth error in the operator lifecycle (once per day per the proactive expiry probe added in P15-043 itself, which even mentions the broken string in its comment at LacerteSessionManager.cs:1325) — the broken remediation hits the daily-friction path. Trivial in-session edit, zero Windows dependency.
verdict.refinedRecommendation:
Rewrite the 5 broken remediation strings to verb-prefix with "Ask the operator to run" (or similar shell-command tag) so the LLM never treats `lacerte_register` as a callable tool. Concrete edits:

(1) SyntheticStatusCodes.cs:145 (AppNotRegistered 9006) — change to:
`"Ask the operator to run the shell command `lacerte-mcp register` once (this is a CLI command, not an MCP tool) to grant consent and sign in."`

Also fix the userMessage on line 144 — it says "Any tool other than lacerte_register was called..." which is doubly wrong (no such tool exists AND there's no MCP tool that can complete registration). Change to:
`"A read/write tool was called before the operator ran the `lacerte-mcp register` CLI command. Registration cannot be performed via MCP — it requires interactive consent against the local Lacerte install."`

(2) SyntheticStatusCodes.cs:151 (LoginExpired 9007) — change to:
`"Ask the operator to run the shell command `lacerte-mcp login` to refresh the auth ticket (consent is one-time; only the 24-hour sign-in needs refresh). `lacerte-mcp register` also works but does more than needed."`

(3) StatusCodes.cs:264 (ConsentDenied 200) — change to:
`"Ask the operator to re-run the shell command `lacerte-mcp register` and click Accept on the Lacerte consent dialog."`

(4) StatusCodes.cs:276 (RegVersionBlocked 202) — change to:
`"Ask the operator to upgrade Lacerte to the minimum supported build, then re-run the shell command `lacerte-mcp register`."`

(5) StatusCodes.cs:282 (NotSignedIn 203) — change to:
`"Ask the operator to run the shell command `lacerte-mcp login` (or open Lacerte and sign in) to refresh the login token."`

(6) SyntheticStatusCodes.cs:193 (ReAuthRequired 9101) — already mostly right, but drop the `(or lacerte_register)` parenthetical since that string also reads as a tool name. Change to:
`"Ask the operator to run the shell command `lacerte-mcp login` to refresh the auth ticket. If that fails, fall back to `lacerte-mcp register`."`

(7) Add a regression seam: a new SyntheticStatusCodesTests case that asserts NO remediation string in StatusCodes.StatusTable or SyntheticStatusCodes.StatusTable matches the regex `\\blacerte_[a-z_]+\\b` UNLESS the substring is the literal name of a registered MCP tool (collect tool names via reflection over `[McpServerToolType]` classes in LacertMCP.Server, transform method names to snake_case). This catches future drift where a new code emits "Run lacerte_xyz" without verifying the tool exists.

(8) Also update the two code-comments that propagate the wrong phrasing so future grep audits don't reintroduce the bug — they're harmless today but they encode the wrong mental model:
   - LacerteSessionManager.cs:1325 comment "Run lacerte_register to re-authenticate" -> "Run `lacerte-mcp login` (CLI) to re-authenticate"
   - BridgeInputValidation.cs:112 comment "Run lacerte_register" -> "Run `lacerte-mcp register` (CLI)"
   - BridgeInputValidationTests.cs:148 comment likewise.

Update any tests that assert on the remediation text substring (SyntheticStatusCodesTests / StatusCodesTests — grep for the old fragments first) to the new phrasing. Pure-string change, no Windows/SDK dependency, all sim-testable.

title: UnknownFieldAccess (9012) remediation references a dead CLI verb AND a tool parameter that doesn't exist
userImpact: Every write to an uncatalogued field returns 9012 with remediation: `Run \`lacerte-mcp field-access discover\` to populate the map, or pass force:true to override.` Both halves are wrong. `field-access discover` was deprecated in P15-029 (exits 3 with a redirect to LacertMCP.FieldAccessDumper.exe). `force:true` is not exposed on any MCP tool (the `force` parameter exists only on the internal `FieldAccessMapLoader.AssertWritable` method). An LLM trying both will fail twice and lose trust before discovering the real path is to run the standalone dumper exe.
description: Today the v1 base shards ship empty by design (per FieldAccessMapLoader and Doctor probe XML doc) — meaning 9012 fires on essentially every write attempt in v0.1 until shards are populated. The most-fired remediation in the write path points at two non-options. The same misdirection is repeated in the file's own doc comment at line 41 (`populate the map with lacerte-mcp field-access discover or override with force:true`).
recommendation: Rewrite the remediation to: `Field is not in the access map. Run \`LacertMCP.FieldAccessDumper.exe --module <X> --table <N>\` on a Windows + live-SDK box to populate the shard, then call \`lacerte_reload_schema\` so the new shard takes effect without restarting (which would invalidate the 24h Intuit ticket). title: `lacerte_client_intake` prompt teaches the LLM a `lacerte_detail_write` call signature that doesn't exist
userImpact: The intake prompt — the most-invoked prompt in the most-invoked operator flow — instructs the LLM to call `lacerte_detail_write` with `{{ clientNumber, row: {{ Series, Code, ... }} }}`. The real tool has 12 required positional params (clientNumber, series, prefix, code, suffix, stateAbbr, cityAbbr, source, tsj, importSrc, amount, description). There is no `row` parameter, and the spec-required strings for prefix/suffix/stateAbbr/cityAbbr/source/tsj/importSrc/description must be passed (most as empty strings). An LLM following this prompt will hit a parameter-binding error on the first detail write of the intake, then have to fish out the real signature from the tool list — defeating the whole point of the prompt.
description: The mismatch is structural: the prompt invents a nested-object shape (`{Series, Code, ...}`) while the tool uses flat positional kwargs. The ellipsis `...` makes the prompt look complete but hides 9 required fields. Same prompt does this only for detail_write — every other tool call uses the actual flat shape. This is the single highest-leverage prompt fix in the codebase (intake is a P0 operator flow per REQUIREMENTS).
recommendation: Rewrite Step 5 to show the actual flat signature explicitly: `lacerte_detail_write({{ clientNumber, series: "11", prefix: "", code: "1", suffix: "", stateAbbr: "", cityAbbr: "", source: "W2", tsj: "T", importSrc: "", amount: 50000.00, description: "Employer A" }})`. Optionally cross-link to `lacerte-mcp tools --name lacerte_detail_write` so the LLM can refresh the exact surface. Add a test that snapshots each prompt's tool-call examples against the real signatures so future param drift fails CI.
rationale: Prior rounds reviewed prompt structure and step ordering but did not validate prompt-embedded tool-call examples against actual tool signatures.

verdict.reasoning:
Verified directly against source. WorkflowPrompts.cs:93 instructs the LLM to call lacerte_detail_write with `{{ clientNumber, row: {{ Series, Code, ... }} }}` — a nested-object shape that does not exist on the tool. DetailsTools.cs:100-117 shows the real signature is 12 required flat positional params (clientNumber, series, prefix, code, suffix, stateAbbr, cityAbbr, source, tsj, importSrc, amount, description) plus 3 optional (replaceIndex, dryRun, idempotencyKey). There is no `row` parameter anywhere on the surface, and none of the nine non-numeric strings are nullable — `prefix`/`suffix`/`stateAbbr`/`cityAbbr`/`source`/`tsj`/`importSrc`/`description` must be passed (most as empty strings). The ellipsis `...` in the prompt hides every required field, so an LLM that follows the prompt literally will emit a malformed call that the MCP binder rejects before reaching the tool body. Notably, every OTHER tool call inside the same prompt uses the correct flat shape — Step 4 even shows lacerte_field_write with the right `{{ table, clientNumber, field, value }}` flat shape. Step 5's nested-row shape is a lone outlier and looks like a stale draft from an earlier API design.

Usability impact is high and concrete: lacerte_client_intake is the canonical onboarding prompt and intake almost always touches detail rows (W-2/1099/Schedule C totals are called out in the Step 5 header itself). On the very first detail write of the very first intake the LLM will spit a binding error, then have to fish out the real signature from the tool list — destroying the prompt's promised determinism. The whole reason this prompt exists (per WorkflowPrompts.cs XML header: "Keep the text concrete + reference real tool names so the agent doesn't fabricate") is undermined by the prompt itself fabricating an unreal call shape.

Duplication check: grepped both audit-findings.json and audit-findings-r2.json for ClientIntake / detail_write / row: / nested / call signature. The closest prior touches are P15-038 (added CSV intake prompt + canonical column mapping) and P14-015 (added README prompts table) — neither validates that prompt-embedded tool-call examples match real tool signatures. The existing WorkflowPromptsTests only check that the string "lacerte_detail_write" appears in the body, never that the call shape is correct. Genuinely new.

Actionability: zero-risk sim-only fix — edit the prompt text + add a snapshot/contract test that links each prompt's documented call examples against the real tool's `[McpServerTool]` parameter list via reflection. Pure docs + test work, no runtime change, all green off-Windows.
verdict.refinedRecommendation:
Two-part fix, both sim-safe, ~30 min of work.

(1) Rewrite WorkflowPrompts.cs:92-94 (Step 5) to emit the actual flat signature with every required field shown explicitly. Drop the nested `row:` wrapper and the `...` ellipsis. Concrete replacement:

```
Step 5 — Seed starter detail rows (W-2 / 1099 / Schedule C totals collected at intake)
  • lacerte_detail_write takes 12 REQUIRED flat params plus 3 optional. Pass empty strings for the codes you don't have. A W-2 row looks like:
      lacerte_detail_write({{ clientNumber, series: ""11"", prefix: """", code: ""1"", suffix: """", stateAbbr: """", cityAbbr: """", source: ""W2"", tsj: ""T"", importSrc: """", amount: 50000.00, description: ""Employer A"" }})
    Series cheat-sheet: 11=W-2, 12=Interest, 13=Dividends, 14=Dependents, 20=Income, 30=State, 40=Partners. tsj is one of T/S/J/"" (taxpayer/spouse/joint/unspecified). stateAbbr is "" or a 2-letter postal code.
  • For idempotent retries pass `idempotencyKey: ""intake-<clientID>-detail-<seriesCode>""`. For a dry-run preview pass `dryRun: true`.
  • The SDK does NOT validate detail-row shape; this tool's client-side validation is the only safeguard. Read the error message verbatim — series/code/stateAbbr/tsj each have a per-field reason if rejected.
```

While you're there, audit the other prompts for the same class of bug — a quick scan suggests Step 3's `lacerte_client_create` example (line 62) and Step 4's `lacerte_field_write` example (line 67) currently use the correct flat shape, but pin that down with a test (next bullet).

(2) Add a contract test at src/LacertMCP.Tests/Prompts/PromptCallExampleSignaturesTests.cs. For each prompt body, extract every `lacerte_<tool>({{ ... }})` example via regex, parse out the kwarg names inside the braces, then reflect over the corresponding `[McpServerTool]` method on its `*Tools` class and assert: (a) every kwarg name in the example matches a real parameter name, (b) no example uses a kwarg the tool doesn't expose, (c) for required parameters (non-nullable, no default) the example actually mentions them. Skip the assertion if the prompt uses prose-style references (no braces) — the test is for concrete call examples only. This is the snapshot the finding asks for and prevents future prompt drift from silently breaking the operator flow. ~60 LOC, off-Windows, no Lacerte/DSN dependency.

Optional polish: append one sentence to each prompt's body — "If a call shape here doesn't match the tool's current signature, run `lacerte-mcp tools --name <tool>` from the shell to print the live signature, and file an issue." This gives the operator a recovery path if drift slips through anyway.
