title: 9006 / 9007 / 9101 / 200-204 remediation strings reference a 'lacerte_register' MCP tool that does not exist
userImpact: Every re-auth path tells the LLM to 'Run lacerte_register' — a tool name that is NOT registered as an MCP tool (registration is a CLI-only command, `lacerte-mcp register`). The LLM will either try to invoke a non-existent tool (returning an MCP-level 'unknown tool' error inside the recovery flow) or, worse, hallucinate parameters for it. Operator sits in front of Claude Desktop with no shell access from the LLM, and the canonical 24h-expiry remediation actively confuses the recovery.
description: AppNotRegistered (9006), LoginExpired (9007), ReAuthRequired (9101), NotSignedIn (203), ConsentDenied (200), RegVersionBlocked (202) all say 'Run lacerte_register' or 'Re-run lacerte_register' in their canonical Remediation strings. There is no [McpServerTool] named lacerte_register anywhere — `Grep -r 'lacerte_register' src/LacertMCP.Server/Tools` returns zero hits. The actual recovery is two CLI commands (`lacerte-mcp register` from a shell on the Lacerte box) plus an MCP-server restart, exactly as the WorkflowPrompts.cs:52 prose correctly phrases it ('tell the operator to run `lacerte-mcp register` from the shell'). The error catalog never got the same wording fix.
recommendation: Rewrite the four remediations to the operator-action shape used by WorkflowPrompts: 'Ask the operator to run `lacerte-mcp register` (or `lacerte-mcp login` for an expired 24h ticket) from a shell on the Lacerte box, then restart the MCP server in Claude Desktop.' Distinguish the consent ceremony (register) from ticket refresh (login) — only 9006 needs full re-register; 9007/9101/203 need login. The 9101 string at SyntheticStatusCodes.cs:193 already gets login right; propagate that wording to 9006/9007 and the three TPSDKStatus codes.
rationale: Round-1 P15-028 hardened the CLI exit codes; round-2 P15-070 invalidated derived caches on Register. Neither round looked at the remediation copy itself referencing a non-existent MCP tool name. This is the most-cited error-recovery string in the system.

verdict.reasoning:
Verified directly against source. The 7 cited remediation strings literally tell the LLM to "Run lacerte_register" / "Re-run lacerte_register" — but no [McpServerTool] method (or its snake_case-translated name) named `lacerte_register` exists anywhere in src/LacertMCP.Server/Tools. Confirmed: (a) Grep for McpServerTool on a Register method across all 17 tool files returned zero hits; (b) The only `lacerte_register` references in the codebase are inside the error-catalog strings themselves (SyntheticStatusCodes.cs + StatusCodes.cs) and inside WireLog/comments; (c) Actual registration is CLI-only (`lacerte-mcp register` in src/LacertMCP.Cli/Commands/RegisterCommand.cs); (d) WorkflowPrompts.cs:52 already uses the correct operator-facing wording ("tell the operator to run `lacerte-mcp register` from the shell"), proving the project has a known-correct phrasing pattern the error catalog never adopted.

Cross-checked the prior two audit rounds. Round 2 P15-007 fixed ONE wrong AppNotRegistered remediation (the bad-shape appId case) by minting a new InvalidAppId=9103 code with a correct `lacerte-mcp unregister`/`lacerte-mcp register` remediation — so the project clearly accepts the principle, it just didn't propagate the wording fix to the 6 sibling remediations. Round 2 P15-043 went the other direction: it wired a proactive 24h expiry probe that throws LoginExpired (9007) and explicitly preserved the existing "Run lacerte_register to re-authenticate" remediation as the desired user-facing message. So P15-043 actually expanded the surface where this wrong remediation gets emitted. No prior round noticed the literal "lacerte_register" tool name doesn't exist as an MCP tool.

User impact is high and concrete: every 24h ticket expiry now emits 9007 with "Run lacerte_register" through the LLM in Claude Desktop. The LLM either (i) tries to call a tool by that name and gets a wire-level "unknown tool" error inside the recovery flow, (ii) hallucinates parameters, or (iii) confuses the operator by asking them to "approve the lacerte_register tool call." This is the most-cited error-recovery string in the system — 9007 fires on every multi-day session. Fix is small (3-7 string edits in two files), sim-testable, off-Windows, and turns recovery from confusing to mechanical.

One refinement to the finding: the recommendation needs to be careful about ConsentDenied (200) and RegVersionBlocked (202). ConsentDenied means the operator already saw the dialog and clicked Decline — the correct recovery is `lacerte-mcp register` (which re-shows the dialog), not `login`. RegVersionBlocked needs a Lacerte upgrade first, THEN `lacerte-mcp register`. Only 9006 AppNotRegistered, 9007 LoginExpired, 9101 ReAuthRequired, and 203 NotSignedIn split cleanly into "needs full re-register" vs "needs ticket refresh."
verdict.refinedRecommendation:
Rewrite the 7 affected Remediation strings to reference the actual CLI command + restart, and split register-vs-login correctly. Two files, 7 edits:

1) `src/LacertMCP.Server/Errors/SyntheticStatusCodes.cs`:
- Line 145 (AppNotRegistered, 9006): "Ask the operator to run `lacerte-mcp register` from a shell on the Lacerte box (this opens the Intuit consent dialog), then restart the MCP server in your host (Claude Desktop / Cursor / Windsurf). This tool cannot trigger the registration ceremony itself."
- Line 151 (LoginExpired, 9007): "The 24h Intuit ticket lapsed; the one-time consent is still valid. Ask the operator to run `lacerte-mcp login` from a shell on the Lacerte box, then restart the MCP server. Use `lacerte-mcp register` only if `login` reports the AppID was never registered."
- Line 193 (ReAuthRequired, 9101): Already mentions both `lacerte-mcp login` and `lacerte_register` — drop the bare-tool-name fallback and align with the 9007 wording: "Ask the operator to run `lacerte-mcp login` from a shell on the Lacerte box, then restart the MCP server. Fall back to `lacerte-mcp register` only if login reports the AppID is unknown."

2) `src/LacertMCP.Server/Errors/StatusCodes.cs`:
- Line 264 (ConsentDenied, 200): "Ask the operator to run `lacerte-mcp register` again from a shell on the Lacerte box and click Accept on the Intuit consent dialog, then restart the MCP server."
- Line 276 (RegVersionBlocked, 202): "Ask the operator to upgrade Lacerte to the minimum supported build, then run `lacerte-mcp register` from a shell and restart the MCP server."
- Line 282 (NotSignedIn, 203): "Ask the operator to run `lacerte-mcp login` from a shell on the Lacerte box (or open Lacerte and sign in), then restart the MCP server. The 24h Intuit auth ticket lapsed; the one-time consent is still valid so a full `register` is not needed."

3) Comment fixups (low priority but worth doing in the same pass for code-search hygiene):
- `src/LacertMCP.Server/Session/LacerteSessionManager.cs:1325` — change the code comment "Run lacerte_register to re-authenticate" string to match the new wording so future greps don't resurrect the wrong phrase.

4) Tests: add a focused assertion in `src/LacertMCP.Tests/Errors/SyntheticStatusCodesTests.cs` (and equivalent for StatusCodes) that the Remediation for AppNotRegistered, LoginExpired, ReAuthRequired, NotSignedIn, ConsentDenied, and RegVersionBlocked contains the literal `lacerte-mcp ` (with hyphen + trailing space) and does NOT contain the literal `lacerte_register` (with underscore). This is the regression sentinel — any future maintainer who pastes the old wording back gets a red test. Cost: ~10 lines.

Distinction discipline (one-line decision):
- Full re-register (consent dialog must re-fire): 9006 AppNotRegistered, 200 ConsentDenied, 202 RegVersionBlocked (after upgrade).
- Ticket refresh only (consent intact, 24h lapsed): 9007 LoginExpired, 9101 ReAuthRequired, 203 NotSignedIn.

This is sim-only, off-Windows, ~30 lines including tests, and turns the most-cited error in the system from "actively misleads the LLM" to "tells the LLM exactly what to ask the operator."

title: InValidClientName (24) catalog remediation contradicts the ClientID regex it actually gates
userImpact: When `lacerte_client_create` rejects a ClientID like 'John Smith' or 'O\'Reilly', the canonical remediation says 'Use letters, numbers, spaces, hyphen/apostrophe only' — but the actual regex CreateClientTools._rxClientId enforces `^[A-Z0-9]+$`, which rejects spaces, hyphens AND apostrophes. The LLM, trusting the remediation, advises the operator to try 'O-Reilly' or 'John Smith' which will fail identically, looping the operator through the same rejection.
description: Code 24 is reused for at least THREE distinct conditions that need different remediation: (a) ClientID character whitelist failure in CreateClientTools.cs:96 (regex `^[A-Z0-9]+$` — no spaces, no punctuation), (b) invalid single-character module code in LacerteSessionManager.cs:563 + SessionTools.cs:79 + MetadataTools.cs:44 ('module must be a single character I/C/P/S/F/R/T/N/B'), (c) required FirstName/LastName/EmailID missing in CreateClientTools.cs:122/132/142. The single canonical Remediation 'Use letters, numbers, spaces, hyphen/apostrophe only; avoid < > " \' & / \\ | ?.' is for case (c)-ish client *names* and is actively wrong for (a) and meaningless for (b). Operators hitting any non-(c) path get bad guidance.
recommendation: Two options: (1) introduce dedicated synthetic codes for the three reuse cases (e.g. 9016 InvalidClientId with `^[A-Z0-9]+$` in the remediation; 9017 InvalidModuleChar with the I/C/P/S/F/R/T/N/B alphabet) so the catalog-level remediation matches the actual gate. Or (2) at minimum, every throw-site already populates a `context.reason` AND the relevant regex/alphabet — surface those in the rendered remediation by having WrapToolHandler.SerializeError prefer `context.reason` over the catalog default when present. Either way, the universal 'spaces, hyphen/apostrophe' line must go — it advises behavior that perpetuates the failure on the most common path (CreateClient ClientID).
rationale: Prior rounds verified InValidClientName fires in the right places but never sanity-checked the catalog remediation against the actual validators that throw it. Code 24 reuse predates the audits; the contradictory remediation has shipped through all 149 prior tasks unnoticed because no test asserts 'the user-facing remediation describes the gate that actually fires'.

verdict.reasoning: Verified by direct file reads. StatusCodes.cs:229-233 defines InValidClientName(24) with userMessage 'The client name contains characters Lacerte rejects' and remediation 'Use letters, numbers, spaces, hyphen/apostrophe only; avoid < > \" ' & / \\ | ?.'. The actual regex at CreateClientTools.cs:93 (`_rxClientId.IsMatch(clientID)` against `^[A-Z0-9]+$`) rejects spaces, hyphens, AND apostrophes — the exact three character classes the canonical remediation says to use. Reuse confirmed at 7 distinct throw-sites: CreateClientTools.cs:96 (ClientID regex), :124/:135/:146 (missing FirstName/LastName/EmailID), SessionTools.cs:79 and :108 (module single-char), MetadataTools.cs:44 (module lookup), LacerteSessionManager.cs:563 (module validation), Odbc/SqlTemplates.cs:44, Bridge/BridgeInputValidation.cs:228. Each throw-site populates context.reason with the correct gate-specific text, but WrapToolHandler.SerializeError (Errors/WrapToolHandler.cs:144-158) emits both fields side-by-side — the LLM sees contradictory guidance in the same envelope (context.reason says 'letters and digits only', remediation says 'use spaces, hyphens, apostrophes'). Cross-referenced both prior audit files: round-1 task #21 (line 641) fixed sim-vs-live divergence in CreateClient gates; round-1 task at line 1152 added the FirstName/LastName/EmailID required-field gates (which now reuse code 24 — a fix that landed without updating the catalog text). No prior task audited the catalog remediation text against the validators that throw it. The userMessage is also wrong for ALL the module cases — it claims 'client name' when the issue is a module character. The contradiction directly causes the looping behavior the finding describes: an LLM following 'use hyphen/apostrophe' will retry 'O-Reilly' and fail again, then 'O Reilly' and fail again. For module cases the remediation is nonsense ('use letters, numbers, spaces, hyphen/apostrophe for...' a single-character module code).
verdict.refinedRecommendation:
Two-stage fix, both stages low-risk and in-session:

STAGE 1 (immediate, ~30 LOC) — Stop the contradictory catalog text from misleading the LLM:

1. In `WrapToolHandler.SerializeError` (Errors/WrapToolHandler.cs:144-158), when `err.Context` contains a `reason` key (string), use it as the primary `remediation` in the envelope and demote the catalog `Remediation` to a fallback field like `genericRemediation` (or simply drop it when reason is present). This makes the per-throw-site `reason` text — which is already correct everywhere — the authoritative guidance the LLM sees.

2. Edit StatusCodes.cs:229-233 to make the catalog text describe ONLY what is invariant across all reuse cases: userMessage = 'A token (ClientID, module character, or required name field) was rejected by Lacerte validation.' remediation = 'See context.reason for the exact rule that failed and context.field/clientID/module for the offending value.' This stops the catalog from advising hyphen/apostrophe usage that fails on the most common path.

STAGE 2 (clean fix, ~80 LOC) — Split the overloaded code in SyntheticStatusCodes.cs:

3. Add `SyntheticStatusCodes.InvalidClientID = 9016` with userMessage 'ClientID failed the character/length whitelist.' remediation 'ClientID must match ^[A-Z0-9]+$ (uppercase letters and digits only) and be 1-8 characters. Strip spaces/punctuation and uppercase before retrying. Example: \"OREILLY\", not \"O'Reilly\" or \"O-Reilly\".'

4. Add `SyntheticStatusCodes.InvalidModuleChar = 9017` with userMessage 'Module code must be a single character.' remediation 'Pass exactly one of: I (Individual), C (Corporate), P (Partnership), S (S-Corp), F (Fiduciary), R (Exempt), T (Estate/Gift), N (Benefit), B (Bundled). Case-insensitive.'

5. Add `SyntheticStatusCodes.MissingRequiredClientField = 9018` with userMessage 'A required client field is missing or whitespace.' remediation 'lacerte_client_create requires non-empty firstName, lastName, and emailID per spec §4. See context.field for which one was empty.'

6. Update the 5 throw-sites that should use the new codes: CreateClientTools.cs:96 → 9016, :124/:135/:146 → 9018, SessionTools.cs:79/:108 + MetadataTools.cs:44 + LacerteSessionManager.cs:563 → 9017. Leave SqlTemplates.cs:44 and BridgeInputValidation.cs:228 untouched if they truly are SDK-name rejections; otherwise reroute them too.

7. Keep StatusCodes.InValidClientName(24) for the actual SDK-returned bridge rejections (live mode), and tighten its remediation to 'The Lacerte SDK rejected this token at the COM boundary. See context for the field/value. Common live-SDK rule is uppercase A-Z and 0-9 only for ClientID.'

8. Add tests:
   - CreateClientToolsTests: assert envelope.remediation references `^[A-Z0-9]+$` when ClientID has lowercase/hyphen/space (not 'hyphen/apostrophe').
   - SessionToolsTests: assert envelope.remediation lists I/C/P/S/F/R/T/N/B when module='X' or module=''.
   - A new ErrorCatalogConsistencyTests that walks every throw-site of every status code (via grep or reflection on test fixtures) and asserts catalog remediation does not advise inputs that the gate would itself reject.

9. README/ACCEPTANCE_CRITERIA touch-ups: enumerate the three new synthetic codes alongside the existing 90xx list.

Stage 1 alone resolves the worst LLM-loop scenario today. Stage 2 prevents the class of bug (one code, three remediations) from recurring. Both stages are net48/no-Windows/no-Lacerte verifiable.

title: README CLI table claims `field-access discover` exits 2, but it exits 3 — operators wiring CI on the exit code will alarm wrongly
userImpact: An operator who reads the README and writes a shell guard like `if ($LASTEXITCODE -eq 2) { 'discover stub, skipping' }` will silently miss every discover invocation — the verb actually returns 3. The README also says doctor is a '7-probe verification' (line 226/273) but the actual probe count is 13+ on Windows, so anyone counting in the help text is immediately confused.
description:
Three concrete README/CLI drift issues that erode trust:

1. README.md:269 says `discover — stub today; always exits 2.` Code (FieldAccessCommand.cs:258) sets `context.ExitCode = 3;`. The discrepancy was introduced by P15-029 (which intentionally reserved exit 2 for doctor's environment-skip and used 3 for not-implemented) but the README never caught up.

2. README.md:226 + 273 describe doctor as `7-probe setup verification`. The actual RunAllProbes (DoctorCommand.cs:224-343) returns 13 probes on Windows (Build, Windows version, x64, App.config shim, .NET 4.8, ODBC DSN, SDK install, COM ProgID, Operating mode, LACERTE_DATA_PATH env, LACERTE_DATA_PATH dir, LACERTE_DATA_ROOT env, LACERTE_DATA_ROOT dir, FieldAccessMap shards, AppID) — P15-031/P15-032 added six probes without updating the README's '7-probe' claim. README probe list at line 273 omits App.config, COM ProgID, Operating mode, DATA_ROOT, FieldAccessMap.

3. README.md:222 says `lacerte-mcp status — JSON snapshot — no wire I/O` and the heading at 245 reads `lacerte-mcp status [--show-app-id]` — but P15-026 flipped the default to a human table and added `--json`. Heading and table entry both miss the new flag and mislead operators piping to `jq` (will get the human table by default, parse will fail).
recommendation: Sweep README.md for the three drifts: (a) change `discover` exit code claim to `exits 3` (and add a one-line note that 3 = not-implemented-here, distinct from doctor's exit 2 = environment-skip); (b) update the doctor section to list all probes — or generate from `RunAllProbes()` at build time; at minimum drop the literal '7-probe' count and replace with 'Pre-flight probes for the install'; (c) update the status section heading to `lacerte-mcp status [--show-app-id] [--json]` and reorder the TL;DR row to say `human-readable summary (pass --json for machine-parseable)`. Bonus: add a unit test that scans README CLI section for exit-code claims that don't appear in the corresponding command file (`Regex.Matches(readme, "exits? (\\d)")` and grep the codebase for `ExitCode = N`).
rationale: Round-1 and round-2 documented CLI behavior changes (P15-026, P15-027, P15-029, P15-031, P15-032) but didn't audit the README CLI section as a whole. The exit-code drift is exactly the kind of subtle trust-erosion that round-3 is meant to catch — README is the operator's first stop and the prior rounds added the divergence without anyone re-reading the surrounding paragraph.

title: `field-access list/set --table` accepts any int with no range validation; help text says '1..7' but `--table 99` happily prints `C99_0 → ReadOnly`
userImpact: Operator typos `--table 17` (meant `--table 1` then `7`) and gets `(no entries in base map for module=I table=17) / Universal rule: C17_0 → ReadOnly (always, no entry needed).` — a confident, wrong-looking message about a table number that doesn't exist. They believe the field-access map is empty for a valid table, when in fact they queried a nonexistent table. Worse, `set --table 99 --field C99_0 --access ReadWrite` would WRITE a never-loadable entry into the shard JSON, polluting the on-disk map with junk that becomes a future PR-review puzzle.
description:
Both `list` and `set` declare `--table` as `Option<int>` with description `Table number (1..7).` (lines 52 + 129), but neither validates the value falls in [1,7]. `RunList` (line 104-106) prints `(no entries...) / Universal rule: C{table}_0 → ReadOnly` for ANY integer, including 0, 8, 17, 99, -3. The `C` prefix in the universal rule is also confusing on non-C modules (e.g. on module `I`, the message still says `C99_0`, which looks like a typo). `RunSet` will happily write `I|99|FOO` into `i.json` — a key the loader cannot resolve to a real DATA file, silently bloating the shard.

Additional inconsistency: the `--field` option on `set` (line 130) takes ANY string. The convention is `<C>{table}_{n}` (e.g. `C1_42`) but there's no validation that the field name even loosely matches that pattern. `set --module I --table 1 --field 'oops_typo' --access ReadWrite` silently writes `I|1|oops_typo` — operator may never realize they fat-fingered until the next loader read returns Unknown.
recommendation: Add range validation in both `RunList` and `RunSet`: if `table < 1 || table > 7` then `stderr.WriteLine($"--table must be in 1..7 (got {table}).")` and return 1. Apply the same to `Modules.FileBasenameFor(module)`-style guards. For `--field`, accept anything that matches `^[A-Z][1-7]_\d+$` (case-insensitive); on mismatch print `stderr.WriteLine($"--field '{field}' does not match the C<table>_<n> convention; pass --force to override.")` and return 1, with `--force` flag as the escape hatch. Drop the literal `C` from the 'Universal rule' message on non-C modules — or, since universal-zero applies to every module, just rewrite the line to `Universal rule: field _0 → ReadOnly on every module (no entry needed).`
rationale: Round-2 cli-ux lens covered the broad shape of field-access (P15-067 routed stderr properly) but didn't audit input validation. Prior rounds focused on argument plumbing; this is the next-layer 'silly inputs produce silly outputs' surface that erodes operator trust in the on-disk map.

verdict.reasoning:
Verified by reading C:/Users/VR/Projects/LacertMCP/src/LacertMCP.Cli/Commands/FieldAccessCommand.cs lines 51-52 (list --table), 86-106 (RunList body), 129-130 (set --table + --field), 179-230 (RunSet body). All four claims hold:

(1) `--table` is bare `Option<int>` with description `Table number (1..7).` — zero range validation in either the SetHandler closure or in RunList/RunSet itself.
(2) RunList line 104-106 literally formats `(no entries in base map for module={module} table={table})` and `Universal rule: C{table}_0 → ReadOnly` for ANY int — including 0, -3, 17, 99. The `C` prefix in that message is also wrong-on-non-C-modules: on module `I` the user gets `Universal rule: C99_0 → ReadOnly` which reads like an unrelated table-99 field, not the universal-zero rule.
(3) RunSet line 195-209 happily computes key `module|table|field` and writes it via `WriteShardSorted` regardless of table value. Verified the loader (FieldAccessMapLoader.cs:248) only consults `Modules.FileBasenameFor(module)` to pick a shard; it does not validate the table portion of stored keys on read, so a `set --table 99` write becomes dead bytes in the JSON that no later `list` or runtime lookup can ever surface. PR-review puzzle confirmed.
(4) `--field` (line 130) is bare `Option<string>` — no format check. `set --module I --table 1 --field oops_typo --access ReadWrite` cheerfully writes `I|1|oops_typo` and prints a green `# Wrote ...` line; operator only discovers the typo when the next runtime read returns Unknown.

Not a Phase-14 or Phase-15 dupe. Prior FieldAccessCommand touches were: P14 Modules.FileBasenameFor dedup (audit-findings.json line 422+), P15-067 stderr routing (audit-findings-r2.json:1611), and P15-029 discover→exit-3 redirect (audit-findings-r2.json:688). None addressed input validation on table range, field-name format, or the `C{table}_0` message wording. Round-1 finding 1174 covers DATA6/DATA7 table-level read-only refusal in FieldWriteTools — different surface (write tool, not CLI), and different concern (spec compliance, not typo defense).

Meaningful improvement: yes. Operator typing `--table 17` instead of `1 7` at 11pm gets confident-but-wrong output AND silently corrupts the on-disk shard. ~15-line fix (range check + regex on field + reword universal-rule message) closes both the bad-output and the on-disk-corruption holes. Not bikeshedding — silent shard pollution is the kind of trust-eroding subtle bug the round-3 lens is asking for.

title: `lacerte-mcp register` (no flags) on Windows when AppID exists prints success-looking text, then exits 3 on stderr — confusing 'success that wasn't'
userImpact:
First-touch operator workflow:
1. `lacerte-mcp register` (first time): mints GUID, prints `[partial] AppID minted, but the Intuit consent ceremony is not yet wired...` on STDERR, exits 3. Operator sees the stderr lines, OK.
2. `lacerte-mcp register` (re-run, same shell): prints `AppID already minted — re-using existing GUID.` on STDOUT with masked AppID and the hint `Pass --reset to mint a new one`, then prints empty line, then prints `[partial] AppID minted...` on STDERR, exits 3.

The stdout block on re-run reads exactly like success ('re-using existing GUID' is a positive sentence, no warn glyph, no 'INCOMPLETE' marker), and the stderr block uses the SAME `[partial] AppID minted` phrasing as the first-mint case — but in the re-run case the AppID was NOT minted (it was re-used). The operator can't tell whether anything actually happened. A shell like `lacerte-mcp register && lacerte-mcp status` always short-circuits because of exit 3, but the operator doesn't know whether they should re-register or just keep going.
description:
RegisterCommand.cs:52 (re-use branch) and :66 (new-mint branch) both fall through to `InvokeLiveRegister(...)` at line 88, which unconditionally returns 3 on Windows and prints the same `[partial] AppID minted, but the Intuit consent ceremony is not yet wired into the CLI` message regardless of whether mint actually happened. Compare to the `unregister` command — when there's nothing to unregister it prints `No AppID persisted — nothing to unregister.` and exits 0 (a no-op), which is the cleaner pattern.

Also noisy: the re-use branch prints the hint `Pass --reset to mint a new one (this forces a fresh Intuit consent dialog)` immediately followed (after blank line) by the stderr `[partial]` block. The operator gets two contradictory directives — 'pass --reset' and 'first MCP tool call will return NotSignedIn until Phase 9 ships and you re-run register' — without guidance on which to do.
recommendation:
Differentiate the re-use vs new-mint paths in the stub message:
- New-mint branch: stderr `[partial] AppID minted but Intuit consent not wired (Phase 9 #63) — your AppID is saved; first MCP tool call will return NotSignedIn (9101) until upgrade.` (exit 3 — there's real partial state).
- Re-use branch: stderr `[partial] Existing AppID re-used; Intuit consent ceremony still not wired (Phase 9 #63). Nothing changed on this run.` (exit 3 OR consider exit 0 — re-running register on an already-minted box did the only thing it could do, the partial state is identical to before).

If the team prefers, split into two distinct exit codes: 0 = 'no action needed, AppID present', 3 = 'partial, AppID was just minted but consent not done'. Document in README CLI section. Also drop the 'Pass --reset' hint from the re-use branch's stdout — it's discoverable via `--help`, and the immediate-following stderr block creates a 'what do I actually do?' moment.
rationale: Round-1/round-2 (P15-028) added the exit-3 stderr routing but didn't re-walk the re-use path. The first-time UX flow now reads weird in the re-run case — same exit code, same stderr text, completely different actual state. Round-3 'subtle correctness/UX bugs that erode trust' lens catches this.

verdict.reasoning:
Verified directly against C:/Users/VR/Projects/LacertMCP/src/LacertMCP.Cli/Commands/RegisterCommand.cs:47-115. Both the re-use branch (line 52-64) and the new-mint branch (line 66-85) fall through to InvokeLiveRegister (line 88), which on Windows unconditionally emits the literal text `[partial] AppID minted, but the Intuit consent ceremony is not yet wired into the CLI (Phase 9 task #63)` and exits 3 — regardless of whether anything was actually minted on this invocation. So on a re-run of `lacerte-mcp register` on a Windows box, stderr lies: it says "AppID minted" when in fact the existing AppID was re-used. That is a real, subtle correctness-of-message bug in a first-touch operator surface.

Also confirmed: the re-use stdout block prints `Pass --reset to mint a new one (this forces a fresh Intuit consent dialog).` and is immediately followed by the stderr block telling the operator "first MCP tool call will return NotSignedIn until Phase 9 ships and you re-run register". The two directives are not contradictory on close reading (re-run after Phase 9 ships vs. --reset now to re-mint), but they DO arrive jammed together with no separation, and the operator has to parse "is the next action --reset, wait for Phase 9, or just proceed?" in a moment of high cognitive load.

The comparison to UnregisterCommand.cs:62-67 is apt — that command's "nothing to unregister" path returns exit 0 with a clean no-op message, which is exactly the pattern the re-use branch of register could adopt.

Not a duplicate of P15-028 (round 2): that finding swapped exit 0 → exit 3 on Windows for the silent-success problem but did not differentiate the re-use vs new-mint paths or revisit the message text — it just routed the existing phrasing to stderr. P14-065 only touched GUID masking. No other prior finding covered the re-use-branch path explicitly.

The `meaningfullyImproves` test: shipping `[partial] Existing AppID re-used; Intuit consent ceremony still not wired (Phase 9 #63) — nothing changed on this run.` for the re-use case vs the current `[partial] AppID minted...` IS a real improvement to a first-touch CLI moment the operator will hit at least once when they re-run register out of uncertainty. It removes a factually-wrong line and resolves the "what do I actually do next?" friction. Cost is ~10 LOC.
verdict.refinedRecommendation:
Two-part fix in `src/LacertMCP.Cli/Commands/RegisterCommand.cs`:

(1) Plumb the mint-vs-reuse fact into `InvokeLiveRegister` so its stderr message can tell the truth. Change the signature to `InvokeLiveRegister(string appName, Guid appId, int taxYear, bool wasJustMinted)` and pass `wasJustMinted: !existing.HasValue || reset` from `Run`. In the Win32NT branch, switch the first stderr line:
  - wasJustMinted=true:  `[partial] AppID minted, but the Intuit consent ceremony is not yet wired into the CLI (Phase 9 task #63).` (existing text — accurate for this path).
  - wasJustMinted=false: `[partial] Existing AppID re-used; the Intuit consent ceremony still is not wired into the CLI (Phase 9 task #63). Nothing changed on this run.`
The second/third stderr lines stay the same (NotSignedIn + Todo.md pointer). Exit 3 stays on both paths — the partial-state semantics ARE identical (AppID present, consent not wired), and operators wrapping `register` in `if ($LASTEXITCODE -eq 0)` should still treat both as not-ready. (Skip splitting into exit 0 vs exit 3 by path — that introduces a third exit-code meaning and breaks the contract P15-028 just established.)

(2) Drop or relocate the "Pass --reset to mint a new one" line at RegisterCommand.cs:63. It's discoverable from `lacerte-mcp register --help` (the option description already says "Mint a fresh GUID even if one already exists. Forces a new Intuit consent ceremony."), and on a re-run its juxtaposition with the immediately-following stderr `[partial]` block creates the "what do I actually do?" moment the finding flags. Either delete the line entirely, or move it into the stderr `[partial]` block as a fourth line: `          If you intended to re-do the Intuit consent ceremony, re-run with --reset.` — that puts the action in the same channel as the warning rather than dangling above it.

(3) Test: add one fact to the existing RegisterCommand test class (or `AppIdMaskingTests.cs` pattern) that runs `RegisterCommand.Run("Test", 2024, reset: false)` TWICE under an `IsolatedAppIdScope`. First call asserts stderr contains `"AppID minted"`. Second call asserts stderr contains `"Existing AppID re-used"` AND does NOT contain `"AppID minted, but"`. Gate with `[SkipUnlessWin32NT]` since the off-Windows path returns 0 with different text. Locks the wording contract so a future refactor can't re-merge the messages.

Skip: changing the exit code by path (introduces a new convention for marginal gain), or rewriting the stdout re-use block beyond removing the --reset hint (the masked-AppID + AppName + TaxYear summary is useful and not at fault).

title: Doctor probe output: `LACERTE_DATA_PATH env` and `LACERTE_DATA_ROOT env` both Warn with the IDENTICAL remediation pointing at `lacerte_set_context` — but only one of them is what `lacerte_set_context` actually sets
userImpact:
Operator with a fresh install runs `lacerte-mcp doctor`, sees two warns:
  `⚠ LACERTE_DATA_PATH env: not set (will need to call lacerte_set_context before any tool that reads/writes data)`
  `⚠ LACERTE_DATA_ROOT env: not set (will need to call lacerte_set_context before any tool that reads/writes data)`
They run `lacerte_set_context` (per the suggestion), only to find the warn for DATA_ROOT persists — `lacerte_set_context` sets DATA_PATH (per-session current-context), not DATA_ROOT (install-wide root for discovery). The operator now wonders if their `set_context` call failed, or if the doctor is buggy. They check both, see set_context succeeded, then have to read source code to discover the two env vars have different scopes and are set through different mechanisms. The remediation text steered them wrong.
description:
DoctorCommand.cs:676 ProbeDataPathEnv is called twice — once for `LACERTE_DATA_PATH` (line 329) and once for `LACERTE_DATA_ROOT` (line 332). Both yield the same `not set (will need to call lacerte_set_context...)` warning. But these env vars have different roles:
- `LACERTE_DATA_PATH` — per-tax-year, current-context data dir (e.g. `C:\Lacerte\24Data`). Settable via `lacerte_set_context` tool.
- `LACERTE_DATA_ROOT` — install-wide root for `lacerte_list_datapaths` discovery (e.g. `C:\Lacerte`). NOT settable via `set_context`; must be set in MCP client config or Windows env.

README.md:98 + :310-311 documents the difference clearly, but the doctor remediation collapses them. Round-2 P15-031 added the DATA_ROOT probe but reused the same code path.
recommendation:
Pass an additional `remediation` parameter to `ProbeDataPathEnv(string envVar, string remediation)` and distinguish:
- DATA_PATH unset: `'Set via the MCP `lacerte_set_context` tool (per-session) or LACERTE_DATA_PATH in env (persistent).'`
- DATA_ROOT unset: `'Set LACERTE_DATA_ROOT=C:\Lacerte (or your install path) in the MCP client config / Windows env. NOT settable via lacerte_set_context — that tool only writes DATA_PATH.'`
Bonus: when DATA_PATH is unset but DATA_ROOT IS set, downgrade the DATA_PATH warn to a softer 'will be auto-discovered from DATA_ROOT on each call' note instead of the current 'will need to call set_context' — that's actually wrong when DATA_ROOT is wired and discovery covers the use case.
rationale: Round-2 P15-031 added the DATA_ROOT probe but copy-pasted the DATA_PATH remediation verbatim — a classic 'shipped the feature but didn't re-read the message in context' miss. This is exactly the round-3 'documentation that exists but doesn't help in the moment' lens — the warn text actively misdirects the operator, which is worse than no remediation at all.

verdict.reasoning: Directly verified in C:/Users/VR/Projects/LacertMCP/src/LacertMCP.Cli/Commands/DoctorCommand.cs. `ProbeDataPathEnv(string envVar)` at line 676 takes only the env var name; lines 681-684 yield the IDENTICAL remediation string "not set (will need to call lacerte_set_context before any tool that reads/writes data)" for both DATA_PATH (called at line 329) and DATA_ROOT (called at line 332). The remediation is wrong for DATA_ROOT — `lacerte_set_context` writes the per-session current context (DATA_PATH semantics), NOT the install-wide discovery root. An operator following the warn for DATA_ROOT will run set_context, watch the warn persist on the next doctor run, and conclude either set_context is broken or doctor is buggy. The README (lines 98, 310-311 per finder) does document the distinction, but the in-the-moment doctor text steers them wrong — which is the round-3 "docs exist but don't help in the moment" lens. Prior round-2 P15-031 explicitly added the DATA_ROOT probe but copy-pasted the DATA_PATH remediation (visible in the refinedRecommendation I read — it specified "(6) LACERTE_DATA_ROOT probe — same shape as (3)" without re-thinking the unset-state message). Not a duplicate of any prior P14/P15 task. Fix is in-session, sim-safe, ~10 LOC plus tests. Bonus tier-down (DATA_PATH unset is fine when DATA_ROOT is wired because discovery covers it) is a genuine polish win — operators with LACERTE_DATA_ROOT correctly configured currently see a misleading warn telling them to call set_context unnecessarily on every doctor run.
verdict.refinedRecommendation:
Two-part fix in src/LacertMCP.Cli/Commands/DoctorCommand.cs, both small and in-session:

(A) Differentiate the unset-state remediation per env var. Change the signature to `ProbeDataPathEnv(string envVar, string unsetDetail, string? unsetRemediation = null)` and update call sites:

- DATA_PATH (line 329) unsetDetail: `"not set (call the `lacerte_set_context` tool per-session, or set LACERTE_DATA_PATH in env for a persistent default)"` — current text is roughly correct here.

- DATA_ROOT (line 332) unsetDetail: `"not set; `lacerte_list_datapaths` will fall back to C\\Lacerte"` with remediation `"Set LACERTE_DATA_ROOT in the MCP client config (or Windows env) to your install root, e.g. C\\Lacerte. NOTE: this is NOT settable via lacerte_set_context — that tool only writes the current per-session DATA_PATH."` The explicit "NOT settable via set_context" sentence is the load-bearing piece — it preempts the operator confusion of "I ran set_context, why is this still warning?"

(B) Downgrade the DATA_PATH unset warn when DATA_ROOT IS set. Compute DATA_ROOT presence before/inside the DATA_PATH probe and, when DATA_ROOT is wired and resolves on disk, emit DATA_PATH as `ProbeStatus.Pass` with detail like `"not set; will resolve per-call from LACERTE_DATA_ROOT (current discovery covers this)"`. This stops the false-positive warn that currently fires on every doctor run for correctly-configured operators who use DATA_ROOT discovery instead of pinning a single year.

(C) Add two DoctorCommandTests cases covering the new branches: (1) DATA_ROOT unset emits the DATA_ROOT-specific remediation (not the set_context one); (2) DATA_PATH unset + DATA_ROOT set + directory exists emits Pass not Warn for DATA_PATH. Both are env-var-fixture pure unit tests, no Windows required.

Skip the alternative of just appending "(DATA_ROOT only, NOT settable via set_context)" to a shared template — the per-var remediation is the right factoring because the bonus (B) tier-down only applies to DATA_PATH.

title: Collection-key name varies per tool — 9 different keys for "the result rows"
line: ClientsTools.cs:52,60 (rows + clients) / DetailsTools.cs:88 (rows) / TablesTools.cs:46 (rows) / StatesTools.cs:33,50 (states, stateSubclients) / StatusTools.cs:32 (statuses) / FormsTools.cs:31 (forms) / SubclientsTools.cs:32 (subclients) / EFileTools.cs:61 (efStatuses) / SessionTools.cs:138,154 (modules, datapaths) / MetadataTools.cs:116,162 (fields, codes)
userImpact: Generic LLM iteration code ("summarise the rows of any read tool") cannot work — the model has to memorise which read tool uses which collection key. Bulk-orchestration prompts grow brittle because the same workflow returns `clients`, `forms`, `statuses`, etc. from sibling calls.
description: Every read tool wraps its results in a domain-named collection key: `clients`, `forms`, `statuses`, `subclients`, `states`, `stateSubclients`, `efStatuses`, `modules`, `datapaths`, `codes`, `fields`. Only the three paginated tools (Clients/Details/Tables) ALSO emit `rows` as a canonical alias. The non-paginated tools do not — so a model that wrote `result.rows` after seeing the paginated shape will get `undefined` from StatesTools/StatusTools/etc. Worst case: `LacerteClientList` returns BOTH `rows` AND `clients` (the legacy alias) with the same content — telling the LLM the spec is inconsistent even within ONE tool.
recommendation: Canonicalize on `rows` as the primary collection key in every read tool. Keep the domain-named alias (`clients`, `forms`, …) as an additive v0.1 back-compat field with the same v0.2-removal note already on ClientsTools.cs:47-49. After P15-047 lands pagination for the seven currently-unpaginated tools, the `rows` key will already be present in all of them — the consistency win is free; just don't drop `rows` in favor of the legacy name like the current Subclients/States/Forms shape does.
rationale: R2 P15-047 paginates the seven tools but its refined recommendation explicitly preserves the legacy collection keys ("keep the legacy top-level collection key (`subclients`/`states`/`forms`/`statuses`/`rows`/`efStatuses`) … for v0.1 back-compat"). It does not require `rows` to be added — so the new shape lands inconsistent unless this finding fixes the canonical-key convention.

verdict.reasoning:
VERIFIED. Read all 9 tool files. Collection-key inconsistency is real and exactly as described:

- Paginated tools (3): ClientsTools emits BOTH `rows` AND legacy `clients` (line 52 + 60); DetailsTools emits `rows` only (line 88); TablesTools emits `rows` only (line 46).
- Unpaginated tools (7): StatesTools emits `states` (33) and `stateSubclients` (50); StatusTools emits `statuses` (32); FormsTools emits `forms` (31); SubclientsTools emits `subclients` (32); EFileTools emits `efStatuses` (61); SessionTools emits `modules` (138) and `datapaths` (154); MetadataTools emits `fields` (116) and `codes` (162).

Net: 11 distinct collection-key names across the read API. ClientsTools' double-emission (`rows` + `clients` with identical content) is genuine signal-loss — an LLM seeing the response can't tell which is canonical and may guess wrong on sibling tools.

Not covered by prior rounds: R1 has no canonical-key entry. R2's P15-047 refinedRecommendation explicitly says to "keep the legacy top-level collection key (subclients/states/forms/statuses/rows/efStatuses) + count for v0.1 back-compat" — it does not mandate `rows` as canonical, so a literal reader could ship the paginated rewrites with only the domain key (the way EFileTools.cs:61 currently looks: `new { count = rows.Count, efStatuses = rows }`).

Usability impact is real for the round-3 lens: a model writing a generic "summarize the rows of the next read call" prompt over sibling read tools currently breaks on every non-paginated tool. The fix cost is trivial — one rule, applied during the work P15-047 already requires — and the post-fix shape gives the LLM a single field name (`rows`) to reach for on every read tool, with domain aliases preserved additively for v0.1.

Not bikeshedding: cross-tool API consistency is exactly the round-3 lens, and locking in the convention now (before P15-047 lands the seven new shapes) prevents the inconsistency from getting worse. Also surfaces a subtler bug — the SessionTools/MetadataTools tools (modules/datapaths/fields/codes) are bounded collections P15-047 deliberately skips, so they'll never gain `rows` unless this finding's broader convention applies to them too.
verdict.refinedRecommendation:
Two-part fix, both sim-only, both small:

(1) Amend P15-047's refined recommendation: when paginating the seven currently-unpaginated DATA-row tools (Subclients/States/StateSubclients/Status/Forms/EFStatus + Details already done), the new envelope MUST expose `rows` as the primary collection key (the natural output of `Pagination.Page<T>().Rows`) AND keep the legacy domain-named key (`subclients`/`states`/`stateSubclients`/`statuses`/`forms`/`efStatuses`) as an additive v0.1 alias with the same v0.2-removal comment that already lives on ClientsTools.cs:47-49. This is what ClientsTools already does; DetailsTools/TablesTools currently emit `rows` only (no domain alias) — the easy unification is to also add domain aliases there for back-compat symmetry, OR leave them and document `rows` as canonical going forward.

(2) Extend the canonical-key convention to the four bounded metadata/session tools P15-047 intentionally skips (SessionTools.LacerteListModules → `modules`; LacerteListDatapaths → `datapaths`; MetadataTools.LacerteFieldAccessMap → `fields`; LacerteReturnCodes → `codes`). These don't need pagination, but they DO need to participate in the same "every read tool returns the row collection under `rows`" convention so an LLM iteration helper works uniformly. Smallest change: add `rows = <existing-collection>` alongside the domain key in each of those four tools. (Note: LacerteFieldAccessMap's `fields` is a `Dictionary<string,string>`, not a list — exempt it from this rule OR project it to `rows = [{ field, access }, …]`; pick one and document the carve-out.)

(3) Add a one-line rule to ARCHITECTURE.md tool-conventions section + ACCEPTANCE_CRITERIA.md: "Every read tool MUST expose its primary collection as `rows`. Domain-named aliases (clients/forms/…) are allowed for v0.1 back-compat but `rows` is the canonical key any new tool/consumer should target." Cross-link this rule from WrapToolHandler.cs so future tool authors see it during code review.

No tests change semantically — existing tests that read `clients`/`forms`/etc. keep working because the aliases stay additive. New convention costs ~7 lines across the codebase and removes a real friction point for LLM bulk-iteration prompts.

title: `stateAbbrev` vs `stateAbbr` — same 2-letter state filter named two different ways across write surfaces
line: DetailsTools.cs:108,207 (stateAbbr) vs FieldWriteTools.cs:48 / UpdateReturnTools.cs:59 / TablesTools.cs:27 / StatesTools.cs:24,41 / FieldWriteBulkTools.cs:73 (stateAbbrev)
userImpact: An LLM that learned `stateAbbrev` from the read/write field tools will pass `stateAbbrev: "CA"` to `lacerte_detail_write` and the SDK will silently see an empty stateAbbr (the model thought it set one). The state-residency tag goes to the federal bucket — quietly wrong on a real return.
description: Every state-filter parameter across the codebase uses `stateAbbrev` (FieldWriteTools, UpdateReturnTools, TablesTools, StatesTools, FieldWriteBulkTools.BulkWriteEntry, EVERY session-manager signature). The single outlier is DetailsTools.LacerteDetailWrite, which calls it `stateAbbr` (no `ev` suffix) — both as the parameter name and as the `field` value in its validation error context. The DBF schema docstring in StatesTools.cs:21 even spells the column "StateAbbrev" — so the data-model authority is `stateAbbrev` and DetailsTools is the typo.
recommendation: Rename `stateAbbr` → `stateAbbrev` in DetailsTools.cs:108 (parameter), :127 (call site), :134 (`StateAbbr:` is the DetailRow record property, leave that), :157 (validator param), :201/207-209 (validator body + error context). Add a one-call wrapper on the manager (or just keep the rename local — the DetailRow property `StateAbbr` belongs to the SDK detail-row shape, but the operator-facing parameter and error `field` key should match the rest of the surface).
rationale: Cross-tool consistency was not surfaced in either prior round. The two prior rounds focused on response shape and pagination, not parameter naming alignment.

verdict.reasoning:
CONFIRMED, but the finding's rationale is partially wrong about the data model.

Read-the-code verdict per cited locations:
- DetailsTools.cs:108, 117 (sig), 127 (validator call), 134 (DetailRow ctor), 157 (validator sig), 201, 207, 209 (validator body) — parameter is `stateAbbr`, no -ev suffix.
- FieldWriteTools.cs:48 — `stateAbbrev`.
- UpdateReturnTools.cs:59 — `stateAbbrev`.
- TablesTools.cs:27 — `stateAbbrev`.
- StatesTools.cs:24, 41 — `stateAbbrev`.
- FieldWriteBulkTools.cs:73 (BulkWriteEntry.StateAbbrev), 197 — `stateAbbrev`.
- BridgeInputValidation.cs:265, 508, ValidateStateAbbrev helper — `stateAbbrev`.
- Schema/Tables.cs:39, 41 — Tables.cs describes the DATA3/4 filter as "StateAbbrev".
- LacerteSessionManager.cs:721, 1497, 1504, 1684 — `stateAbbrev` / `StateAbbrev` / `StateAbbrevRequired`.

The finding's claim "the data-model authority is `stateAbbrev`" is WRONG in one respect: SqlTemplates.cs:258 shows the detail-file column is literally `StateAbbr` (no -ev) and DetailRow.cs (SimulationStore.cs:51) carries `StateAbbr` to match. So there ARE genuinely two different underlying DBF column names: detail files use `StateAbbr`, DATA3/4 tables use `StateAbbrev`. DetailsTools' `stateAbbr` parameter naming faithfully mirrors the detail-file column.

BUT — and this is why the finding still lands — operator/LLM doesn't know or care about this Intuit-side naming quirk. Across 6 tool surfaces, 5 say `stateAbbrev` and 1 says `stateAbbr`. An LLM doing in-context learning from FieldWriteTools/UpdateReturnTools/TablesTools/StatesTools/FieldWriteBulkTools (the heavily-used surfaces) will form a `stateAbbrev` prior. When it calls `lacerte_detail_write` with `stateAbbrev: "CA"`, the MCP framework binds parameters by name — `stateAbbr` stays default (null/empty), the extra `stateAbbrev` is silently ignored, and a state-residency detail row gets written into the federal bucket with no error. On a real return this is a quiet bookkeeping defect on a tax filing.

Verified NOT a duplicate. Prior `stateAbbr` mentions in audit-findings.json (lines 1086-1196) and audit-findings-r2.json (lines 45, 871-872, 973) reference the validation logic's "field": "stateAbbr" error context or the regex name `_rxStateAbbr` — none of them flag the cross-surface parameter-name divergence as a usability issue.

Meaningfully improves UX because: silent ignored-param bug on a write tool is exactly the trust-erosion class — operator can't audit because the MCP call returned status=1. The fix is small (rename DetailsTools.LacerteDetailWrite's `stateAbbr` parameter to `stateAbbrev`, keep internal DetailRow.StateAbbr field as-is since that maps to the DBF column).
verdict.refinedRecommendation:
Make `lacerte_detail_write`'s state parameter accept what the rest of the surface uses. Two-line change with one small follow-on:

1) DetailsTools.cs:108 — rename the parameter `stateAbbr` to `stateAbbrev`. Update its `[Description]` to: `"State abbreviation for the row's tax bucket — 2-letter postal code if non-empty (validated against ^[A-Z]{2}$). Maps to the DBF column StateAbbr internally."` (mentioning the internal name preempts the LLM wondering why responses come back with `StateAbbr` while requests take `stateAbbrev`).

2) DetailsTools.cs:127 — update the call site `ValidateDetailWrite(series, code, stateAbbrev, tsj)`.

3) DetailsTools.cs:134 — keep `StateAbbr: stateAbbrev ?? ""` (the DetailRow property name maps to the DBF column and must stay; this is the one place the rename should NOT propagate).

4) DetailsTools.cs:157 — rename the validator's local param to `stateAbbrev`.

5) DetailsTools.cs:201, 207, 209 — update body to use `stateAbbrev` for both the variable reference and the `["field"] = "stateAbbrev"` error context, and tweak the reason string to: `"stateAbbrev must be empty OR a 2-letter uppercase postal code (e.g. CA, NY)."` (matches the operator-facing param name, not the internal DBF column).

6) Add one DetailsToolsTests test: `LacerteDetailWrite_StateAbbrevParam_BindsCorrectly` that invokes the tool with `stateAbbrev: "CA"` and asserts the written DetailRow has `StateAbbr == "CA"` — this pins the rename so a future drift won't regress it.

Do NOT add a backward-compat alias. The current `stateAbbr` parameter has never appeared in any documented operator workflow (it's only been LLM-discoverable for ~weeks since the tool landed), and silently accepting two names long-term keeps the LLM-confusion alive. Rename clean.

Verify off-Windows: `dotnet build src/LacertMCP.sln` + `dotnet test src/LacertMCP.Tests` should stay green at 1006+/1016. Sim-only fix, no Lacerte install needed.

title: Write tools split parameter name: `field` (single-write) vs `fieldName` (bulk-write) for the exact same value
userImpact: An LLM that drafts a single-call to `lacerte_field_write` then refactors to `lacerte_field_write_bulk` for a batch will copy-paste `field:` into every entry and the bulk call will reject every row with a NullRef or empty-field error. The user sees "all 50 rows failed" with no clear cause.
description: FieldWriteTools.LacerteFieldWrite and UpdateReturnTools.LacerteUpdateReturn take a parameter literally called `field`. The bulk wrapper FieldWriteBulkTools.BulkWriteEntry uses `FieldName` (which serializes as `fieldName`). The bulk tool's description even references "`{clientNumber, fieldName, value, subClientID?, stateAbbrev?}`" verbatim — so a model that read both descriptions sees the rename explicitly with no explanation. The bulk tool's per-row response then echoes `fieldName` too, but the single-write response (via FieldWriteCore.cs:59) echoes `field`. Two write tools, one concept, two names.
recommendation: Rename `BulkWriteEntry.FieldName` to `Field` (will serialize as `field`), update FieldWriteBulkTools.cs:63 description, :80 entries-array description (`{clientNumber, field, value, subClientID?, stateAbbrev?}`), :85 idempotency-key shape (`{prefix}-{clientNumber}-{field}`), and the per-item response shape on lines 153, 207, 220, 242. Alternatively rename the single-write `field` parameter to `fieldName` everywhere — but that breaks every prompt in WorkflowPrompts.cs which spells it `field`. The cheaper direction is bulk → `field`.
rationale: Cross-tool naming inconsistency was not surfaced before. FieldWriteBulkTools landed as P15-008 in the post-round-1 wave and introduced the new name without any audit catching the drift.

verdict.reasoning: CONFIRMED at the code level. FieldWriteTools.cs:45 ('field'), UpdateReturnTools.cs:56 ('field'), and FieldWriteCore (the shared body) all use 'field' as the canonical parameter name. FieldWriteBulkTools.cs ships 'FieldName' (line 64) as the per-row property, which serializes to 'fieldName'. The tool description literally documents the rename twice — line 80 ('{clientNumber, fieldName, value, subClientID?, stateAbbrev?}') and line 85 (idempotency-key shape '{prefix}-{clientNumber}-{fieldName}') — and the per-row response objects on lines 154, 171, 207, 220, 242 echo 'fieldName' back to the caller, while the single-write response goes through FieldWriteCore and presumably echoes 'field'. An LLM that drafts with the single-write tool then switches to bulk will reasonably copy 'field:' into entry rows; the System.Text.Json default binder will silently leave BulkWriteEntry.FieldName as string.Empty, and every row will be rejected once it hits WriteField/AssertWritable. Operator sees 'all rows failed' with no obvious cause — the bulk tool's batch-error envelope makes the silent name-mismatch even harder to debug than a single-call failure. This is not a duplicate: audit-findings.json has no matches for fieldName/FieldName/BulkWriteEntry, and the only r2 hits are inside P15-008 (the original ask for a bulk tool) and P15-017 (unrelated wire-redaction split). P15-008's refined recommendation actually proposed a different schema entirely (one shared 'field' at the tool level + per-row BulkWriteTarget with no field property); the shipping implementation diverged to a per-row 'fieldName' to support multi-field batches, but no prior audit caught the resulting cross-tool drift. Fix is small (rename property + update 4 description strings + update per-row response shape on 4 lines + idempotency-key docstring), in-session, and lands the consistency before more prompts/tests crystallize around 'fieldName'.
verdict.refinedRecommendation:
Rename `BulkWriteEntry.FieldName` → `Field` in FieldWriteBulkTools.cs:64 so it serializes as `field`, matching the single-write tools. Concrete edits (one file, ~8 lines):

1. Line 63-64: rename property `FieldName` to `Field` and update its [Description] to match the single-write tool verbatim ("Field name (e.g. C1_1, C2_15, C4_G3). Must be a writable field in the access map.").

2. Line 37 (XML doc): change `'$"{idempotencyKey}-{clientNumber}-{fieldName}"'` and the prose "Suffixing with both clientNumber and fieldName" to say `field`.

3. Line 77 (tool description): change `each row uses '{prefix}-{clientNumber}-{fieldName}'` to `'{prefix}-{clientNumber}-{field}'`.

4. Line 80 ([Description] on `entries`): change `{clientNumber, fieldName, value, subClientID?, stateAbbrev?}` → `{clientNumber, field, value, subClientID?, stateAbbrev?}`.

5. Line 85 ([Description] on `idempotencyKey`): change `'{prefix}-{clientNumber}-{fieldName}'` → `'{prefix}-{clientNumber}-{field}'`.

6. Lines 153-154, 170-171, 206-207, 219-220, 241-242: change every `fieldName = entry?.FieldName` (and the null-row version) to `field = entry?.Field` so the per-row response echoes `field` — matches the single-write response shape.

7. Line 187 + 194 + 196: usages `entry.FieldName` and `$"...-{entry.FieldName}"` simply update to `entry.Field` — pure rename, behavior identical.

Add one FieldWriteBulkToolsTests case that JSON-deserializes a payload with `"field":"C1_1"` (not `fieldName`) and asserts it round-trips — this locks the LLM-facing wire name and catches any future drift in CI. Update WorkflowPrompts.cs if its `lacerte_bulk_field_update` prompt body references either name (grep confirms it does NOT currently mention `fieldName` since it predates P15-008, but the prompt should be touched to recommend the bulk tool with the `field` key explicitly).

Why this direction (bulk → field) not the reverse (single → fieldName): WorkflowPrompts.cs and ARCHITECTURE.md both use `field` throughout, and renaming the single-write parameter would break every shipped prompt — also `field` is the shorter, more conventional name used in the SDK Developer Instructions. Two write tools with one canonical name eliminates the silent-failure trap for LLMs refactoring single→bulk.

title: Module parameter typed as `char` in one tool, `string` in two others — JSON binding traps the LLM
userImpact: An LLM calling `lacerte_field_access_map` with `module: "I"` (the natural JSON spelling, learned from every OTHER tool) hits the .NET JSON binder's char-from-string path — works on the modern System.Text.Json but is famously fragile (some MCP hosts deserialize char as int / first-char of array / etc.). The same value typed `string module` in SessionTools just works. Confusing inconsistency that surfaces only when the model picks the "wrong" tool first.
description: MetadataTools.LacerteFieldAccessMap (line 34) declares `char module` as the parameter type. SessionTools.LacerteSetContext (line 72) and SessionTools.LacerteCanUseNewApis (line 102) declare `string module` (then both immediately validate `.Length == 1` and take `module[0]`). The parameter description for all three is identical: "Single-character module code: I/C/P/S/F/R/T/N/B." The schema (Modules.GetByChar) takes a `char`. The chosen surface is therefore a model-facing implementation leak — and the divergence means JSON-Schema generators that key off the parameter type emit a 1-char string constraint for one tool and a free string for the others.
recommendation: Change MetadataTools.cs:34 to `string module` and add the same Length-1 guard SessionTools uses (lines 76-85). Mirrors the existing two tools, eliminates the char-binding fragility, and makes the JSON-Schema for all three tools identical (a one-char string).
rationale: Type-level cross-tool inconsistency was not surfaced in either prior round. Both rounds focused on naming and response shape, not parameter type alignment.

verdict.reasoning:
Verified directly against source. MetadataTools.cs:34 declares `[Description("Single-character module code: I/C/P/S/F/R/T/N/B.")] char module`, while SessionTools.cs:72 and :102 declare the SAME parameter with the SAME description as `string module` (then guard `module.Length == 1` and pass `module[0]` to the schema layer). All three tools end up calling code that expects a `char`, but the model-facing parameter type differs.

Why this is a real usability bug, not bikeshedding:
1. The MCP SDK (ModelContextProtocol 0.3.0-preview.4, confirmed in csproj) emits JSON-Schema from the C# parameter type. `char` and `string` produce different schemas — the LLM sees one tool whose `module` field has a different shape than the other two with identical descriptions. That divergence on the schema surface is exactly what makes a multi-tool API feel slapped together, and it's the kind of subtle thing the model can latch onto when it picks the wrong tool first.
2. System.Text.Json char-from-string binding works on modern runtimes but is historically fragile — different MCP host implementations (Claude Desktop, Cursor, Windsurf, third-party) wrap deserialization differently, and char primitives are an off-the-happy-path corner. The SessionTools path of string+length-1-guard is the project's own preferred idiom (used in 2 of 3 sites); the third site is an oversight.
3. The three tools were clearly meant to be uniform — identical Description text proves intent. The type drift is a model-facing implementation leak.

Not a duplicate of any prior task:
- P14-058 (round 1) touched MetadataTools.cs for moduleName casing only — explicitly did not change the parameter type.
- P15-047 (round 2) grouped MetadataTools.cs into an unbounded-result-set pagination finding.
- No prior round audited parameter-type alignment across tools. Both rounds focused on response shape, naming, and remediation strings — not parameter declarations.

The fix is in-session, sim-friendly, ~6 lines (change `char` to `string`, add the same null/length guard SessionTools.cs:76-85 already uses, adjust the `Modules.GetByChar(module)` call to `Modules.GetByChar(module[0])`, and update `["module"] = module.ToString()` to `["module"] = module ?? ""`). MetadataToolsTests.cs at lines 20/33/42/51 passes `'I'`/`'Z'`/`'I'` (chars) directly — these would need conversion to strings, but that's a one-character edit per test. Build stays green.

Meaningfully improves UX: the metadata tool is the one an LLM hits first to discover field-access policy before attempting writes — failure or schema-confusion at the discovery step blocks the entire write flow. Aligning the three tools' parameter types means schema-driven tool selection is uniform across the lacerte_field_access_map / lacerte_set_context / lacerte_can_use_new_apis trio, which is the only group that takes a single-char module input.

title: README ships stale prompts table — `lacerte_csv_intake` exists in code but is invisible to operators
userImpact: An operator scanning the README for guided workflows sees only three prompts (`lacerte_client_intake`, `lacerte_review_ef_status`, `lacerte_bulk_field_update`). The fourth registered prompt — `lacerte_csv_intake` — ships in WorkflowPrompts.cs lines 240-305 and is the single most operator-relevant prompt because it maps to REQUIREMENTS §1.3 (Tax-Organizer CSV bootstrapping), but a tax pro reading the README would never know it exists and would re-derive the workflow by hand or chain `lacerte_client_intake` per row.
description: README line 158 says 'Three first-class MCP prompts' and lists three rows. The `[McpServerPromptType]` class actually carries FOUR `[McpServerPrompt(Name=...)]` methods: `lacerte_client_intake`, `lacerte_review_ef_status`, `lacerte_bulk_field_update`, AND `lacerte_csv_intake`. The CSV one is the only prompt directly addressing the most common operator workflow (bulk client onboarding from a Tax Organizer export) and it is silently absent from both the count and the table. Same staleness in the task list reference in line 166 ('Canonical step lists live in...').
recommendation: Update README line 158 to 'Four first-class MCP prompts' and append a row to the table: `| `lacerte_csv_intake` | Bulk-onboard clients from a CSV / Tax-Organizer export with one-shot column→field mapping, per-row idempotency, stop-on-first-error. | `sourceLabel?: string`, `rowCount: int = 0` |`. Add a check to the McpDiscoveryRoundtripTests (which already exists per the grep — `src/LacertMCP.Tests/Integration/McpDiscoveryRoundtripTests.cs`) that asserts the README prompts table row count equals the count of `[McpServerPrompt]` methods discovered at runtime, so this drift fails CI the next time a prompt is added without README sync.
