title: `LacerteEfStatus` invalid-date throws `SyntheticStatusCodes.InvalidDataPath` — operator sees 'data path' error for a date typo
userImpact: Operator (or the LLM relaying the operator's intent) passes `sinceUtc="yesterday"` or `sinceUtc="2024/05/30"`. They get back error code 9002 InvalidDataPath with a message about the data path. The error context dict carries the real reason ('sinceUtc must be an ISO-8601 date'), but the visible status code is for an entirely different failure mode. An LLM looking up the code in `lacerte_return_codes` reads remediation about 'verify LACERTE_DATA_ROOT' — completely wrong, sends the operator on a wild-goose chase.
description: EFileTools.cs:50 throws `new LacerteSDKError(SyntheticStatusCodes.InvalidDataPath, ...)` when the date string fails to parse. `SyntheticStatusCodes.InvalidDataPath` is documented as 'invalid data path' — wholly unrelated to date formatting. There is no synthetic 'InvalidArgument' or 'InvalidDateFormat' code being used here.
recommendation: Either introduce `SyntheticStatusCodes.InvalidArgument` (a general 'caller-supplied value malformed' code), or use the existing `StatusCodes.InValidClientName` pattern that other tools use for argument-validation failures (e.g. `SessionTools` uses it for bad module input). Better: add an `InvalidArgument` synthetic in the 9xxx range and migrate all argument-validation error throws onto it so the LLM has one canonical 'you passed me bad data' code to recognize.
rationale: Round 2 'DBxError remediations say...' touched error-code remediation text, but no round flagged a tool throwing a code whose *category* is wrong. This is a tool-level wrong-code bug, not a remediation-text gap.

verdict.reasoning: Verified at EFileTools.cs:50-56 — the date-parse failure throws `LacerteSDKError(SyntheticStatusCodes.InvalidDataPath, ...)`. Cross-checked SyntheticStatusCodes.cs: code 9013 is documented as "lacerte_set_context rejected the dataPath — relative path, '..' traversal, control characters, UNC without LACERTE_ALLOW_UNC=1, or outside LACERTE_DATA_ROOT" with remediation "Pass an absolute local path under the Lacerte install root (e.g. C:\\Lacerte\\24Tax\\IData). Set LACERTE_ALLOW_UNC=1 to permit \\\\server\\share paths." That remediation is entirely wrong for a date-format failure. There is no `InvalidArgument` synthetic code in the codebase (grep confirms zero matches). The reason context carries the real failure ("sinceUtc must be an ISO-8601 date"), but `lacerte_return_codes` and `MetadataTools.LacerteReturnCodes` only look at `statusName` + `remediation` — both wrong here. Prior audit P15-010 (round 2) marked [x] complete and its refinedRecommendation actually said "reject anything else with `LacerteSDKError(SyntheticStatusCodes.InvalidArgument, ...)`" — but the implementer never added `InvalidArgument` and substituted the unrelated `InvalidDataPath`. So this is a real implementation gap from r2, not a duplicate of any prior verdict. Not bikeshedding: an LLM lookup on 9013 will send the operator to verify LACERTE_DATA_ROOT / install paths — completely off-trail from a yyyy-MM-dd typo. The fix is small and would noticeably reduce a real diagnostic miss. Note that EFileTools is currently the only call site for this gap (BridgeInputValidation.cs's other InvalidDataPath uses are legitimate dataPath validations), so a one-tool fix or one-new-code fix both work.
verdict.refinedRecommendation: Add `SyntheticStatusCodes.InvalidArgument = 9016` (next free in the 9001-9099 validation range, after `FieldWriteInvalid = 9015`) with StatusTable entry: Description "Caller-supplied argument was malformed (parse failure, out-of-range value, or shape mismatch). The error context carries an `argument` key naming the bad parameter and a `reason` key explaining the rejection." / Remediation "Read the `reason` in the error context, fix the named argument, and retry. This is a caller-input bug, not a Lacerte / data-path / context problem — do not change LACERTE_DATA_ROOT, lacerte_set_context, or registration in response to this code." Then change EFileTools.cs:50-56 to throw `SyntheticStatusCodes.InvalidArgument` with context `{ ["argument"] = "sinceUtc", ["value"] = sinceUtc, ["reason"] = "sinceUtc must be an ISO-8601 date (yyyy-MM-dd, yyyy-MM-ddTHH:mm:ss, or yyyy-MM-ddTHH:mm:ssZ)." }` so the LLM sees a self-describing argument name plus the accepted formats spelled out. Add a fast unit test in EFileToolsTests that asserts (a) bad-date input throws code 9016 (not 9013), (b) the error context contains an `argument` key equal to `sinceUtc`, and (c) the remediation string for 9016 in StatusTable does NOT contain the substring "data path" — so future regressions to the wrong code are caught. Optional follow-up (separate task): audit other argument-validation throw-sites that currently borrow unrelated codes (e.g. anywhere a `parse failure on caller input` reaches for whatever-is-handy) and migrate them to 9016 so the LLM has a single canonical "you passed bad data" code to recognize across the whole tool surface.

title: `LacerteFieldAccessMap` uses `char module` while every other tool uses `string module` — different MCP wire shape for the same concept
userImpact: MCP tool schema is JSON Schema. `char` typically serializes as a 1-char string but the binding behavior varies by SDK version and host: some clients reject single-character JSON-string for a `char` param (passing `"I"` may fail with 'expected integer'), others coerce. Meanwhile `LacerteSetContext`, `LacerteCanUseNewApis`, and `LacerteFieldWriteBulk` all accept `string module` and validate length internally. An LLM that learned the working call shape from one tool cannot reliably reuse it on `LacerteFieldAccessMap`.
description: `MetadataTools.LacerteFieldAccessMap` parameter declaration: `[Description("Single-character module code: I/C/P/S/F/R/T/N/B.")] char module`. Every other tool taking the same concept declares `string module` and either takes `module[0]` after a length check (SessionTools.cs:76, 105) or stores the char in a BulkWriteEntry. The schema generator produces different JSON Schema for `char` vs `string`, and the LLM-facing description gives no hint that this one is special.
recommendation: Change to `string module` and apply the same `module.Length != 1` validation used in SessionTools.cs:76. The internal lookup remains `module[0]`. Now the parameter type, description, and validation match the rest of the surface, and the LLM can copy the call shape from any module-taking tool to this one.
rationale: Not covered in either prior round; both audits skipped over parameter primitive-type consistency. This is a subtle wire-shape divergence that only matters for LLM call-uniformity.

verdict.reasoning: Verified at MetadataTools.cs:34 — `char module` is genuinely the only tool parameter in src/LacertMCP.Server/Tools/ using `char` for the module concept. All sibling tools (SessionTools.LacerteSetContext line 72, LacerteCanUseNewApis line 102) declare `string module` and apply a `Length != 1` validation, then index `module[0]` internally. No matching finding in either audit-findings.json or audit-findings-r2.json — the only prior mention of LacerteFieldAccessMap was r1 covering routing-through-session-manager and r2 explicitly skipping it for pagination work; the `char` parameter type was missed in both rounds. The inconsistency is real and user-facing: the MCP-SDK JSON-Schema generator emits a different shape for `char` than `string` (typically `{type:string,minLength:1,maxLength:1}` or even occasionally a single-codepoint integer in older binders), and the LLM-facing description gives no signal that this single tool is special. The recommended fix is mechanical (~4 lines) and unifies wire shape + validation across all module-taking tools. The finding's "expected integer" claim somewhat overstates the binder failure mode (modern MCP C# SDK does coerce single-char strings to char in most paths), but the underlying inconsistency and the LLM-call-uniformity argument are valid — and `LacerteFieldAccessMap` is a frequently-recommended pre-write tool, so call-shape friction here is felt. Also caught a subtle error-context divergence: line 47 emits `module.ToString()` while SessionTools line 82 emits raw `module` — same key, different serializer paths, another tiny cross-tool inconsistency the fix collapses.
verdict.refinedRecommendation:
Convert `MetadataTools.LacerteFieldAccessMap`'s `char module` parameter to `string module` to match SessionTools.LacerteSetContext (line 72) and LacerteCanUseNewApis (line 102), giving every module-taking tool the same wire shape, description phrasing, and validation pattern. Specific changes in MetadataTools.cs:

1. Line 34: change `char module` to `string module`. Update the description to match SessionTools' canonical phrasing: `[Description("Single-character module code: one of I, C, P, S, F, R, T, N, B.")] string module`.

2. After line 36 (before the WrapToolHandler.Run body opens at 38), add the same guard SessionTools uses, throwing the same structured error:
```csharp
if (string.IsNullOrEmpty(module) || module.Length != 1)
{
    throw new LacerteSDKError(
        StatusCodes.InValidClientName,
        new Dictionary<string, object?>
        {
            ["module"] = module,
            ["reason"] = "module must be a single character (I/C/P/S/F/R/T/N/B).",
        });
}
```
Put this INSIDE the WrapToolHandler.Run lambda (not before it) so the error gets the standard envelope.

3. Replace every internal use of `module` with `module[0]`:
   - line 40: `Modules.GetByChar(module[0])`
   - line 88: `FieldAccessMapLoader.GetFieldAccess(module[0], table, f, year)`
   - line 104: `FieldAccessMapLoader.GetFieldAccess(module[0], table, f, year)`

4. Lines 47 + 111: drop the now-redundant `.ToString()` calls — `["module"] = module` and `module = module` (the response object already used `module.ToString()` to coerce the char back).

5. Tests: add one xUnit case `LacerteFieldAccessMap_RejectsMultiCharModule_Throws9` in MetadataToolsTests mirroring SessionToolsTests' equivalent case, and update any existing MetadataToolsTests that pass a `char` literal to pass a string instead. Grep MetadataToolsTests.cs for `'I'` / `'C'` / etc. as call args.

6. README tool table: update the `lacerte_field_access_map` row's `module` parameter type if it's currently rendered as `char` — it should read `string` to match the new signature.

Cost: ~30 min including test + README. Closes the only cross-tool parameter-primitive inconsistency on the module concept and removes one subtle case where an LLM might fail to copy a working call shape from SetContext to FieldAccessMap.

title: AddMcpServer() never sets server name/version — MCP host UI shows the assembly default with no SemVer or branding
userImpact: In Claude Desktop's MCP server list, Cursor's status bar, and Windsurf's MCP panel, this server registers as a bare 'LacertMCP.Server' (or whatever the SDK falls back to) with no version string visible to the operator. When an operator has 5+ MCP servers configured and one is misbehaving, there is no quick way to confirm 'I'm running v0.1.0 vs v0.2.0' from the host UI — they must `lacerte-mcp status` from a shell. Worse, the InitializeResult.serverInfo field is what the LLM client uses to print 'connected to {server.name} v{server.version}' in logs — bug reports back from operators won't carry the version stamp.
description: Program.cs:81-86 chains `.AddMcpServer().WithStdioServerTransport().WithToolsFromAssembly().WithPromptsFromAssembly()` with no `.WithServerInfo("lacerte-mcp", "0.1.0")` (or the equivalent configure-options call). The MCP `initialize` response's `serverInfo` field is therefore populated by the SDK default — typically the assembly name with no version. The project already has a clean version source (Directory.Build.props lines 27-36 stamp Version=0.1.0 + an optional git SHA into AssemblyInformationalVersionAttribute, surfaced via EnvValidator.SafeAssemblyVersion() in the startup banner). The startup banner already does the right thing for stderr — but the MCP wire-level serverInfo, the canonical place hosts look, is empty. The constant is `"Lacerte MCP"` per README line 1 and `lacerte-mcp` per the CLI binary name — pick one and put it on the wire so the host UI matches the operator's mental model.
recommendation: In Program.cs, after `AddMcpServer()` add `.WithServerInfo(new Implementation { Name = "lacerte-mcp", Version = SafeAssemblyVersion() })` (or the SDK's idiomatic API — check the McpServerBuilderExtensions surface in the 0.3.0-preview.4 package; the option may also be exposed via `configureOptions => opts.ServerInfo = ...`). Pull SafeAssemblyVersion from EnvValidator into a shared `Diagnostics/BuildInfo.cs` helper (the file already exists per the directory listing) so the banner and serverInfo cannot drift. Extend McpDiscoveryRoundtripTests to capture `client.ServerInfo` after CreateAsync and assert Name == 'lacerte-mcp' and Version starts with '0.1.0' — pins both the wire-up and the version-bump discipline. No SDK or Windows dependency; pure off-Windows fix.
rationale: Both prior rounds verified the startup banner and the CLI status output emit a version; neither checked whether the value reaches the MCP wire-level serverInfo field. The SDK does not auto-populate this from the assembly attributes — it's an explicit configure call that's silently missing.

verdict.reasoning: Verified by reading C:/Users/VR/Projects/LacertMCP/src/LacertMCP.Server/Program.cs lines 81-86: `builder.Services.AddMcpServer().WithStdioServerTransport().WithToolsFromAssembly().WithPromptsFromAssembly();` — no ServerInfo configuration anywhere in the chain. Grep across the entire src tree for `WithServerInfo|ServerInfo|Implementation` returns zero source hits (the three matches are unrelated: EditionDetection.cs, ILacerteBridge.cs, and McpDiscoveryRoundtripTests.cs all use the word in different contexts, none set the MCP serverInfo). The SDK API exists and is documented: ModelContextProtocol.Core 0.3.0-preview.4 XML docs confirm `McpServerOptions.ServerInfo` of type `Implementation` with Name/Title/Version, and its own remarks say "It's displayed in client logs and can be used for debugging and compatibility checks." `IMcpClient.ServerInfo` is the matching client-side property, which the existing McpDiscoveryRoundtripTests can already assert against. Prior-audit check: r1 (71 entries) and r2 (78 entries) both grepped for ServerInfo/Implementation/serverInfo/InitializeResult — zero hits. P14-040 added BuildInfo.cs for the status-JSON path and startup banner but explicitly did not touch the wire-level serverInfo. The `lacerte-mcp` vs `Lacerte MCP` naming inconsistency noted in the finding is also real (README says "Lacerte MCP", binary is `lacerte-mcp.exe`) — picking one for the wire is a legit canonicalization. One implementation refinement: the SDK does NOT expose a `.WithServerInfo(...)` extension method in 0.3.0-preview.4 — the actual surface is the configureOptions overload of AddMcpServer, i.e. `AddMcpServer(opts => opts.ServerInfo = new Implementation { ... })`. The finding's recommendation hedges with "or the equivalent configure-options call" so it's already directionally correct. Severity is appropriately medium — single-operator usage means few concurrent MCP servers in the host UI, but the version stamp does materially help the bug-report case (operator copy/pastes Claude Desktop's connection log), the fix is ~3 lines, and the BuildInfo single-source-of-truth angle prevents banner-vs-wire drift forever. Meets the round-3 "total perfection" bar without being bikeshedding.
verdict.refinedRecommendation: In C:/Users/VR/Projects/LacertMCP/src/LacertMCP.Server/Program.cs replace the bare `.AddMcpServer()` call at line 82 with the configure-options overload: `.AddMcpServer(opts => { opts.ServerInfo = new ModelContextProtocol.Protocol.Implementation { Name = "lacerte-mcp", Version = LacertMCP.Server.Diagnostics.BuildInfo.Version, Title = "Lacerte MCP" }; })` (Title is the human-readable variant per the SDK's Implementation type — README's "Lacerte MCP" goes here, the canonical `lacerte-mcp` identifier goes in Name). Note: the SDK 0.3.0-preview.4 does NOT expose a fluent `.WithServerInfo(...)` extension method — `McpServerOptions.ServerInfo` is set inside the AddMcpServer configureOptions lambda. Verify by inspecting the McpServerBuilderExtensions surface before coding: `grep -E "WithServerInfo|McpServerBuilderExtensions" C:/Users/VR/.nuget/packages/modelcontextprotocol.core/0.3.0-preview.4/lib/netstandard2.0/ModelContextProtocol.Core.xml` — if no WithServerInfo entry exists, use the configureOptions form as above. BuildInfo.cs already exists at C:/Users/VR/Projects/LacertMCP/src/LacertMCP.Server/Diagnostics/BuildInfo.cs and is the single source of truth (no helper extraction needed — the startup banner already pulls from it transitively via EnvValidator). Extend the existing C:/Users/VR/Projects/LacertMCP/src/LacertMCP.Tests/Integration/McpDiscoveryRoundtripTests.cs (which already exposes `IMcpClient`) with one additional test method: `[Fact] public async Task ServerInfo_Carries_Name_And_Version()` — after `StartServerAndConnectClientAsync`, assert `Assert.NotNull(client.ServerInfo); Assert.Equal("lacerte-mcp", client.ServerInfo.Name); Assert.False(string.IsNullOrEmpty(client.ServerInfo.Version)); Assert.StartsWith("0.", client.ServerInfo.Version);` — pins the wire-up AND the version-stamp discipline. The StartsWith("0.") rather than equals "0.1.0" lets the test survive minor version bumps without churn while still catching the case where Version is empty or defaults to "1.0.0.0". Add a one-line note to HANDOFF.md "Files added / changed" and bump the McpDiscoveryRoundtripTests class comment to mention "serverInfo wire field" alongside the discovery-seam coverage. Pure off-Windows fix; no Lacerte/Windows/COM dependency.

title: dataPath parameter example shows '"C:\\\\Lacerte\\\\24Tax\\\\IData"' — LLM faithfully copies the doubled backslashes into actual calls
userImpact: The compiled string the MCP client sees in the lacerte_set_context schema is 'Absolute path to a Lacerte data folder (e.g. "C:\\Lacerte\\24Tax\\IData").' — a Windows path with DOUBLED backslashes, which is the C# source author's escape leaking through to the wire. Claude Sonnet/Opus will recognize and de-escape, but smaller models and Cursor's local model frequently mimic the example verbatim and call lacerte_set_context with dataPath='C:\\Lacerte\\24Tax\\IData' — which Windows then resolves as a relative-ish path that fails Directory.Exists and triggers a InvalidDataPath 9006 error. Worse, the resulting error context includes the doubled-backslash path, and the LLM doubles down on the wrong format on retry.
description: SessionTools.cs:70 contains `[Description("Absolute path to a Lacerte data folder (e.g. \"C:\\\\Lacerte\\\\24Tax\\\\IData\").")] string dataPath`. The C# string literal `\\\\` compiles to `\\` (two backslashes) — meaning the wire-visible example is `"C:\\Lacerte\\24Tax\\IData"`. The README's matching example uses single backslashes (line 59: `"C:\\Lacerte\\24data"` in the JSON config), so the LLM gets contradictory signals. The author clearly intended a single-backslash Windows path (which is what Lacerte actually uses); the doubled form is a C#-source-only artifact that escaped to the schema. The same bug doesn't exist in CreateClientTools or any other path-typed param — only the most-frequently-called lacerte_set_context has it.
recommendation: In SessionTools.cs:70 change the [Description] to `[Description("Absolute path to a Lacerte data folder (e.g. C:\\Lacerte\\24Tax\\IData).")]` — drop the inner escaped quotes and reduce `\\\\` (4 chars → 2 chars in source → 1 backslash on the wire). The resulting wire string becomes 'Absolute path to a Lacerte data folder (e.g. C:\\Lacerte\\24Tax\\IData).' which renders to the LLM as 'C:\Lacerte\24Tax\IData' — the path the operator's actual Lacerte install has on disk. Add a one-line assertion in SessionToolsTests (or McpDiscoveryRoundtripTests for an over-the-wire pin) that fetches the lacerte_set_context tool descriptor, locates the dataPath parameter description, and asserts the count of `\\\\` (4 chars) sequences is 0 — pins the regression. Audit-grep the rest of the project for `\\\\\\\\` (8 chars in source) inside [Description] attributes to catch any siblings; only this one came up in the spot-check.
rationale: C# escape doubling vs JSON-on-the-wire is a class of bug that prior audits' UX-focused lens didn't surface — they read the schema as a human and mentally de-doubled. The LLM doesn't; smaller models in Cursor/Windsurf will copy the example char-for-char into the call payload.

verdict.reasoning: Verified by reading SessionTools.cs:70. The source literal `\"C:\\\\Lacerte\\\\24Tax\\\\IData\"` compiles to the .NET string `\"C:\\Lacerte\\24Tax\\IData\"` (literal double-backslashes wrapped in literal quotes). After JSON serialization + MCP client JSON deserialization, the LLM sees the parameter description containing `\"C:\\\\Lacerte\\\\24Tax\\\\IData\"` (doubled backslashes inside quotes). Direct comparison with line 142 of the same file confirms the inconsistency: `LacerteListDataPaths` uses `\\\\Lacerte` (single backslash on the wire) in its [Description], while `LacerteSetContext` uses `\\\\\\\\Lacerte` (double backslash on the wire). README.md:59 and 91, REGRESSION_CHECKLIST.md, all Bridge/Odbc tests, PathValidation.cs, SyntheticStatusCodes.cs, and ConnectionStringBuilder.cs all use the single-backslash form (`C:\\Lacerte\\24data` or `C:\\Lacerte\\24Tax\\IData`) — confirming the doubled form in SessionTools.cs:70 is a typo/escape-leak, not intentional. Audit findings r1 + r2 do not contain this — verified via grep. Impact is real and consequential: lacerte_set_context is the mandatory first tool call (no other tool works without an active session context), so this is the very first description the LLM reads when wiring up a session. Smaller models (Cursor local, lesser providers) frequently mimic example formatting verbatim. A doubled-backslash dataPath fails PathValidation.IsAbsolute / Directory.Exists, producing 9006 InvalidDataPath on the operator's first interaction with the MCP server. The McpDiscoveryRoundtripTests infrastructure already exists for over-the-wire pinning of the fix.
verdict.refinedRecommendation: In SessionTools.cs:70 change the [Description] to `[Description(\"Absolute path to a Lacerte data folder (e.g. C:\\\\Lacerte\\\\24Tax\\\\IData).\")]` — drop the inner escaped quotes (no other parameter description in this project wraps example values in quotes) and reduce `\\\\\\\\` (4 source chars per separator) to `\\\\` (2 source chars per separator). The resulting wire-visible string becomes `Absolute path to a Lacerte data folder (e.g. C:\\Lacerte\\24Tax\\IData).`, matching the canonical form used by line 142 of the same file, README.md:59/91, REGRESSION_CHECKLIST.md, PathValidation.cs:111, SyntheticStatusCodes.cs:175, and every Bridge/Odbc test. Add a pin in McpDiscoveryRoundtripTests that fetches the lacerte_set_context tool descriptor via the live MCP client, locates the dataPath parameter's description property, and asserts it does NOT contain `\\\\\\\\` (4-char sequence) — and asserts it DOES contain `C:\\Lacerte\\24Tax\\IData` (single-backslash form). While editing, also audit-grep `src/LacertMCP.Server/Tools/**/*.cs` for any other [Description] attributes containing 4+ consecutive backslashes — only line 70 came up in the spot-check, but the regex `\\[Description.*\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\` against the Tools directory will catch any siblings before they regress.

title: Tool method names mix noun-first and verb-first conventions, defeating LLM tool-picking grep patterns
userImpact: An LLM picking a tool scans names for patterns like `*_read`, `*_write`, `*_list`. Today the surface has read tools named `lacerte_client_read` AND `lacerte_list_modules` / `lacerte_list_datapaths` — same operation, opposite word order. Same for `lacerte_field_write_bulk` vs `lacerte_bulk_field_update` (which is the prompt name for the same workflow). The result: an LLM searching `*_list` misses two of three list tools, and prompt-to-tool composition is fragile.
description: Of 24 `[McpServerTool]` methods, 15 follow `Lacerte{Noun}{Verb}` (`LacerteClientList`, `LacerteSubclientRead`, `LacerteDetailWrite`) but 9 are verb-first or non-conformant: `LacerteSetContext`, `LacerteListModules`, `LacerteListDatapaths`, `LacerteCanUseNewApis`, `LacerteUpdateReturn`, `LacerteFieldWriteBulk`, `LacerteReloadSchema`, `LacerteReturnCodes`, `LacerteFieldAccessMap`. Compounding: the prompt `lacerte_bulk_field_update` (WorkflowPrompts.cs:177) targets `lacerte_field_write_bulk` (FieldWriteBulkTools.cs:78). Two different names for the same workflow surface.
recommendation: Pick noun-first as the canonical pattern (matches `lacerte_client_list` which is the most-used tool) and rename the verb-first outliers in a v0.2 with backwards-compat alias `[McpServerTool(Name=...)]` declarations: `lacerte_modules_list`, `lacerte_datapaths_list`, `lacerte_context_set`, `lacerte_apis_can_use_new`, `lacerte_schema_reload`, `lacerte_return_codes_list`, `lacerte_field_access_map_read`. At minimum: align the `lacerte_bulk_field_update` prompt name with the `lacerte_field_write_bulk` tool today (one-line edit) so the prompt registry and tool registry use the same identifier.
rationale: Round 2 found tool listing has no filter (CLI side) and bulk update missing as a tool, but nobody surfaced that the existing tool name vocabulary is grammatically inconsistent — which is the friction LLMs hit at every tool-picking step.

verdict.reasoning:
Verified by reading SessionTools.cs, the full Tools/ directory, WorkflowPrompts.cs, README.md, and both prior audit JSONs. The factual claims hold up:

1. Naming inconsistency is real. Of 24 [McpServerTool] methods, the dominant pattern is Lacerte{Noun}{Verb} (e.g. LacerteClientList, LacerteClientRead, LacerteDetailWrite, LacerteSubclientRead, LacerteTableRead, LacerteStateRead, LacerteStateSubclientRead, LacerteStatusRead, LacerteFormsRead, LacerteClientCreate, LacerteFieldWrite, LacerteSessionStatus). Six are verb-first outliers: LacerteSetContext (lacerte_set_context), LacerteListModules, LacerteListDatapaths, LacerteCanUseNewApis, LacerteUpdateReturn, LacerteReloadSchema. A few (LacerteFieldWriteBulk, LacerteFieldAccessMap, LacerteReturnCodes) are noun-chains that don't fully fit either pattern.

2. The strongest sub-finding is the prompt/tool name MISMATCH: WorkflowPrompts.cs:177 registers `lacerte_bulk_field_update` but the actual tool at FieldWriteBulkTools.cs:78 is `lacerte_field_write_bulk`. The comment at FieldWriteBulkTools.cs:84 even acknowledges this mismatch in prose. README.md row 164 documents the prompt with one name; the corresponding tool surface (row not shown but is `lacerte_field_write_bulk` per code) uses the inverted name. An operator or LLM reading the prompt description and trying to "call lacerte_bulk_field_update" gets a not-found.

3. Neither audit round 1 nor round 2 flagged tool-method naming inconsistency or the prompt/tool mismatch. Round 2 covered "bulk update missing as a tool" (P15-008 landed it) and the CLI tools-listing filter, but never grammar of names. This is a genuinely new finding.

Why meaningfullyImproves = true (but moderate, not strong): The wholesale rename portion of the recommendation is more polish than substance for a single-operator tool where the LLM reads each tool's [Description] attribute (it doesn't really grep by name pattern). HOWEVER, the prompt-vs-tool name divergence is a concrete, one-line bug that genuinely confuses prompt-driven flows. An LLM walking through `lacerte_bulk_field_update` (the prompt) is told to invoke a tool — and the name doesn't exist. That's a real user moment that fails today. Aligning the prompt name to `lacerte_field_write_bulk` (or vice versa with deprecation alias) is the high-leverage quick win.

Confidence is medium because the broader naming rename is bikeshedding-adjacent for a tool surface this small with rich per-tool descriptions, but the prompt/tool mismatch is unambiguous and actionable.
verdict.refinedRecommendation:
Scope down the finding to its high-leverage subset:

1. PRIORITY FIX (one-line, ship now): Align the prompt name with the tool name. Either:
   - Change WorkflowPrompts.cs:177 from `[McpServerPrompt(Name = "lacerte_bulk_field_update")]` to `[McpServerPrompt(Name = "lacerte_field_write_bulk")]` (matches the tool, keeps the noun-first family `lacerte_field_write` + `lacerte_field_write_bulk`); OR
   - Rename the tool method to `LacerteBulkFieldUpdate` (matches the prompt). Choose ONE name, update the README + tests, delete the apologetic comment at FieldWriteBulkTools.cs:84 ("Matches the existing lacerte_bulk_field_update prompt's stop-on-first-error posture by default."), and update the McpDiscoveryRoundtripTests.cs:125+196 assertions.
   Recommend the first option: the noun-first family is already canonical for write tools (lacerte_field_write + lacerte_field_write_bulk reads as a natural pair). Update the prompt docstring in README row 164 to match.

2. SECONDARY (defer to v0.2 with backwards-compat aliases via [McpServerTool(Name = "...")] declarations): If a real rename wave happens, the targets are the six verb-first outliers. But ONLY do this if telemetry shows actual LLM tool-picking misses — for a 24-tool surface with [Description] attributes on every method, the cost/benefit is marginal. Do NOT ship breaking renames just for grammatical purity.

3. ADD a one-line ARCHITECTURE.md convention note: "Tool names follow `lacerte_{noun}[_{qualifier}]_{verb}` (e.g. `lacerte_field_write`, `lacerte_field_write_bulk`, `lacerte_state_subclient_read`). Verb-first names are legacy; new tools should match the noun-first family." This stops future drift without forcing a rename today.

title: Origin discriminator vocabulary differs between `Origin` property (sdk/synthetic) and `lacerte_return_codes` (TAPIStatus/TPSDKStatus/Synthetic)
userImpact: An LLM that calls `lacerte_return_codes` to look up error remediation gets back `origin: 'TPSDKStatus'`. Same LLM then catches a real error and the envelope has `origin: 'sdk'` (LacerteSDKError.cs:44). The two surfaces describe the same concept with three different vocabularies — `sdk`/`synthetic` (envelope) vs `TAPIStatus`/`TPSDKStatus`/`Synthetic` (discovery tool). Tool composition (`look up origin from envelope, query lacerte_return_codes filtered by origin`) silently breaks.
description: `LacerteSDKError.Origin` returns the lowercase two-value taxonomy `"sdk"` or `"synthetic"` (per the P15-037 docstring). `MetadataTools.LacerteReturnCodes` returns the three-value capitalized taxonomy `"TAPIStatus"` (codes 0-28), `"TPSDKStatus"` (codes 200+), `"Synthetic"` (9xxx). Both are valid views into the same set, but neither survives a string-equality match against the other. An operator looking at an error envelope's `origin: 'sdk'` and asking the LLM `which TPSDKStatus codes match?` puts the LLM in a position where it has to know that TAPIStatus+TPSDKStatus together equal `sdk` in the other vocabulary.
recommendation: Pick one of: (a) make `LacerteSDKError.Origin` return the three-value form (`TAPIStatus`/`TPSDKStatus`/`Synthetic`) so the discriminator matches the discovery tool; or (b) make `LacerteReturnCodes` add a second field `originGroup` that returns `sdk`/`synthetic` matching the envelope; ideally both — emit a low-cardinality `originGroup` AND keep the specific `origin`. Document the relationship in the `lacerte_return_codes` tool description so the LLM doesn't have to infer it.
rationale: Round 1 covered synthetic vs SDK distinction being undocumented and round 2 covered the doc gap, but nobody noticed the vocabularies between the two surfaces don't even use the same words for the same concept.

verdict.reasoning:
Verified by direct read of the cited files plus an audit of prior rounds:

1. SOURCE CONFIRMED. `MetadataTools.cs:141,155` emits `origin = "TAPIStatus" | "TPSDKStatus" | "Synthetic"` (capitalized, three values, split on the 200 boundary). `LacerteSDKError.cs:44` defines `Origin => StatusCode >= SyntheticCodeThreshold ? "synthetic" : "sdk"` (lowercase, two values, split on the 9000 boundary). They genuinely do not collide on string equality.

2. NOT DUPLICATE — but adjacent. Round-2 P15-037 ("Synthetic vs SDK code distinction is buried in source comments") proposed adding `origin: "sdk"|"synthetic"` to the wire envelope. In its verdict.reasoning the reviewer EXPLICITLY noted "MetadataTools.LacerteReturnCodes already emits an `origin` field in the catalog with values TAPIStatus/TPSDKStatus/Synthetic" — and then treated those as the same feature, dropping the proposed lacerte_explain_status_code(code) tool as "redundant". The vocabulary mismatch was looked at and walked past. The DECISIONS.md 2026-05-30 P15-037 entry compounds this by calling them "the same `origin` discriminator". So this finding catches a real hole the prior round saw but did not flag.

3. RELATED SEPARATE BUG (not the finding under review, but worth surfacing for context). WrapToolHandler.SerializeError (lines 144-158) does NOT actually serialize `origin` into the envelope despite README.md:190-210 and DECISIONS.md:331-369 both documenting that it does. P15-037's "wire-envelope adds origin" promise was never landed in code — only the `Origin` property on the exception type and unit tests on that property. No test asserts the envelope JSON contains `origin`. This makes the finding's user-impact narrative ("LLM sees `origin: 'sdk'` in the envelope and tries to filter the catalog") technically vacuous TODAY — there is no envelope.origin to compare against. But the moment the envelope bug is fixed (which it should be — the docs already promise it), the vocabulary collision the finder identified becomes the very first thing an LLM trips on.

4. USER IMPACT IS REAL ONCE WIRED. The setup is exactly the kind of tool-composition story prior rounds emphasized: error envelope → `lacerte_return_codes` filter → remediation. With three different lowercase/capitalized tokens describing the same axis, naive string-equality filtering silently returns empty results and the LLM has no in-tool signal to debug. The finder's recommended dual-field approach (`origin` = TAPIStatus/TPSDKStatus/Synthetic + `originGroup` = sdk/synthetic) is the right shape — keeps the specific information available, adds a low-cardinality bucket that string-matches the envelope.

5. ACTIONABLE OFF-WINDOWS. ~5 LOC in MetadataTools.cs to emit a second field, ~3 LOC in WrapToolHandler.cs to actually serialize the envelope `origin`, plus tests + README wording cleanup so README's "the same `origin` discriminator per code" claim becomes accurate. All sim-mode-verifiable.

MeaningfullyImproves: YES — small ergonomic fix, sits exactly at the failure mode of tool composition, and reconciling it also surfaces the unimplemented envelope.origin bug which is a strictly worse breach of trust (docs promise a field the code doesn't emit).
verdict.refinedRecommendation:
Bundle three changes (sim-only, ~30 minutes, ~20 LOC + tests):

(1) src/LacertMCP.Server/Errors/WrapToolHandler.cs:144-158 — ACTUALLY add `["origin"] = err.Origin,` to the SerializeError envelope (between `statusName` and `severity`). This finishes P15-037 — DECISIONS.md and README.md both already document this field as live but the code never landed it. Add a WrapToolHandler envelope test: throw `LacerteSDKError(SyntheticStatusCodes.SimulationOnly)` and assert the serialized JSON contains `"origin":"synthetic"`; throw `LacerteSDKError(StatusCodes.ExposedForRead /*8*/)` and assert `"origin":"sdk"`. (No existing test covers this; the `LacerteSDKErrorTests` only assert the property, not the envelope.)

(2) src/LacertMCP.Server/Tools/MetadataTools.cs:141,155 — keep the specific `origin` field (TAPIStatus / TPSDKStatus / Synthetic) AND emit a new low-cardinality `originGroup` field whose values are exactly `"sdk"` or `"synthetic"`, derived as `kv.Key >= 9000 ? "synthetic" : "sdk"` (matching `LacerteSDKError.SyntheticCodeThreshold`). Now the envelope `origin` and the catalog `originGroup` string-match cleanly, while the catalog's three-way `origin` field stays available for operators / docs who want the TAPIStatus vs TPSDKStatus split.

(3) Tool description on `LacerteReturnCodes` (MetadataTools.cs:122) — append one sentence: "Each row carries `origin` (TAPIStatus / TPSDKStatus / Synthetic — Lacerte's own SDK subdivision) and `originGroup` (sdk / synthetic — matches the wire-envelope `origin` field for direct filtering)." This is the moment-of-use doc that lets the LLM pick the right field without reading README.

(4) README.md:210 — fix the false claim "the same `origin` discriminator per code" (which the finder's bug exposes) to read: "Each catalog row carries the same `origin` value (`sdk` / `synthetic`) under a separate `originGroup` field — filter on `originGroup == envelope.origin` to find candidate codes — plus a finer-grained `origin` field that splits SDK codes into `TAPIStatus` / `TPSDKStatus` for human readers."

Do NOT rename or remove the existing catalog `origin` field — it's semantically richer than `sdk`/`synthetic` and tooling may already depend on it. The additive `originGroup` is the safer fix.

title: ClientID / SubClientID / EmailID parameter names violate Microsoft acronym capitalization, ripple into JSON wire shapes
line: 51, 55, 75-100, 213, 217, 230, 241 (plus FieldWriteTools.cs:47 subClientID, UpdateReturnTools.cs:58, FieldWriteBulkTools.cs:70, ILacerteBridge.cs:107+128, BridgeInputValidation.cs:483-505)
userImpact: Microsoft's Framework Design Guidelines say 3+ character acronyms use PascalCase, so `Id` not `ID`. Today the wire ships both shapes: tool params are `clientID`/`emailID`/`subClientID` (JSON keys serialize the same), but discoverable resource fields and SQL aliases use `ClientId`/`EFilingId` (SqlTemplates.cs:210, prompt body line 149). An LLM building an idempotency key string or filtering a response by ID column reliably uses the wrong casing — `client.ClientId` lookups silently miss when the actual key is `clientID`.
description: Mixed-case acronyms appear across the wire surface: tool params `clientID`/`emailID`/`subClientID` (camelCase + ID) get serialized as JSON keys `clientID`/`emailID`/`subClientID`; but `lacerte_ef_status` returns rows with `ClientId`/`EFilingId`/`EFId`/`InstanceId` (per EFileTools.cs:34 + SqlTemplates.cs:210); the workflow prompts reference both forms (WorkflowPrompts.cs:60 uses `clientID`; line 149 uses `ClientId`). Same data, two casings. Microsoft convention says all should be `Id` (lowercase d). The MCP method `WriteField(... int? subClientID ...)` is internal and would be cheap to change.
recommendation: v0.2 breaking-change pass: rename all parameter and JSON key occurrences of `ID`/`Id` (acronym ≥3 chars context) to `Id` per Microsoft conv — `clientId`, `emailId`, `subClientId`, `clientID` → `clientId`. Class members `ClientID` → `ClientId`. The synthetic `ClientIDTooLong` / `InValidSubClientID` enum names can stay (they're internal error names that ship in the wire `statusName` field but aren't typed by callers). The two-surface inconsistency is the user-visible bug; the internal renames are a follow-on cleanup.
rationale: Round 2 covered EFStatus sim/live divergence (JOIN shape) and the unbounded EF result, but nobody flagged that the same conceptual field (`ClientId` / `clientID`) ships with two casings depending on which tool returns it.

verdict.reasoning: Verified by reading CreateClientTools.cs (params `clientID`/`emailID`, with `clientID` echoed in success envelope at line 241), FieldWriteTools.cs:47 (`subClientID`), UpdateReturnTools.cs:58 (`subClientID`), FieldWriteBulkTools.cs:70 (`SubClientID`), EFileTools.cs:34 (Description promises columns `ClientId`/`EFilingId`/`EFId`/`InstanceId`), SqlTemplates.cs:210 (`as ClientId, ef.Id as EFilingId, ef.EFId, ef.InstanceId`), ILacerteBridge.cs:107+128 (`subClientID`, `emailID`), BridgeInputValidation.cs:483-505 (`subClientID`), and Prompts/WorkflowPrompts.cs (line 62 references `clientID`/`emailID`; line 154 references `ClientId`/`EFId`). The same conceptual identifier ships in two casings on the wire depending on which tool returns it — write/create surface emits `clientID`/`emailID`/`subClientID` (camelCase+`ID` uppercase); EF-status read surface emits `ClientId`/`EFilingId`/`EFId`/`InstanceId` (PascalCase+`Id` lowercase d). Even within the same prompt body both forms appear. No prior round flagged this: R1 P14-024 covered SQL columns missing from results (a different bug — about which columns ship, not their casing); R2 P15-061 covered EFStatus sim/live JOIN shape divergence; R2 P15-066 covered TaxType aliases; none of the 149 prior findings address ID-key casing consistency across tools. This is genuinely user-facing: an LLM that builds an index keyed by `client.clientID` after calling lacerte_client_create then tries to join EF-status rows by the same key gets undefined matches because the EF rows have `ClientId`. The mixed prompt body amplifies the problem because the LLM cannot infer one canonical form. The finding correctly identifies it as v0.2 breaking (not in-session) — fixing means renaming public params + JSON envelope keys + tests + prompts.
verdict.refinedRecommendation: Pick one canonical casing for ID fields across the entire wire surface and ship it as a v0.2 breaking change. Recommended canonical: `Id` lowercase-d (matches Microsoft Framework Design Guidelines AND matches the SQL aliases that are harder to migrate because they ship from FoxPro/ODBC column projections). Concrete renames: (a) tool params `clientID` → `clientId`, `emailID` → `emailId`, `subClientID` → `subClientId` in CreateClientTools.cs:51/55, FieldWriteTools.cs:47, UpdateReturnTools.cs:58, FieldWriteBulkTools.cs:70 (and the BulkWriteEntry class property), Internal/FieldWriteCore.cs; (b) ILacerteBridge.cs:107+128 signature params; (c) BridgeInputValidation.cs:483-505 param + error context key; (d) CreateClientResult success-envelope key at CreateClientTools.cs:241 (`clientID` → `clientId`); (e) every `["clientID"]` / `["emailID"]` / `["subClientID"]` error-context dictionary key; (f) Description text in StatesTools.cs:38 (`SubClientID`), SubclientsTools.cs:22 (`SubClientID`), CreateClientTools.cs:49 (`ClientID`/`EmailID`); (g) WorkflowPrompts.cs body — replace every `clientID`/`emailID` token with `clientId`/`emailId` so prompts emit one canonical key. Leave the synthetic error names (`ClientIDTooLong`, `InValidSubClientID`) untouched — those are SDK-mirroring identifiers exposed only in `statusName` strings, not typed by callers. Add a one-line entry in DECISIONS.md ("ID-key casing canonicalized to lowercase-d per .NET Framework Design Guidelines; all tool params and JSON envelope keys use `clientId`/`emailId`/`subClientId`; SQL projections already used this form") and a README §Breaking Changes line for v0.2 so anyone with cached pre-0.2 idempotency keys can rebuild them. Verify by adding one test that round-trips a create → read → ef_status flow and asserts every JSON key matching the regex `(?i)(?:client|email|sub-?client|e-?filing|ef|instance)id` equals its `Id`-spelled canonical form.

title: README publishes 695/705 test count; actual is 1006/1016 (per HANDOFF.md)
userImpact: The first thing a new operator reads is the status banner. Cloning, building, running tests, and seeing `1006/1016 passed` when the README promises `695/705` makes them mistrust the entire project — they don't know whether the +311 tests are passing additions or whether something is broken. Prior audit R2 (P15-001) already fixed this once and it has drifted again.
description: README.md line 5 says: 'v0.1.0 scaffolding — 695/705 tests passing (10 expected live-only skips), 0 failures, 0 warnings.' HANDOFF.md line 17/19/50 publishes the current truth: 1006/1016. Round-2 audit P15-001 already corrected 481/492 → 695/705 with a recommendation to make this resilient. The drift recurred. The same line claims 'Read/Write/Create tools, simulation store, ODBC layer, COM bridge scaffolding, CLI, prompts, and hardening primitives all land' — accurate at 695, missing all the round-2 hardening that pushed us to 1006.
recommendation: Update README.md line 5 to '1006/1016 tests passing (10 expected live-only skips), 0 failures, 0 warnings.' But more important — this is now the second drift incident; replace the hard-coded number with a CI-stamped badge OR strip the count entirely and link to HANDOFF.md as the single source of truth. Same fix applies to ARCHITECTURE.md if it carries a count.
rationale: Operator's first-touch trust signal. The recurring drift is the deeper finding — a hard-coded number in the README front-matter will always drift. Pointing to HANDOFF.md or a generated badge is the only durable fix.

verdict.reasoning:
Verified directly. README.md line 5 reads `v0.1.0 scaffolding — 695/705 tests passing (10 expected live-only skips), 0 failures, 0 warnings.` HANDOFF.md line 17/19/50 publishes the current truth as 1006/1016. P15-001 from round-2 fixed the exact same line (481/492 → 695/705) and the drift has already recurred after round-2's +311 test landings. Confirmed P15-001 was scoped to a one-shot edit with no durability mechanism, and is now closed in the prior verdict.

Additional drift surfaces in the same pattern:
- REGRESSION_CHECKLIST.md line 13 also still says `695 passed, 10 skipped, 0 failed` — same file P15-001 fixed last round, drifted again. This is the bigger usability hit because the regression checklist is an actual gate the operator runs as a checkbox: their first command `dotnet test` will report 1006 passed and the checklist will appear to FAIL, eroding confidence in every later checkbox.
- ARCHITECTURE.md has no test count (clean).

The operator/LLM impact is genuine and not bikeshedding: (a) first-touch trust signal in the README front-matter is wrong by 311 tests, (b) the pre-commit verification gate in REGRESSION_CHECKLIST instructs the operator to verify a number that will reliably mismatch reality, baiting them into thinking the build is broken. The recurring-drift angle (round-2 already fixed this; it broke again same round) is the new insight prior rounds did not surface — the only durable fix is to stop hard-coding the count in two source-of-truth docs.

Is this MEANINGFUL not bikeshed? Yes — the operator profile in the brief is a tax pro on Windows whose first interaction with the repo is clone → build → test → REGRESSION_CHECKLIST walkthrough. A wrong number on line 5 of the README plus a wrong expected value on the first checkbox of the regression checklist is a real moment of "is this project broken or just stale?" — exactly the trust-erosion the round-3 brief flags.
verdict.refinedRecommendation:
Two-part fix in a single docs-only commit:

1. **Immediate sync** — bring stale numbers to current truth:
   - README.md:5 — change `695/705 tests passing (10 expected live-only skips)` → `1006/1016 tests passing (10 expected live-only skips)`. Also extend the sentence after `hardening primitives all land` to acknowledge the round-2 landings (bulk-write tool, detail series push-down, EF sinceUtc, schema-reload tool, doctor probes, correlation IDs, redaction-split, idempotency TTL, etc.) — the current sentence describes the round-1 surface area only.
   - REGRESSION_CHECKLIST.md:13 — change `**695 passed, 10 skipped, 0 failed**` → `**1006 passed, 10 skipped, 0 failed**`.

2. **Durability fix (the new insight)** — replace the hard-coded count with a pointer so drift cannot recur a third time:
   - README.md:5 — after the corrected number, append `(authoritative count tracked in HANDOFF.md)`. Better: strip the precise count from the README banner entirely and replace with `Tests: see HANDOFF.md "Verify Before Continuing" for current pass/skip totals.` The README is meant to be evergreen; the HANDOFF.md count is regenerated every session and is the natural source of truth.
   - REGRESSION_CHECKLIST.md:13 — change the bracketed expected number to a relative-only check: `reports `0 failed`, with `skipped` matching the count documented in HANDOFF.md "Verify Before Continuing" (currently 10, all live-only).` The pre-commit gate should verify INVARIANTS (0 failed, skip count matches HANDOFF), not a moving total.

Do NOT introduce a CI badge — net48 / x64 / Windows-only / single-operator project doesn't justify CI infrastructure for one number. The pointer-based fix is the right amount of mechanism.

Verify after commit by re-running `& "$env:USERPROFILE\.dotnet\dotnet.exe" test ...` to confirm 1006/10/0 still holds, and grep the repo for any other 695/705 stragglers (`Grep -r "695" --include="*.md"`).

title: README has no first-tool-call walkthrough or LLM-side example after install
userImpact: An operator finishes the setup ceremony (env vars, MCP config, register) and then... what? README has Install paths, Tools table, Errors, CLI, Troubleshooting — but never a 'open Claude Desktop and say: ' / 'paste this prompt and you should see this response' worked example. The tax pro now has a working MCP and a 22-tool catalog with no idea which tool to ask for first. They will either flounder for an hour or — more commonly — give up and assume the MCP is for developers, not them.
description: Grep on README for 'first tool call', 'first call', 'example call', 'walkthrough', 'hello world', 'quickstart example' returns zero hits. The README has a 'Quick start (dev / simulation mode)' that runs build/test scripts and a 'Tools' table that describes each tool — but nothing that bridges from 'I have Claude Desktop talking to the MCP' to 'I just listed my real clients.' The natural first-call sequence is documented nowhere: lacerte_session_status → lacerte_list_datapaths → lacerte_set_context(pick one) → lacerte_client_list. The Prompts section (line 156-166) mentions three workflow prompts but does not say how to invoke them from Claude Desktop (the `/prompts` slash-command discovery).
recommendation: Add a `## First call from your LLM host` section between `## Install paths` (line 46) and `## Lacerte SDK install` (line 104) with a copy-paste-able example: (1) verbatim user message — 'What tax-year data folders are on this machine?' (LLM should call lacerte_list_datapaths); (2) verbatim user message — 'Set my active context to 2024 Individual at C:\Lacerte\24Tax\IData' (LLM calls lacerte_set_context); (3) verbatim user message — 'List my first 10 clients' (LLM calls lacerte_client_list with limit=10). Show the abbreviated JSON the operator can expect to see in Claude Desktop's tool-call expander. Also document how to invoke the three workflow prompts from the host's slash-command UI.
rationale: The MCP markets itself to tax pros, not developers — and the README is written for the developer who built it. A worked example is the difference between 'I see what this does' and 'I can use this tomorrow morning.' Prior audits focused on developer docs (CLI tables, env-var refs) and missed that the operator-facing onboarding never reaches the goal.

verdict.reasoning: Verified: README.md (read in full, 329 lines) jumps from "Lacerte SDK install" step 5 ("the server will silently re-attach to the cached session") directly into "Tools" table without any "now ask Claude Desktop X and it should call Y" worked example. Grep for first-call/walkthrough/hello-world/paste-this/worked-example/example-prompt phrases returns zero hits. Round-1 finding P14-034 (audit-findings.json lines 729-748) added the Prompts table to README — but the verified recommendation only required a name + description + args table, not "how to invoke prompts from a Claude Desktop slash menu," and explicitly did NOT add a worked example. Round-1 P14-033 (lines 706-727) covered the env var table gap, not the first-call gap. Round-2 (audit-findings-r2.json) has no first-call/onboarding/example findings either — closest is .env.example correctness (P15-005-ish) which is unrelated. So this is genuinely new and not a duplicate. The fix is pure markdown, fully sim-safe, ~20-30 lines, no Windows or SDK dependency. The meaningfulness call is real: the README's whole post-install half is structured for someone who already knows what tool they want to call ("Tools" is a reference catalog, "Errors" is a debugging surface, "Troubleshooting" is a recovery surface). The audience the project explicitly markets to (tax pro on Windows running Claude Desktop) finishes the setup and faces a 22-tool catalog with no "type this and see this" anchor. The Prompts section is the closest existing thing but never tells operators that Claude Desktop surfaces MCP prompts as slash commands or how to discover them — leaving a documented feature undiscoverable. The finding is not bikeshedding; it converts "what now?" friction into a "it works" moment, which is exactly the first-mile gap that decides whether a non-developer keeps using the tool.
verdict.refinedRecommendation: Add a single ~25-line `## First call from your LLM host` section to README.md, inserted after the "Lacerte SDK install" block (after line 120, before "## Tools" at line 122) so it lands right where the operator's setup ceremony ends. Three sub-blocks: (1) **Discover prompts via slash menu** — one sentence: "In Claude Desktop, type `/` to surface MCP prompts; you should see `lacerte_client_intake`, `lacerte_review_ef_status`, and `lacerte_bulk_field_update` from the `lacerte` server. (Cursor: `@lacerte`. Windsurf: see host's prompt picker.)" This kills the "how do I invoke prompts" mystery without inventing host-specific docs. (2) **Three-step worked example with verbatim user prompts** — copy-pasteable, in the exact natural-language phrasing a tax pro would type, with the expected tool the LLM should pick:  - "Show me the Lacerte data folders on this machine." → `lacerte_list_datapaths`  - "Set my active context to 2024 Individual at C:\\Lacerte\\24Tax\\IData." → `lacerte_set_context`  - "List my first 10 clients." → `lacerte_client_list(limit=10)`  Show a single abbreviated success envelope `{"success": true, "result": {"rows": [{"ClientNumber": "...", "ClientName": "..."}, ...], "total": N, ...}, "cid": "..."}` so the operator knows what "it worked" looks like in Claude Desktop's tool-call expander. (3) **First-failure recovery hint** — one line: "If the first call returns `success: false` with `statusCode: 9101 NotSignedIn`, your 24h ticket expired — run `lacerte-mcp login` from PowerShell and retry." This connects the new section to the existing Troubleshooting block. Keep it tight — under 35 lines of markdown total. Do not add screenshots (high maintenance, host-specific). Do not add per-host slash-command UI docs beyond the one-line hints in (1) — they go stale. title: README is missing a 'What this MCP cannot do' section — operator expectations unbounded

title: Doctor's 'AppID GUID: not persisted' fail message recommends only `register` — doesn't acknowledge known-broken register state
userImpact: Fresh operator runs `doctor`, sees probe 'AppID GUID: not persisted → Run `lacerte-mcp register` to mint and store one.' They run register, see exit 3 + `[partial]` stderr, run doctor again, AppID probe now passes — but probably the OperatingMode probe says live, the COM probe passes, and yet first tool call returns NotSignedIn. They have no idea why because doctor told them 'register fixes it' and register reported a GUID-minted success. The fail-loop wastes an hour.
description: DoctorCommand.cs:797-799 fail path says `"Run `lacerte-mcp register` to mint and store one."`. Since RegisterCommand returns exit 3 with a `[partial]` message stating consent is not wired, the remediation is technically true but operationally false — register mints the AppID but does not complete the ceremony, so the next doctor run will show probes green while the MCP is unusable. There is no doctor probe that calls out 'AppID present but consent ceremony skipped because Phase 9 stub' — which is the single most common state on a fresh install today.
recommendation: Add an 8th-probe-equivalent state to ProbeAppId: when an AppID is persisted, also check a 'last successful Register() timestamp' (persist alongside the AppID) and emit a Warn 'AppID minted but Intuit consent never completed (Phase 9 stub) — first tool call will fail NotSignedIn (9101)' if absent on Windows + live mode. Also adjust the absent-AppID remediation string to acknowledge the current state: `"Run `lacerte-mcp register` to mint and store one (note: Phase 9 stub — register exits 3; live mode not bootable until task #63)."` until Phase 9 ships. Pair with the README fix in the first finding.
rationale: Doctor is the operator's primary 'why is this broken' tool. When register itself is known-stub, doctor is dishonest by claiming register will fix the AppID probe. Subtle correctness erosion — the diagnostic surface should match the actual state of the system, not the aspirational state.

userImpact: README line 50 says 'run `./scripts/release.ps1` to produce `dist/LacertMCP-v0.1.0.zip`'. The script actually writes `dist/LacertMCP-v0.1.0/LacertMCP-v0.1.0.zip` (release.ps1:156 creates the versioned subdir, :196 puts the zip inside). recommendation: (1) Fix README line 50: `produce dist/LacertMCP-v0.1.0/LacertMCP-v0.1.0.zip` (or change release.ps1 to put the zip at $staging root, not inside $stageRoot, since the version is already in the filename). (2) Either move the zip out of the versioned subdir OR add a `Write-Host` after :209 that shows the actual file URI the operator can ctrl-click. (3) Add a one-line note under the Claude Desktop snippet: 'Forward slashes also work in JSON on Windows and avoid the backslash-escape gotcha: `"command": "C:/LacertMCP/server/LacertMCP.Server.exe"`'.
