title: Error envelope omits `origin` (sdk|synthetic) even though LacerteSDKError exposes it for exactly this purpose
userImpact: An LLM reading an error envelope has to compare `statusCode >= 9000` against the SyntheticCodeThreshold to know whether the remediation lives in Intuit's SDK docs (sdk-origin) or in this MCP's config knobs (synthetic). LacerteSDKError.Origin was added in P15-037 specifically so the wire could carry the discriminator — but SerializeError never reads it. Worse, `lacerte_return_codes` invents a THIRD vocabulary ('TAPIStatus'/'TPSDKStatus'/'Synthetic') for the same concept, so an LLM that learned 'synthetic' from one place sees 'Synthetic' (capital S) or 'TAPIStatus' in another and may not realize they mean the same thing.
description: WrapToolHandler.SerializeError builds the error envelope with success/statusCode/statusName/severity/userMessage/remediation/context/cid — but skips `err.Origin`. The Origin property at LacerteSDKError.cs:44 is defined precisely to surface this on the wire ('don't have to memorize the 9000+ range'). Meanwhile MetadataTools.cs:141 + 155 emit 'origin' with a different vocabulary: 'TAPIStatus' / 'TPSDKStatus' / 'Synthetic'. Three independent serialization sites disagree on whether origin appears at all, and when it does, what its values are.
recommendation: Add `["origin"] = err.Origin` to the error envelope in SerializeError. Then update MetadataTools.LacerteReturnCodes to use the same {sdk, synthetic} vocabulary (or document the table-vs-error semantic explicitly). Goal: an LLM that learned the discriminator in one place recognizes it everywhere.
rationale: Round 1 did not surface this; P15-037 (DECISIONS) acknowledges Origin should ride the envelope but the change never landed in WrapToolHandler. The MetadataTools origin-vocabulary divergence is also unflagged by either round.

verdict.reasoning: Verified the gap directly: WrapToolHandler.cs:144-158 builds the error envelope as {success, statusCode, statusName, severity, userMessage, remediation, context, cid} — no `origin`. LacerteSDKError.cs:44 defines `Origin => StatusCode >= 9000 ? "synthetic" : "sdk"`, and LacerteSDKErrorTests.cs unit-tests the property in 9 cases. DECISIONS.md 2026-05-30 (P15-037) explicitly chose this as the design, with the Downstream bullet stating verbatim "WrapToolHandler.SerializeError reads err.Origin and emits it in the error envelope". README.md:184-210 already documents the `origin` field as user-facing (sample envelope includes `"origin": "synthetic"`). Todo.md:661 marks P15-037 as `[x]` complete. The implementation never landed — the envelope ships without `origin`, breaking a documented contract. Neither audit-findings.json nor audit-findings-r2.json contains a closed task referencing the missing `err.Origin` emission or the MetadataTools vocabulary divergence (grep for "origin"/"Origin"/"SerializeError"/"P15-037" in both files returned only the original P15-037 task definition itself, never a re-flag of the missed wire emission). Vocabulary divergence is also real: MetadataTools.cs:141,155 emits "TAPIStatus"/"TPSDKStatus"/"Synthetic" (three values, capitalized) while DECISIONS.md/README promise the two-value {sdk, synthetic} (lowercase). An LLM that picks up the README/envelope contract sees mismatched values when calling lacerte_return_codes. Meaningfully improves: an LLM hitting a 9203 SyntheticInternalServerError today gets no machine-readable signal that the remediation is MCP-side config, not Intuit SDK docs — it must memorize the 9000+ threshold or call a second tool. This is the exact friction P15-037 was meant to eliminate, and the fix is ~6 lines.
verdict.refinedRecommendation: Two-part sim-only fix, ~15 minutes: (1) In WrapToolHandler.cs:146-156, insert `["origin"] = err.Origin,` between `["statusName"]` and `["severity"]` so the envelope matches the documented shape in README.md:190-210 and the DECISIONS.md P15-037 downstream contract. Add a WrapToolHandlerTests assertion: throw a `LacerteSDKError(StatusCodes.DBError)` and a `LacerteSDKError(SyntheticStatusCodes.InternalServerError)`, deserialize the envelope, assert `origin == "sdk"` and `"synthetic"` respectively — pins the contract so a future refactor of SerializeError cannot silently drop it again. (2) In MetadataTools.cs:141,155, normalize the `origin` column emitted by `lacerte_return_codes` to the same two-value {sdk, synthetic} vocabulary the envelope uses, and add a sibling column (e.g. `sdkClass = "TAPIStatus" | "TPSDKStatus" | null`) if the SDK-subrange info is still useful for callers. Update the README Errors section's `lacerte_return_codes` mention to match. Net result: an LLM that learns `origin` from one site recognizes it everywhere — the discriminator becomes truly load-bearing instead of two parallel half-implementations.

title: SessionMode enum serialized inconsistently — PascalCase in session_status, lowercase in health and heartbeat
userImpact: A switch statement an LLM writes against `result.mode === 'simulation'` after seeing lacerte_health will silently fail when it inspects lacerte_session_status (which returns 'Simulation'). Operators piping the heartbeat file through `jq '.mode == "live"'` will get a true result, but the same query against session_status returns false. The same field, with two different casings, in tools the operator will compose freely.
description: SessionMode enum (Simulation/Live) is serialized via .ToString() in SessionTools.LacerteSessionStatus producing 'Simulation' / 'Live' (PascalCase), but via .ToString().ToLowerInvariant() in HealthTools.LacerteHealth producing 'simulation' / 'live'. HeartbeatWriter.BuildPayload also lowercases. The SessionStatusSnapshot.Mode field flows through to both call sites unchanged — the difference is purely the serialization decision per tool author. The error envelope's `severity` field consistently lowercases ('error'/'warn'/'info'), so the inconsistency is real even by the codebase's own pattern.
recommendation: Standardize on lowercase across the wire (it's the more common JSON convention and matches the severity casing already used by error envelopes). Update SessionTools.cs:51 to `mode = s.Mode.ToString().ToLowerInvariant()`. Add a regression test pinning the casing across all three sites.
rationale: Neither round flagged this. The asymmetry is exactly the kind of cross-tool subtlety prior rounds were told to surface and missed.

verdict.reasoning:
Verified by direct file reads of all three cited sites:

- SessionTools.cs:50 — `mode = s.Mode.ToString()` (PascalCase: 'Simulation' / 'Live')
- HealthTools.cs:52 and :60 — `mode = _session.Mode.ToString().ToLowerInvariant()` ('simulation' / 'live')
- HeartbeatWriter.cs:159 — `mode = _session.Mode.ToString().ToLowerInvariant()` ('simulation' / 'live')

The inconsistency is real. Three operator-visible surfaces — lacerte_session_status (MCP tool), lacerte_health (MCP tool), and the heartbeat file (watched by external scripts) — all emit the same logical field `mode` derived from the same `SessionMode` enum, but the session_status tool is the lone PascalCase outlier.

The finding's claim about codebase convention is corroborated: `Severity.ToString().ToLowerInvariant()` is used consistently at three other sites (FieldWriteBulkTools.cs:224, MetadataTools.cs:138 and :152). The lowercase wire convention is established; SessionTools.cs:50 is the only deviation.

Not a duplicate of any Phase-14 or Phase-15 task. Grepped both audit files for Mode.ToString, casing, PascalCase, lowercase, ToLowerInvariant, heartbeat, mode-pascal/lower variants, enum-casing — no overlap. The closest prior items are P14 health-tool wrapping (round-1 entry that wrapped LacerteHealth in WrapToolHandler.Run and added the {mode,status} shape — but did not pin the casing across all three sites) and P15-030 (mode-resolution warning when LACERTE_LIVE+SIMULATION both set — orthogonal concern). Neither closes this gap.

MeaningfullyImproves=true: an LLM (or operator's jq pipeline) writing `result.mode === 'live'` after observing one tool will silently get false from the other. The bug only manifests on a cross-tool composition path, which is exactly the path the LLM is asked to take. Cost-of-fix is one `.ToLowerInvariant()` token plus one regression test pinning the casing — under 20 LoC including the test. Trust-eroding cross-tool subtlety; correct lens for round 3.

title: `lacerte_health` and `lacerte_session_status` disagree on the casing of the same `mode` value
userImpact: The first probe call most LLMs make is `lacerte_health` — it returns `{ mode: "simulation", status: "reachable" }` (lowercase). The second probe is `lacerte_session_status` — it returns `{ mode: "Simulation", ... }` (PascalCase). An LLM that branches on `result.mode === "simulation"` against the wrong tool silently takes the wrong branch. An operator pasting both responses into a bug report sees mojibake-feeling inconsistency in the first 30 seconds with the tool.
description: HealthTools.cs lines 52 and 60 use `_session.Mode.ToString().ToLowerInvariant()`. SessionTools.cs:50 uses bare `s.Mode.ToString()`. The disk heartbeat file (HeartbeatWriter.cs:159) lowercases. Doctor (DoctorCommand.cs:645) Title-cases (`"Live"`/`"Simulation"`). Four surfaces, three different casings of the same two-value enum. This is the kind of detail that makes the API feel slapped-together on the LLM's first contact.
recommendation: Pick one canonical casing (lowercase is the prevailing JSON-API convention and matches the existing `severity` field's `ToLowerInvariant()`), apply at the SessionMode enum's serialization seam, and lock with a test. Concretely: change SessionTools.cs:50 to `s.Mode.ToString().ToLowerInvariant()` and add an xUnit assertion that the `mode` field on every tool envelope round-trips to lowercase. Doctor's human-readable text can keep PascalCase (it's prose, not JSON).
rationale: Prior rounds focused on response envelope shape (success/error split, cid stamping) but did not audit per-field value casing across tool boundaries. This is the cheapest possible fix with outsized perception payoff.

verdict.reasoning: Verified directly in the cited files: HealthTools.cs:52 and :60 use `_session.Mode.ToString().ToLowerInvariant()` returning lowercase `"simulation"`/`"live"`, while SessionTools.cs:50 uses bare `s.Mode.ToString()` returning PascalCase `"Simulation"`/`"Live"`. HeartbeatWriter.cs:159 also lowercases. DoctorCommand.cs:645 uses PascalCase but that string is human-readable prose, not a structured `mode` field, so it's defensibly separate. The `lacerte_health` and `lacerte_session_status` tools — the two most common LLM probes — emit a `mode` JSON field with different casing for the same enum value. An LLM that learns the lowercase form from `lacerte_health` (or from the public README/heartbeat) and branches `result.mode === "simulation"` against `lacerte_session_status` silently falls through to the wrong branch. A grep of the audit-findings*.json files for "casing", "PascalCase", "lowercase", "Mode.ToString", and "Mode.ToLower" returned no prior task covering this. Prior casing findings were about a totally different concern (case-insensitive `C{t}_0` field-name comparison in r1; WireLog redaction key casing in r2). The fix is one line + one round-trip xUnit assertion — outsized perception payoff for near-zero engineering cost, and it cures a real LLM correctness footgun, not just bikeshedding.
verdict.refinedRecommendation: Change `src/LacertMCP.Server/Tools/SessionTools.cs:50` from `mode = s.Mode.ToString()` to `mode = s.Mode.ToString().ToLowerInvariant()` so the `mode` field is lowercase everywhere it appears in a JSON envelope (HealthTools, SessionTools, HeartbeatWriter all align on lowercase, matching the prevailing `severity` / JSON-API convention). Add an xUnit regression in `SessionToolsTests` (or a new `ModeCasingContractTests`) that calls both `LacerteHealth()` and `LacerteSessionStatus()`, parses each envelope, and asserts `mode == "simulation"` (and a parallel live-mode assertion). Leave `DoctorCommand.cs:645` PascalCase — it's prose ("resolved: Simulation"), not a structured field — but note the divergence in a one-line code comment on the SessionTools fix so future contributors don't re-introduce the bug. Optional sweep: grep for `Mode.ToString()` (without `.ToLowerInvariant()`) and confirm only WireLog internal telemetry remains in PascalCase, which is acceptable since it's diagnostic-only.

title: lacerte_field_write_bulk pre-flight reuses 9009 ContextNotSet for year/readOnly MISMATCH — the canonical remediation 'Call lacerte_set_context first' is wrong when context IS set
userImpact: When the caller passes `year=2024` to lacerte_field_write_bulk while the active context is on TY2023, the tool throws 9009 ContextNotSet. Operator/LLM sees `userMessage: 'A read/write tool was called before lacerte_set_context provided Datapath + TaxYear + ReturnType'` and `remediation: 'Call lacerte_set_context first.'` But context IS set — the LLM dutifully calls lacerte_session_status, sees a non-null context, and gets stuck. The actually-useful `context.reason` + `context.expectedYear` + `context.actualYear` keys carry the truth, but they're buried under a confidently-wrong userMessage/remediation.
description: FieldWriteBulkTools throws SyntheticStatusCodes.ContextNotSet in three branches: (a) Context==null — correct usage, (b) year mismatch with active context — wrong code, (c) readOnly mismatch with active context — wrong code. The 9009 catalog entry's userMessage and remediation are written for case (a) and actively lie for (b) and (c). The structured context dict has the right info, but the top-level fields (which the LLM weighs most heavily because they sit at envelope-root) say 'context not set' when the actual diagnosis is 'context mismatch'. This is exactly the friction the bulk tool was designed to *prevent* via its pre-flight validation (FieldWriteBulkTools.cs:90 comment 'fail loudly BEFORE iterating').
recommendation: Either (a) mint a dedicated synthetic code for context-mismatch (e.g. 9010 ContextMismatch with remediation 'The active context does not match the value you passed for {year/readOnly}. Call lacerte_set_context with the correct {field}, or remove the assertion from this tool call.'), or (b) keep 9009 but rewrite remediation to cover both shapes and switch on context.reason. The mismatch branches already build the right reason text; surface it as userMessage instead of the catalog default for these branches.
rationale: P15-008 added the pre-flight gate; nobody audited that its 9009 reuse contradicts the catalog message. The pre-flight feature inverts its own value when its error message points the LLM at the wrong corrective action.

verdict.reasoning:
Verified at the source. FieldWriteBulkTools.cs:99-133 throws SyntheticStatusCodes.ContextNotSet (9009) in three semantically distinct branches: (a) ctx==null, (b) year-mismatch, (c) readOnly-mismatch. LacerteSDKError (Errors/LacerteSDKError.cs:51-61) always reads UserMessage and Remediation from the catalog at construction — there is NO per-throw override surface — so all three branches emit identical wire-level userMessage "A read/write tool was called before lacerte_set_context provided Datapath + TaxYear + ReturnType" and remediation "Call lacerte_set_context first" (SyntheticStatusCodes.cs:159-163). For the year/readOnly mismatch branches that lie is real: the context IS set, just for a different year/readOnly value. The LLM weighs the top-level userMessage/remediation more than the buried context.reason dict; "Call lacerte_set_context first" plus a follow-up lacerte_session_status that returns a non-null context creates an exact debug loop on the path the preflight was designed to streamline.

Not duplicated: P15-008 (audit-findings-r2.json:191) created the FieldWriteBulk tool and added the year/readOnly preflight params; that finding's verdict and refinedRecommendation never audited the chosen synthetic code. No r1 or r2 finding mentions ContextMismatch, expectedYear, the year.HasValue branch, or the readOnly.HasValue branch.

Meaningfully improves: yes. The year/readOnly params exist specifically to catch "I set context to TY24 but meant TY23" mistakes (parameter description line 81 says so explicitly). On a 300-client bulk update, getting the year wrong and seeing "Call lacerte_set_context first" when context is set is the worst possible time to misdirect — the operator is mid-batch on a high-stakes path and the LLM either loops (re-calling set_context with the same wrong year) or escalates to the operator with a misleading question. The fix is small and high-leverage: it directly improves the error story on the exact failure mode the feature was built to prevent.

One minor refinement note for the parent: the finding suggests code 9010, but 9010 already exists as BridgeUnavailableLegacy (SyntheticStatusCodes.cs:69 area per r2 finding referenced above) — the next clean slot in the 9001-9099 validation cluster is 9016. The fix should either (a) mint 9016 ContextMismatch with a precise remediation, or (b) accept that 9009's catalog default is for case (a) only and have the bulk-tool branches construct LacerteSDKError + a follow-up code wrapper (more invasive). Option (a) is cleaner — one catalog row, one constant — and matches the existing pattern where 9003/9014 split TaxYearTooOld/TaxYearTooNew and 9006/9009/9013 split AppNotRegistered/ContextNotSet/InvalidDataPath at the same family-of-failures granularity.
verdict.refinedRecommendation:
Mint a new `SyntheticStatusCodes.ContextMismatch = 9016` (next unused slot in the 9001-9099 validation cluster — note 9010/9011 are taken by the deprecated BridgeUnavailableLegacy/SimulationOnlyLegacy aliases per r2 finding, so do NOT reuse those even though they're functionally dead). Catalog entry:

```csharp
[ContextMismatch] = new StatusInfo(
    "ContextMismatch",
    Severity.Error,
    "The active session context does not match a caller-supplied assertion (year or readOnly).",
    "Re-call lacerte_set_context with the correct year/readOnly, OR remove the mismatching assertion from your tool call. Do NOT just re-call set_context with the same values — that's the value you asserted against."),
```

Then in `FieldWriteBulkTools.cs:109-133`, change the two mismatch branches to throw `SyntheticStatusCodes.ContextMismatch` instead of `ContextNotSet`. Keep the (ctx==null) branch on lines 97-107 as ContextNotSet — that branch's wire message is correct for that case. Keep the existing context dict shape (reason, expectedYear, actualYear, expectedReadOnly, actualReadOnly) — the structured payload is already right, only the catalog default was lying.

Tests in `FieldWriteBulkToolsTests.cs` (sim-only, off-Windows actionable, ~30 lines):
1. Set context to TY2024, call LacerteFieldWriteBulk with year=2023, assert wire envelope `statusCode == 9016`, `statusName == "ContextMismatch"`, `userMessage` does NOT contain "Call lacerte_set_context first", `context.expectedYear == 2023`, `context.actualYear == 2024`.
2. Same shape for readOnly mismatch.
3. Regression: with no context set, assert the (ctx==null) branch STILL returns 9009 ContextNotSet — that branch should not regress.

Also audit the other two ContextNotSet emitters (`LacerteSessionManager.cs:513` and `:1319`) to confirm they're the genuine null-context case — both are inside RequireContext-style helpers per the grep, so they're fine and need no change.

Skip the alternative "rewrite 9009's remediation to cover both shapes" route — that produces a paragraph-shaped remediation that's worse for the LLM to act on than two narrow codes with sharp remediations. The codebase already uses the split-by-family pattern (9003/9014, 9006/9009/9013) so this is consistent.

Document the new code in the README error-codes table next to ContextNotSet and add a one-line entry to DECISIONS.md noting the 9009-vs-9016 split rationale (so future audits don't merge them).

title: Bulk-write envelope omits firstFailureIndex / nextResumeIndex / resume-with-same-key hint — recovery requires the LLM to scan perItem and reinvent retry strategy
userImpact: When a 300-row bulk-write trips at row 47 with continueOnError=false (the default), the response includes errorCount=1, successCount=46, and 253 entries each with `skipped: true, reason: 'stop-on-error: a prior row failed and continueOnError is false.'` The LLM has to scan perItem to find the index of the first non-skipped failure, then realize that resubmitting the whole batch with the same idempotencyKey will replay the 46 successes from cache and re-execute the failed row. That resume strategy is never stated; an under-prompted LLM is likely to either retry row 47 standalone (losing the bulk envelope's audit trail) or send entries[48..] (losing the safety of replaying through the same idempotency umbrella).
description: The bulk envelope returns `{table, dryRun, continueOnError, totalCount, successCount, errorCount, perItem}`. It does NOT carry: (a) `firstFailureIndex` — the index where the loop stopped, so the LLM doesn't have to scan; (b) `firstFailure` — a copy of that one perItem row hoisted to envelope level for easy LLM extraction; (c) `resumeStrategy` — a structured hint like `{ method: 'retry-same-batch', expectedReplays: 46, expectedExecutions: 254, idempotencyNote: 'rows 0..46 will return cached results; row 47 onward will re-execute' }`. The per-row idempotency key shape `'{prefix}-{clientNumber}-{fieldName}'` makes the retry-same-batch strategy safe but the operator/LLM has to derive that from the docstring rather than the response.
recommendation: Add three top-level keys to the bulk envelope: `firstFailureIndex` (int? — null on success), `firstFailure` (a hoisted copy of perItem[firstFailureIndex] or null), and `recoveryHint` (a short structured object: `{ canResumeViaSameBatch: bool, idempotencyKeyPrefix: string?, note: 'Resubmitting the same entries[] with the same idempotencyKey replays succeeded rows from cache and re-executes failed/skipped rows.' }`). The information is already known at envelope-construction time (the for-loop knows `i` when stopped is set; idempotencyKey is in scope). The cost is ~5 lines of code; the win is the LLM gets the resume strategy without having to scan or reason about idempotency semantics.
rationale: P15-008 added the bulk tool itself with the cascade safeguards; the audit rounds verified WriteField chokepoint integrity, not the envelope's UX as a recovery surface. The cascade safeguards are correct — but the response shape doesn't surface them in a way that survives the LLM's per-call summarization.

verdict.reasoning: Verified directly against FieldWriteBulkTools.cs:253-262 — the bulk envelope is literally {table, dryRun, continueOnError, totalCount, successCount, errorCount, perItem}, with no firstFailureIndex, no hoisted firstFailure, no recoveryHint. Confirmed the stop-on-error branch (lines 146-159) marks every subsequent row as `{skipped:true, reason:'stop-on-error: a prior row failed and continueOnError is false.'}` — meaning a 300-row batch tripping at row 47 returns 252 indistinguishable skipped entries the LLM must linearly scan to find the failure index. Confirmed the per-row idempotency key shape `{prefix}-{clientNumber}-{fieldName}` (lines 181-187) makes the retry-same-batch strategy safe (resubmit replays successes from cache + re-executes the failed/skipped rows), but this property is only documented in the parameter description at line 85 — the response itself never surfaces it. Grep across audit-findings.json and audit-findings-r2.json: zero matches for firstFailureIndex/firstFailure/recoveryHint/resumeStrategy. P15-008 added the tool but its verdict.refinedRecommendation only specified `{table, field, dryRun, total, succeeded, failed, skipped}` — it never called out exposing a structured recovery hint. Bonus reinforcement: WorkflowPrompts.BulkFieldUpdate (lines 193-220) still walks the LLM through the OLD per-row `lacerte_field_write` loop and does not reference `lacerte_field_write_bulk` at all — so the model gets zero prompt-side coaching about the bulk envelope or its replay semantics either. The recovery moment is real and high-stakes: it's the #2 operator scenario in REQUIREMENTS §1.2 (bulk mailing-address sweeps, EF flag toggles, preparer assignments across hundreds of clients) and under per-call summarization pressure the LLM commonly picks the wrong recovery strategy (retries just row N standalone, losing audit trail; or sends entries[N+1..], losing the idempotency umbrella). Fix is ~5-10 lines in the for-loop that already knows `i` at the moment `stopped` is set; cost-to-value is excellent.
verdict.refinedRecommendation: Add three top-level keys to the FieldWriteBulkTools.cs:253-262 envelope: (1) `firstFailureIndex` (int? — the `i` captured when `stopped` is first set to true, null when errorCount==0), (2) `firstFailure` (a hoisted copy of `perItem[firstFailureIndex]` or null — saves the LLM from a linear scan over up to 300 entries), and (3) `recoveryHint` — only emit when errorCount>0, shape: `{ canResumeViaSameBatch: bool, idempotencyKeyPrefix: string?, perRowKeyShape: "{prefix}-{clientNumber}-{fieldName}", note: "Resubmitting the same entries[] with the same idempotencyKey replays succeeded rows from cache and re-executes failed/skipped rows. Do NOT slice entries[] — that loses the cache replay and the audit envelope.", retryRowsCount: int (errorCount+skippedCount), replayedRowsCount: int (successCount) }`. Set `canResumeViaSameBatch=true` only when `idempotencyKey` was supplied AND `dryRun==false` (without a prefix the cache is bypassed; in dryRun mode "resume" is meaningless). Implementation: track `firstFailureIndex` as a local `int?` initialized null, set it on the first non-success branch (the LacerteSDKError catch, the generic Exception catch, AND the null-entry guard at line 162), then include all three keys in the final anonymous object. The for-loop already has `i` in scope and `idempotencyKey` is the method parameter — no new state plumbing needed. Add 2 FieldWriteBulkToolsTests.cs cases: (a) inject a failure at index 2 of 5 entries with idempotencyKey supplied, assert response.firstFailureIndex==2, firstFailure.clientNumber matches entries[2], recoveryHint.canResumeViaSameBatch==true, recoveryHint.replayedRowsCount==2, recoveryHint.retryRowsCount==3; (b) same scenario with idempotencyKey==null, assert recoveryHint.canResumeViaSameBatch==false and idempotencyKeyPrefix==null. Companion change (same task): update WorkflowPrompts.BulkFieldUpdate (Prompts/WorkflowPrompts.cs:193-220) to recommend `lacerte_field_write_bulk` as the primary path and to tell the model "on failure, read response.firstFailureIndex + response.recoveryHint — resubmit the SAME entries[] with the SAME idempotencyKey to safely retry" — without this prompt update the LLM may never reach the bulk tool in the first place and the new envelope keys won't be exercised. Also add one line to README's tools table describing the recovery hint contract.

title: BridgeUnavailable (9201) and InternalServerError (9203) remediations name LACERTE_DEBUG_WIRE but don't tell the operator how to find the log file, and never reference the cid that's on the same envelope
userImpact: When the bridge crashes or the server throws an internal error, the envelope carries `cid: 'a1b2c3d4'` — the 8-hex correlation ID that ties the failure to its nested WireLog records (per WrapToolHandler.cs:84-90). The remediation says 'inspect logs/lacerte-YYYYMMDD.log for the bridge stderr' but: (a) never mentions the cid as the grep token to use, (b) gives a relative path 'logs/...' that resolves against Claude Desktop's launch CWD (typically `C:\Program Files\Claude` or similar) — invisible to the operator who started Claude from the Start menu, (c) doesn't tell the operator that LACERTE_DEBUG_WIRE has to be set BEFORE the failure (re-running with it on means re-triggering the failure). Operator hits a 9201 and has no usable path from 'I see this error' to 'I have the relevant log lines'.
description: Two failures of operator-facing observability: (1) the cid is the whole point of WrapToolHandler's P15-052 correlation work but the remediation strings never close the loop by saying 'grep `cid=<your-cid>` in the log'. (2) The log path 'logs/lacerte-YYYYMMDD.log' is computed by WireLog.cs:1130 as `Path.Combine(Directory.GetCurrentDirectory(), 'logs')` and can be overridden with LACERTE_DEBUG_LOG_PATH — but the operator has no way to know the resolved absolute path from inside an MCP error response (lacerte_session_status doesn't surface it either, see separate finding). The remediation reads like 'go find a file somewhere' instead of 'here's the absolute path; grep this cid'.
recommendation: (1) Rewrite the BridgeUnavailable + InternalServerError remediations to: 'If LACERTE_DEBUG_WIRE=1 is enabled, grep `cid=<the cid in this envelope>` in {resolved-log-path} to find the failed bridge call. Otherwise, set LACERTE_DEBUG_WIRE=1 in your Claude Desktop config, restart, and reproduce.' (2) Add an `effectiveLogPath` (or `wireLogPath`) field to the StatusInfo's context for these codes — compute via the same resolver WireLog uses — so the operator sees the absolute path inline. (3) Stamp `cid` into the remediation template via simple string-replace at SerializeError time (WrapToolHandler.cs:144) so each rendered remediation already names the grep token. Without these changes the cid is a write-only forensic device.
rationale: Round-1 P15-035 split 9203 from raw Error=0; round-2 P15-052 added cid stamping. Both treated the cid as a forensic primitive without closing the loop on how an operator (or LLM) is meant to USE the cid in the moment. The information is already on the envelope; the recovery copy doesn't activate it.

verdict.reasoning:
All factual claims verified against source:

(1) SyntheticStatusCodes.cs:207-223 — confirmed the 9201 BridgeUnavailable remediation says "re-run with LACERTE_DEBUG_WIRE=1 and inspect logs/lacerte-YYYYMMDD.log for the bridge stderr" and 9203 InternalServerError says "re-run with LACERTE_DEBUG_WIRE=1, and file an issue with the wire log timestamp." Neither mentions cid as the grep token.

(2) WrapToolHandler.cs:84-101,144-157 — confirmed cid is stamped on BOTH success envelopes (line 100) AND SerializeError envelopes (line 155) but is purely a write-only forensic field; nothing in the remediation strings references it.

(3) WireLog.cs:1124-1162 — confirmed default log path is computed as Path.Combine(Directory.GetCurrentDirectory(), "logs"), which when Claude Desktop spawns the MCP via stdio resolves to whatever CWD it inherits (typically Claude's install dir or the user profile root, never something an operator can find by intuition). LACERTE_DEBUG_LOG_PATH override exists but is also not surfaced anywhere.

(4) SessionTools.cs:42-65 — confirmed lacerte_session_status returns mode/registration/expiry/context/appName/appId but NOT the resolved log path or the LACERTE_DEBUG_WIRE state. So the operator has no in-band way to discover where the log file even lives.

(5) Prior audits: P15-052 (r2) added the cid plumbing AsyncLocal mechanism and stamped it on envelopes; P15-035 (r1) split 9203 from raw Error=0 and wrote the original remediation copy. Neither closed the loop on USING cid in remediation text or surfacing the resolved log path. Cross-checked grep for effectiveLogPath/wireLogPath/grep.*cid/cid.*grep — no hits in either audit file. This is genuinely a new angle on incomplete prior work.

UX meaningfulness is high, not bikeshedding: when an operator hits a 9201/9203 inside Claude Desktop, the LLM reads them the remediation copy. Today the copy is "go find a log file somewhere and look for something" — the operator has neither the absolute path nor the search term. After the fix it becomes "grep cid=a1b2c3d4 in C:\Users\you\AppData\...\logs\lacerte-20260530.log" — a copy-pasteable recipe. The information already exists on the envelope; activating it in copy is ~10 lines of work for a tangible "first time you hit this, you can actually fix it" win. Also fixes the subtle gotcha that LACERTE_DEBUG_WIRE has to be set before the failure (re-running with it on just produces a different failure context if the bug isn't deterministic).

title: lacerte_session_status omits debug-log state — operator hitting BridgeUnavailable remediation 'inspect logs/lacerte-YYYYMMDD.log' cannot tell whether LACERTE_DEBUG_WIRE is on or where logs go
userImpact: When a tool fails with a 9201/9203 telling them to 'inspect logs/lacerte-YYYYMMDD.log', the operator's first move is to call lacerte_session_status to confirm the environment. The snapshot returns mode, isRegistered, expiry, context, appName, edition, buildVersion, modeResolutionReason, defaultTaxYear — but NOT `debugWireEnabled` and NOT `wireLogPath`. So the operator doesn't know whether logging is even on (it defaults off) or where it would write if turned on. Worst case they enable LACERTE_DEBUG_WIRE=1, reproduce, and still can't find the log because Claude Desktop launched the server from an unfamiliar CWD.
description: WireLog.IsActive (line 378) and the resolved log dir from ResolveConfig (lines 1124-1162) are private — the SessionStatus tool surface has no observable handle on the diagnostic state operators are being asked to consult. Other env surfaces (modeResolutionReason, defaultTaxYear) were added precisely to close this kind of 'the docs say to use this env var but no tool tells me whether it took' gap (P15-030, P15-004). LACERTE_DEBUG_WIRE has the same problem and is more frequently load-bearing for incident recovery.
recommendation: Add `debugWireEnabled: bool` and `wireLogPath: string?` to SessionStatusSnapshot (and the SessionTools.LacerteSessionStatus tool response). `debugWireEnabled` comes straight from `WireLog.IsActive`; `wireLogPath` is the absolute path WireLog would write to today (compute via the same resolver — when IsActive is false, return the would-be path for when the operator turns the flag on). This makes the 9201/9203 remediation actually executable.
rationale: Audit rounds added defaultTaxYear and modeResolutionReason to close the same class of 'is my env var actually taking effect' UX gap. The pattern is established; LACERTE_DEBUG_WIRE was left out and is the most impactful one because it gates the only audit trail operators have when bridge/internal failures occur.

verdict.reasoning: Verified by direct file read. SessionStatusSnapshot.cs lines 20-46 carries Mode/IsRegistered/Context/AppName/AppId/Edition/BuildVersion/ModeResolutionReason/DefaultTaxYear — NO debugWireEnabled, NO wireLogPath. SessionTools.LacerteSessionStatus (SessionTools.cs:44-65) only projects mode/isRegistered/registeredAt/expiresAt/minutesUntilExpiry/context/appName/appId — strict subset of the snapshot, also missing the debug-wire surface. The remediation gap is load-bearing: SyntheticStatusCodes.cs:211 (BridgeUnavailable 9201) literally instructs operators to "re-run with LACERTE_DEBUG_WIRE=1 and inspect logs/lacerte-YYYYMMDD.log for the bridge stderr." and :223 (InternalServerError 9203) gives the identical guidance. The operator's natural follow-up is calling lacerte_session_status — which can't tell them whether logging is on, nor where logs will/do land. The precedent the finding cites is real: P14-040 added BuildVersion, P15-004 added DefaultTaxYear, P15-030 added ModeResolutionReason — all to close "is my env var actually taking effect" UX gaps with operator-facing fields on the same surface. WireLog.IsEnabled (line 379) and WireLog.CurrentLogPath (line 382) are already public — wiring them in is purely additive plumbing. Cross-checked both audit-findings.json (R1, 71 entries) and audit-findings-r2.json (R2, 78 entries) plus Todo.md: no prior task projects WireLog state onto SessionStatus. Two adjacent tasks were considered and rejected as not closing this gap: (a) P15-033 startup banner prints debugWire=on|off + debugLogPath to stderr ONCE at process boot, but Claude Desktop swallows stderr and the operator can't read it mid-session; (b) P15-054 heartbeat file is for external process supervisors, not the LLM mid-tool-call. The remaining nuance for the implementer: WireLog.CurrentLogPath returns null when disabled, so to fulfill the "where it WOULD write if turned on" requirement, the impl should expose a separate ResolvedLogDir helper that calls the same path-resolution logic regardless of LACERTE_DEBUG_WIRE state (i.e. defaultDir = Path.Combine(cwd, "logs") OR the validated LACERTE_DEBUG_LOG_PATH override) so the operator can be told "your log WOULD be at C:\Users\…\logs\lacerte-YYYYMMDD.log if you enable it." Meaningfully improves the operator UX: in the exact 9201/9203 moment the remediation text describes, the operator's next call IS lacerte_session_status — and today the snapshot stays silent about the only diagnostic lever the error message mentions. The fix turns the remediation from "follow these two steps, then guess" into "follow these two steps, then look at this exact path." Real moment, not bikeshedding.
verdict.refinedRecommendation: Add two fields to SessionStatusSnapshot (after DefaultTaxYear): `bool DebugWireEnabled` and `string? WireLogPath`. Populate both in LacerteSessionManager.SessionStatus(): DebugWireEnabled = WireLog.IsEnabled, WireLogPath = active path when enabled OR the would-be path when not (so the operator can enable the flag, restart, and immediately know where to grep). Project them as `debugWireEnabled` + `wireLogPath` in SessionTools.LacerteSessionStatus's anonymous object. Implementation detail the finding glosses over: WireLog.CurrentLogPath returns null when disabled. Add a sibling helper `WireLog.ResolvedOrWouldBeLogPath` that runs the same default-dir + LACERTE_DEBUG_LOG_PATH + PathValidation.ValidateLogDir + Path.Combine(dir, FilenameForToday()) chain unconditionally (env-flag-independent) — when LACERTE_DEBUG_LOG_PATH is set but rejected by PathValidation, fall back to the default ./logs dir to mirror the WireLog runtime behavior so the operator's expectation tracks reality. Tests in SessionTools / SessionStatusSnapshot test files: (a) snapshot reports DebugWireEnabled=false + a non-null WireLogPath when LACERTE_DEBUG_WIRE is unset (path-is-where-it-would-go contract), (b) reports DebugWireEnabled=true + matching CurrentLogPath when EnableForTests is active, (c) rejected LACERTE_DEBUG_LOG_PATH override results in WireLogPath pointing at the default ./logs dir (matches WireLog fallback). Also update the BridgeUnavailable + InternalServerError remediation strings in SyntheticStatusCodes.cs to add a one-line breadcrumb: "Call lacerte_session_status to see whether LACERTE_DEBUG_WIRE is on and the resolved wire log path." — closing the loop so the LLM seeing the error envelope knows the lookup tool exists. Out of scope: do NOT add an Edition.IsActive-style enum or a structured WireLogStatus subobject — two flat fields preserves the snapshot's compact shape and mirrors the precedent (BuildVersion + ModeResolutionReason + DefaultTaxYear are all flat scalars).

title: `tools --name <missing>` exits 1, but `tools --filter <matches-nothing>` exits 0 with `0 registered` — same negative result, opposite exit code
userImpact:
Operator/script that runs `lacerte-mcp tools --filter '^lacerte_ef_'` to assert e-file tools exist (CI smoke before a release) gets exit 0 + `0 registered` if a refactor accidentally drops the prefix — the assertion silently passes. The same intent expressed as `--name lacerte_ef_status` correctly fails with exit 1. The two flags are presented as parallel filters but behave under opposite exit conventions.

Also: `tools --filter X --json --names-only` silently picks one winner (`--names-only`) without telling the user. They get partial output that doesn't match either of their requested formats.
description:
ToolsCommand.cs:127 — when `--name` doesn't match a tool, the code returns 1 with `No tool matched name '<X>'.` ToolsCommand.cs:181 — when `--filter` matches nothing, code prints `lacerte-mcp tools — 0 registered` and returns 0. These are the same negative semantics (operator asked 'is this tool here?' and the answer is no) with mismatched exit codes.

Additionally, the inline comment at line 156-157 says 'Mutually exclusive with --json; --names-only wins (documented)' — but the help text on `--names-only` (line 55) doesn't say this, nor does `--json` warn the user. Combining the two silently drops --json. A user piping `--json` into `jq` gets a single non-JSON line per tool.
recommendation: Two small cleanups: (a) `--filter` with zero matches should print to stderr `No tools matched filter '<X>'.` and return 1 (mirror --name behavior); add a `--allow-empty` flag for scripts that legitimately expect zero matches. (b) Reject the explicit combo of `--json` + `--names-only` with `stderr.WriteLine("--json and --names-only are mutually exclusive — pick one.")` and return 2 (usage error). Same treatment for `--name` + `--filter` (they overlap weirdly today — `--filter X --name Y` reduces to Y only if Y matches, silently dropping the filter).
rationale: Round-2 P15-066 added the filter/name/names-only options as a feature; this round catches the cross-flag consistency the feature dropped. Power-users running these in shell pipelines deserve consistent exit semantics so a single `if ($?) { ... }` pattern works for both flags.

verdict.reasoning: Verified directly in C:/Users/VR/Projects/LacertMCP/src/LacertMCP.Cli/Commands/ToolsCommand.cs. All three sub-claims hold: (1) `--name` no-match returns 1 with stderr message (lines 127-132); `--filter` no-match prints `lacerte-mcp tools — 0 registered` and returns 0 (lines 121, 181, 200). Same negative semantics, opposite exit codes. (2) `--names-only` is checked before `--json` at lines 157-164 / 166, so combining them silently drops `--json`; the help string on line 55 doesn't mention this — the only mention is an inline code comment at line 156. (3) `--filter` is applied (line 121) before the `--name` lookup runs against the filtered set (line 127), so `--filter X --name Y` silently requires Y∈X — undocumented overlap. Prior round-2 task P15-066 (audit-findings-r2.json:1582-1608) explicitly added these three flags but its refinedRecommendation only said "Mutually exclusive with `--json` (or `--names-only` wins — document and test)" without enforcing it as a usage error, and never addressed `--filter` empty-match exit code. So this is a genuine gap left by P15-066, not a duplicate. The exit-code asymmetry has real CI impact: an operator script `lacerte-mcp tools --filter '^lacerte_ef_'; if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { fail }` silently passes when a refactor removes the e-file prefix — a trust-eroding silent-pass for the exact "sanity-check before pasting into Claude Desktop config" workflow the XML doc (lines 28-32) advertises. The `--json + --names-only` silent winner produces non-JSON output when piped into `jq` — small but real polish. Fix is isolated, pure off-Windows, ~15 lines plus 3 tests.
verdict.refinedRecommendation:
Land three small cleanups in src/LacertMCP.Cli/Commands/ToolsCommand.cs, all enforced by tests in ToolsCommandTests.cs:

(1) **Exit-code parity for `--filter` no-match.** After the filter-apply at line 121, if `!string.IsNullOrEmpty(filter) && tools.Count == 0`, write `stderr.WriteLine($"No tools matched filter '{filter}'.");` and `return 1;` BEFORE the `--name` / `--names-only` / `--json` / table branches. This mirrors the `--name` no-match contract on line 131 so a single `if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0)` pattern works for both flags in operator CI scripts. Skip the `--allow-empty` escape hatch the original recommendation suggested — YAGNI for a single-operator tool; if it's ever needed, add it then. Update help text on line 52: append " — exit 1 if zero matches."

(2) **Reject `--json` + `--names-only` as a usage error, not silent-pick.** At the top of Run() after parsing args (before line 106 DiscoverTools), if `asJson && namesOnly`: `stderr.WriteLine("--json and --names-only are mutually exclusive; pick one.");` and `return 2;` (matches the invalid-regex exit-2 convention on line 119). Delete the misleading inline comment on lines 155-156. Update both help strings (lines 47-48 and 55-56) to mention the exclusion.

(3) **Document `--name` + `--filter` interaction in help text** — don't change semantics (the current "filter narrows the pool, then name picks within" is defensible), but the help on line 53-54 should read: "Print one tool's full surface (all parameter descriptions). Exit 1 if no match. When combined with --filter, the name must also satisfy the filter."

Tests to add in C:/Users/VR/Projects/LacertMCP/src/LacertMCP.Tests/Cli/ToolsCommandTests.cs:
- `Filter_NoMatches_ReturnsExit1_WithStderrMessage` — `Run(asJson:false, filter:"^no_such_prefix_zzz_", nameExact:null, namesOnly:false, stdout, stderr)` asserts exit==1, stderr contains "No tools matched filter", stdout is empty.
- `JsonAndNamesOnly_RejectedWithExit2` — `Run(asJson:true, filter:null, nameExact:null, namesOnly:true, stdout, stderr)` asserts exit==2, stderr contains "mutually exclusive", DiscoverTools not invoked (no output on stdout).
- `NameWithinFilterScope_ExcludedNameReturnsExit1` — `Run(asJson:false, filter:"^lacerte_health$", nameExact:"lacerte_client_list", namesOnly:false, stdout, stderr)` asserts exit==1 (name is real but excluded by filter), stderr contains "No tool matched name".

Total diff ≈ 15 production lines + 3 tests. No README change beyond the help-string updates which appear in --help automatically.

title: `status --json` emits `"buildVersion": "0.1.0+7b4af..."` — JSON-escaped `+` makes the build hash unreadable when an operator pastes it into a bug report
userImpact: Operator runs `lacerte-mcp status --json | jq .buildVersion` to capture the build for a bug report; jq DOES de-escape so jq output is fine — but a copy-paste of the raw JSON (which is what `lacerte-mcp status --json > status.json` produces) shows `0.1.0+7b4af...` instead of `0.1.0+7b4af...`. The maintainer reviewing the report has to mentally decode `+` to recognize this is the same string they see in the human `status` output (`0.1.0+7b4af...`). Small thing, but the JSON output of every other status field is verbatim — only the version field stutters.
description: System.Text.Json's default `JsonEncoder` escapes ASCII characters in the 'unsafe' set including `+`. The human `status` command prints `Build      : 0.1.0+7b4af...` cleanly (StatusCommand.cs:122), but the JSON branch (line 94) serializes via `new JsonSerializerOptions { WriteIndented = true }` with no Encoder override, producing `"buildVersion": "0.1.0+7b4af..."`. Same issue would hit any field containing `+`, `<`, `>`, `&` (e.g. if a future AppName included an ampersand). The doctor's `--json` payload has the same exposure for `buildVersion` and any remediation strings with `<startup>` tags (DoctorCommand.cs:485 has `'{configPath}'` and remediation text contains `<supportedRuntime>` which would render as `<`).
recommendation: Pass `Encoder = JavaScriptEncoder.UnsafeRelaxedJsonEscaping` on the `JsonSerializerOptions` for both `status --json` (StatusCommand.cs:94) and `doctor --json` (DoctorCommand.cs:158-163) and `tools --json` (ToolsCommand.cs:171-176). This is the standard advisory for human-readable JSON output that's not destined for HTML embedding. Add a one-line code comment that the CLI's JSON output is for shell/terminal consumption, not browser embedding.
rationale: Round-1/round-2 added the JSON output modes (P15-026 for status, P15-027 for doctor) but accepted the default System.Text.Json encoder. The escaped-`+` is the kind of small-but-unmistakable polish issue that round-3 perfection-pickiness should catch — pasted bug reports look amateurish with `+` peppered through them.

verdict.reasoning:
Verified by reading StatusCommand.cs:94, DoctorCommand.cs:158-167 + 416-421, ToolsCommand.cs:171-176, FieldAccessCommand.cs:265-279, BuildInfo.cs:42-46, and Directory.Build.props:35 (confirming the `+` appears in `$(Version)+$(SourceRevisionId.Substring(0,7))`). All four CLI JSON emitters use the default `JsonSerializerOptions` with no `Encoder` override, so they use `JavaScriptEncoder.Default` which escapes `+`, `<`, `>`, `&`, single-quote, and many other ASCII characters as `\uXXXX` for HTML-safety the CLI does not need.

The finding's `buildVersion` example is the small visible case — `0.1.0+abc1234` becomes `0.1.0+abc1234`, which is mildly ugly but not catastrophic. The real bite is in doctor's App.config remediation (DoctorCommand.cs:416-421): the canonical fix-it text literally contains `<startup useLegacyV2RuntimeActivationPolicy="true">` and `<supportedRuntime version="v4.0" />`. Through the default encoder these render as `\u003Cstartup ...\u003E` and `\u003CsupportedRuntime ...\u003E` — the operator's most important moment with the doctor (a failed App.config probe in live mode) hands them back unreadable angle-bracket gibberish when they pipe to a file for a bug report. That's a clear erosion of the recovery experience that doctor exists for.

Not duplicated: grepping audit-findings.json + audit-findings-r2.json for `JavaScriptEncoder`/`UnsafeRelaxed`/`encoder`/`escape` returned zero hits. P14-040 added the buildVersion field; P15-026 split status into human + --json; P15-027 added doctor --json; none touched the encoder. The fix is single-file additive — `Encoder = JavaScriptEncoder.UnsafeRelaxedJsonEscaping` on the four JsonSerializerOptions sites — and the name `UnsafeRelaxed` is itself misleading: the only thing it relaxes is HTML-context escaping, which CLI output doesn't need. Tradeoff cost is zero (CLI output is shell/terminal/jq-bound, never embedded in a webpage).

Meaningfully improves: yes — operator pasting a doctor remediation into a bug-report shows readable XML instead of `\u003C` noise. The buildVersion `+` polish is the visible smoke; the doctor remediation is the fire.
verdict.refinedRecommendation:
Add `Encoder = JavaScriptEncoder.UnsafeRelaxedJsonEscaping` to the four JsonSerializerOptions sites in the CLI:

1. StatusCommand.cs:94 — fixes `buildVersion` `+` rendering.
2. DoctorCommand.cs:158-163 — the HIGH-VALUE site; fixes `<startup>` / `<supportedRuntime>` in the App.config remediation text that operators paste into bug reports after a failed probe.
3. ToolsCommand.cs:171-176 — fixes any tool description containing `<`, `>`, `+`, `&` (some tool descriptions reference URL templates / type signatures).
4. FieldAccessCommand.cs:265-279 — same reason; some FieldAccessMap shard values contain non-ASCII text that the default encoder also escapes to `\uXXXX`.

Add `using System.Text.Encodings.Web;` to each file. Drop one shared two-line comment on each site: `// Encoder = UnsafeRelaxedJsonEscaping: CLI JSON is shell/terminal/jq-bound, never embedded // in HTML. The default encoder turns App.config <startup>/<supportedRuntime> remediation // text into \u003C noise that is unreadable when an operator pastes it into a bug report.`

Do NOT factor a shared helper for these four sites — each emitter has slightly different needs (status uses positional anon-object camelCasing-by-naming; doctor needs JsonStringEnumConverter; field-access needs AllowTrailingCommas + ReadCommentHandling for the read-side). A shared helper would over-couple them; a one-line addition per site is plenty.

Add two tests:
- `StatusCommandTests`: assert `--json` output for a project where SourceRevisionId is non-empty contains literal `+` and not `\u002B`.
- `DoctorCommandTests`: synthesize a failing App.config probe result and assert the JSON `remediation` field contains literal `<startup ...>` and not `\u003Cstartup`.

Explicitly out of scope: the MCP-tool-side JSON envelopes (WrapToolHandler.Run) — those are JSON-RPC payloads consumed by the MCP client which de-escapes them itself, so the operator never sees the wire form. The CLI commands are the only emitters where a human directly reads the raw bytes.

title: Tax-year parameter named `taxYear` in some tools, `year` in others — and the response always re-emits it as `year`
line: SessionTools.cs:71,101,118 (taxYear in/taxYear out) vs MetadataTools.cs:36,114 (year in/year out) vs FieldWriteBulkTools.cs:81 (year in)
userImpact: An LLM that calls `lacerte_set_context` with `taxYear: 2024`, then tries `lacerte_field_access_map(module, table, taxYear: 2024)` gets a parameter-not-found error — the model has to remember which tools spell it `taxYear` and which spell it `year`. SessionTools.LacerteSessionStatus and LacerteSetContext both ECHO BACK `year` (not `taxYear`) in the response, deepening the confusion: the input is `taxYear` and the output is `year`.
description: `LacerteSetContext` and `LacerteCanUseNewApis` take `taxYear` as the input parameter name; `LacerteCanUseNewApis` even echoes it back as `taxYear`. `LacerteFieldAccessMap` takes the same value as `year`, and echoes it as `year`. `LacerteFieldWriteBulk` takes the validator-only year as `year`. SessionTools.LacerteSessionStatus and LacerteSetContext echo their context's year as `year` (not `taxYear`) — so SetContext is asymmetric within itself (input `taxYear`, output `year`).
recommendation: Pick one. The cleanest choice is to keep `taxYear` as the input EVERYWHERE (signals the domain — "2024" alone is ambiguous in a financial product where calendar year ≠ tax year for fiscal-year filers) and emit `taxYear` in every response. Renames: MetadataTools.cs:36, :114 (`year` → `taxYear`); FieldWriteBulkTools.cs:81 (`year` → `taxYear`); SessionTools.cs:58, :92 (response field `year` → `taxYear`). Keep the old key as an additive alias for one release with a deprecation note in DECISIONS.md.
rationale: Cross-tool parameter-name drift on the most fundamental Lacerte concept (the tax year) — not flagged in either prior round. The within-tool input/output drift (SetContext takes `taxYear` but emits `year`) is a particularly sharp instance.

verdict.reasoning:
Verified by direct file inspection. The split is exactly as described:

INPUT params:
- SessionTools.cs:71 LacerteSetContext takes `int taxYear`
- SessionTools.cs:101 LacerteCanUseNewApis takes `int taxYear`
- MetadataTools.cs:36 LacerteFieldAccessMap takes `int year`
- FieldWriteBulkTools.cs:81 LacerteFieldWriteBulk takes `int? year = null`

RESPONSE fields:
- SessionTools.cs:58 LacerteSessionStatus emits `year`
- SessionTools.cs:92 LacerteSetContext emits `year` — asymmetric with its own `taxYear` input
- SessionTools.cs:118 LacerteCanUseNewApis emits `taxYear` (the one consistent tool)
- MetadataTools.cs:114 LacerteFieldAccessMap emits `year`

Cross-checked both prior audit JSON files (round 1 and round 2). Prior taxYear-related findings exist (TaxYearTooNew ceiling, LACERTE_DEFAULT_TAX_YEAR wiring, fence-post enforcement) but NONE address the parameter-name spelling drift between tools or the within-tool input/output asymmetry. This is a genuinely new cross-tool-consistency finding.

Why meaningfullyImproves=true: an LLM that successfully reads `lacerte_session_status` sees `year` in the JSON, then naturally guesses `year:` as the param for `lacerte_set_context` — which throws parameter-not-found because the input is `taxYear`. The reverse path (use `taxYear` after seeing the SessionStatus shape) also fails for `lacerte_field_access_map`. Both are concrete moments where the model wastes a tool call on a friction error that pure naming consistency would eliminate. The within-tool asymmetry on SetContext (takes `taxYear`, emits `year`) is the sharpest instance — round-tripping the response shape back as the next input is exactly what a tool-using LLM does, and here it breaks. Fix is mechanical (four param renames + two response key renames, with one-release aliasing per the recommendation) and improves a recurring real moment, not a hypothetical one. Not bikeshedding — wrong-parameter-name errors are observably the most common class of LLM tool failure.
verdict.refinedRecommendation:
Standardize on `taxYear` everywhere — both as the input parameter name and as the response field key. The domain word "tax year" disambiguates from calendar year (matters for fiscal-year filers) and the existing `LacerteCanUseNewApis` tool already echoes `taxYear` in its response, so the rest of the surface should align to that precedent rather than to `year`.

Concrete changes:
1. MetadataTools.cs:36 — rename param `int year` to `int taxYear`; update both [Description] copy and line 114 response field `year` → `taxYear`.
2. FieldWriteBulkTools.cs:81 — rename param `int? year = null` to `int? taxYear = null`; update line 109 reference (`year.HasValue / year.Value`), the [Description], and error-context keys `expectedYear`/`actualYear` → `expectedTaxYear`/`actualTaxYear` for consistency with `expectedReadOnly`/`actualReadOnly`.
3. SessionTools.cs:58 — LacerteSessionStatus response: `year = s.Context.Year` → `taxYear = s.Context.Year`.
4. SessionTools.cs:92 — LacerteSetContext response: `year = ctx.Year` → `taxYear = ctx.Year`. Fixes the within-tool input/output asymmetry.

Backwards-compat: For one release, additionally emit the legacy `year` key in SessionStatus + SetContext + FieldAccessMap responses (anonymous-object with both `taxYear` and `year` pointing at the same value) so any operator script that key-paths into the old shape doesn't break. Do NOT add an `year` parameter alias on the input side — MCP tool schemas don't support param aliases without a custom binder, and an LLM that hits "year not allowed; did you mean taxYear?" learns the right name on retry. Add a dated entry to DECISIONS.md explaining the rename + the one-release legacy-key window, and update the README tool table to show `taxYear` consistently. Update tests: SessionToolsTests + MetadataToolsTests + FieldWriteBulkTests will fail on the response shape — update assertions to read `taxYear` while keeping a single regression test per response confirming the legacy `year` key still appears for the deprecation window. Cost: ~30 min including tests and DECISIONS.md.

title: `SchemaReloadTools` returns inner `success` field — duplicates WrapToolHandler's outer envelope key
userImpact: Operators looking at the JSON see `{"success":true, "result":{"success":true, "modulesReloaded":...}}` — two `success` keys at different nesting levels. A naive consumer checking `response.success` always gets the outer one (transport-level success) and never sees a real reload failure if the inner one disagrees. The tool's own description ("Returns { success, modulesReloaded, overlaysReloaded }") implies `success` is part of the tool's contract, but ALL tools always have `success` via WrapToolHandler — it is meaningless here.
description: Every tool is wrapped by WrapToolHandler.cs:96-102, which already emits `{"success": true, "result": <handler return>, "cid": ...}` on the outer envelope. SchemaReloadTools.cs:47 adds an INNER `success = true` field to its handler return, which then nests under `result.success`. No other tool does this — every other Lacerte*Tools handler returns the payload directly. The description on line 39 documents the inner `success` as part of the tool contract, which it should not be.
recommendation: Drop `success = true` from line 47. Update the description on line 39 to read "Returns { modulesReloaded, overlaysReloaded, schemaRoot } — the counts are how many cache entries were evicted (the next lookup will repopulate them from disk)." The outer WrapToolHandler envelope's `success` field already carries the success/failure signal; the operator does not need a redundant inner copy.
rationale: Round-1 and round-2 audits never inspected SchemaReloadTools' specific response shape against WrapToolHandler's envelope contract. This is a fresh instance of envelope-leak that survived both passes.

verdict.reasoning: Verified by reading C:/Users/VR/Projects/LacertMCP/src/LacertMCP.Server/Tools/SchemaReloadTools.cs (line 47 emits `success = true` inside the handler's anonymous return) and C:/Users/VR/Projects/LacertMCP/src/LacertMCP.Server/Errors/WrapToolHandler.cs lines 96-101 (envelope already carries `success: true`). The shape on the wire is literally `{"success":true,"result":{"success":true,"modulesReloaded":...,"overlaysReloaded":...,"schemaRoot":...},"cid":"..."}`. Grep for `success\s*=\s*true` across the entire Tools folder returns exactly two hits: SchemaReloadTools.cs:47 (the bug) and FieldWriteBulkTools.cs:208 — but the latter is a legitimate per-row status field inside a `perItem` bulk-response collection, not a duplicate of the envelope. So SchemaReloadTools really is the only outlier. Confirmed not addressed in either prior round: grep over both audit-findings.json files returns no hits for `SchemaReload`, `ReloadSchema`, or `modulesReloaded`. Meaningfully improves because (a) the tool description on line 39 misrepresents the contract — it tells the LLM that `success` is part of the return shape, but the inner `success` is a hardcoded constant that never flips to false (any failure throws and is serialized by WrapToolHandler.SerializeError on a completely different path), so a defensive consumer checking `response.result.success` gets a meaningless tautology; (b) the description also misses the much more useful fact that the counts are eviction counts, not load counts, which is exactly what an operator wonders when they see `modulesReloaded: 0` after running the dumper; (c) this is the only handler in the codebase that returns its own envelope-shaped field, so fixing it restores cross-tool consistency. Fix is one line of code + one description edit, off-Windows, no test churn.
verdict.refinedRecommendation:
Two-part fix in src/LacertMCP.Server/Tools/SchemaReloadTools.cs.

1) Line 47: remove the `success = true,` line from the anonymous object returned by the handler. The outer WrapToolHandler envelope already supplies `success` — this nested copy was always true (any reload failure throws and goes through SerializeError on a different code path), so it provides zero signal and creates a `response.success` / `response.result.success` ambiguity that no other tool in the codebase has (verified via grep — FieldWriteBulkTools.cs:208 is the only other `success = true` site and it's legitimately per-row inside a bulk perItem array).

2) Line 39: rewrite the description to: `"Drop the in-process FieldAccessMap caches so freshly written shards on disk take effect. Call this after running LacertMCP.FieldAccessDumper.exe so the new shards take effect without restarting the server (which would invalidate the Intuit 24h auth ticket). Returns { modulesReloaded, overlaysReloaded, schemaRoot } — the counts are how many cached entries were evicted (NOT how many shards exist on disk); the next field-write or lookup will lazily repopulate the cache from disk."` The "evicted, not loaded" clarification is the operator-facing payoff — without it, a `modulesReloaded: 0` response right after running the dumper looks like the reload failed, when really it means the cache hadn't been populated yet (no field operations had happened, so GetOrAdd never fired).

No new test required; if there's an existing SchemaReloadToolsTests asserting on the inner `success` field, drop that one assertion. Update README/docs only if the response shape is documented there verbatim (grep README.md and ARCHITECTURE.md for `modulesReloaded`).

title: `LacerteClientRead` description claims "Returns null if no such client exists" — actually returns a found-false envelope; LLM rejection logic will be wrong
userImpact: An LLM that reads the description literally will check `if (result == null)` to detect a missing client — and will NEVER fire, because the actual return is `{ clientNumber, found: false, client: null }` (which is non-null even after WrapToolHandler unwraps). The model then treats the empty record as a valid hit, prints `client: null` to the user, or worse silently proceeds to a follow-up tool with a stale ClientNumber.
description: The [Description] on line 65 says "Returns null if no such client exists." The handler on line 72 returns `new { clientNumber, found = row != null, client = row }` — a three-field envelope where `client` is null but the envelope itself is not. This makes the description directly contradictory to behavior. The not-found pattern is also unique to this tool: every other read tool that could return zero hits (StatesTools, SubclientsTools, FormsTools, StatusTools) just returns an empty array — no `found:false` sentinel.
recommendation: Two-line fix: update the description on line 65 to "Returns `{ clientNumber, found, client }` — `found` is false and `client` is null if no such client exists in the active context." Then to align with the rest of the read surface, consider dropping the `found` field — it duplicates `client == null` — but the description rewrite is the minimum to stop the LLM from writing wrong null-check logic.
rationale: Doc-vs-behavior mismatch on the most-called single-client tool. Neither prior round flagged the LacerteClientRead description against its actual return shape; the cross-tool angle (every other read tool uses empty-array, not found-sentinel) makes it a consistency issue, not just a doc bug.

verdict.reasoning:
Verified directly in C:/Users/VR/Projects/LacertMCP/src/LacertMCP.Server/Tools/ClientsTools.cs lines 64-73. Line 65 [Description] says "Returns null if no such client exists." Line 72 actually returns `new { clientNumber, found = row != null, client = row }` — a 3-field envelope that is never null. WrapToolHandler.Run serializes this to JSON, so the LLM literally sees `{"clientNumber":"9999","found":false,"client":null}` — i.e. a JSON object, not JSON null. An LLM that trusts the description and codes `if (result == null) ...` will skip the missing-client path entirely, then either (a) print `client: null` to the user as if it were a real record, or (b) feed the original clientNumber into a follow-up write tool (LacerteWriteFields, EFile, etc.) where the missing client manifests as a confusing DBxError/OutOfIndex deep in the call chain instead of a clean upfront not-found.

Cross-tool consistency claim is also correct. Grepping `found = ` across src/LacertMCP.Server/Tools/*.cs returns ONE hit — this exact line — confirming that no other read tool uses a found-sentinel envelope. The other zero-hit read paths (StatesTools, SubclientsTools, FormsTools, StatusTools, EFileTools, DetailsTools) all return `{ count, rows }` shapes where an empty result is `count: 0, rows: []`. So this tool's shape is genuinely an outlier — and the description compounds that by lying about it.

Prior-audit dedup: Searched audit-findings.json and audit-findings-r2.json for "LacerteClientRead" and ClientsTools.cs hits. Round 1 (audit-findings.json:290) covered the pagination/int.MaxValue overfetch on LacerteClientList — different tool, different issue. Round 2 (audit-findings-r2.json:1140) discussed pagination consistency across read tools but explicitly NOT LacerteClientRead. No prior finding touches the description-vs-return-shape mismatch or the found-sentinel-vs-empty-array consistency angle. New.

Meaningful: LacerteClientRead is the single highest-traffic read tool — the LLM calls it before nearly every write, every detail read, every state/subclient query. A wrong null-check pattern here silently degrades every multi-step flow that starts with "look up client 1001". The fix is a one-line description rewrite that costs nothing and forecloses a real LLM reasoning bug. The secondary recommendation (drop the redundant `found` field) is reasonable but breaking; the description rewrite alone resolves the user-facing harm.

One minor sharpening of the finding's framing: the original recommendation says "drop the `found` field — it duplicates `client == null`". That's true but `found` is also load-bearing for LLMs that handle a non-null sentinel object more reliably than they handle the absence of a key — so keeping `found` and just fixing the description is arguably the safer two-line change. I would NOT recommend dropping `found`.
verdict.refinedRecommendation:
Minimal one-line fix in src/LacertMCP.Server/Tools/ClientsTools.cs line 65: replace the [Description] string with `"Read one client by ClientNumber from DATA1 in the active context. Returns an envelope { clientNumber, found, client } — when no such client exists in the active context, `found` is false and `client` is null. The envelope itself is never null; check `found` (or `client != null`), not the top-level result."`. Do NOT drop the `found` field — it's the only sentinel the LLM has, and removing it would be a breaking surface change for downstream prompts already coded against it.

Optional consistency hardening (defer to a separate phase if it adds churn): pin the not-found-envelope shape with a one-paragraph note in README's tool table for LacerteClientRead so the cross-tool inconsistency (every other single-row read tool wraps results in `{ count, rows }`, this one alone wraps in `{ found, client }`) is at least documented. Even better, if Phase 16 touches the read surface, consider migrating LacerteClientRead to `{ count, rows }` (where rows is 0-or-1) for true cross-tool symmetry — but that's a v0.2 breaking change, not a same-session fix.

Test addition: add a one-line ClientsToolsTests assertion that the JSON-serialized not-found result contains `"found":false` and `"client":null` AND is a JSON object (not null) — pin the contract so a future "simplify" pass can't quietly null-out the envelope and break LLM prompts in the wild.

title: Doctor command's failure-mode help never mentions the 'next thing to run' (status / tools / register)
userImpact: When `lacerte-mcp doctor` exits with code 1 or 2, the final lines just say `'Result: FAIL...'` / `'Result: PARTIAL...'`. The remediation under each probe says 'Run lacerte-mcp register' for the AppID one but it doesn't roll up into the bottom-of-output 'now do X' guidance. description: DoctorCommand.cs lines 188-197 print only the single-line result. The README Quick Start section lists `status`, `doctor`, `register`, `tools` as related verbs, but the doctor CLI output doesn't cross-reference siblings. Specifically: (a) green doctor (exit 0) is a great place to suggest `lacerte-mcp tools` next ('here's what the server exposes'); (b) red doctor (exit 1) with AppID missing should mention `lacerte-mcp register`; (c) partial doctor (exit 2 — off-Windows expected) should mention 'this is normal off-Windows; the Windows-only probes are skipped; you can still develop in sim mode' and point at `LACERTE_SIMULATION=1` + `lacerte-mcp tools` for off-Windows development.
